full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of an order of the learned Munsif, Cox's Bazar dismissing the Miscellaneous Case No. 81 of 1983 filed under Order 9, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the petitioner for setting aside an ex-parte order dated 10.4.1982 made in the Miscellaneous case No. 342 filed under section 96 of the Slate Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for pre-empting certain land. 

2. The petitioner who was preempted in the aforesaid pre-emption case filed an application under Order 9, Rule 13 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for selling aside the ex-parte order dated 10.4.1982 allowing the Miscellaneous case No. 342 of 1980 stating, inter alia, that the preemptor-opposite parties Nos. I to 3 in collusion with the process server suppressed the summons of the aforesaid pre-emption case and upon such suppression obtained the ex-parte order on 10.4.1982. The petitioner further Slated that he was a business man and used to stay away from his house at Ramu Bazar from dawn to dusk and as such the summons shown to have been served by hanging on refusal to accept the same by the petitioner was not at all delivered to him for service. The petitioner further stated that he came to know about the ex-parte order for the first time on 23.6.1982 from one Golam Hossain and on the following day he filed the application. The opposite parties-pre-emptors contested the case on the ground that the summons of the preemption case was duly served upon the petitioner and the petitioner had knowledge of the case from the very beginning. They further contended that after the ex-parte order was passed they started Execution ease No. 114 of 1982 and got possession of the land under pre-emption through court. 

3. Mr. Abdul MomenChowdhury in support of this Rule vehemently urges before me that there was no service of summons on the petitioner in the eye of law and the learned Court below was wrong in dismissing the Misc. Case No. 81 of 1983. He further submits that the court's finding as to service of summons was the result of misreading of evidence on record. The learned Advocate for the petitioner drawing my attention to the statement of D.W.2 Kabir Ahmed submits that D.W.2 Kabir Ahmed did not state that the summons was offered to the petitioner and D.W. 2 was unable to say that who were the attesting witnesses to the summons and who were present at the time of serving the summons. Mr. Momen also contends that D.W. 2 also was unable to say that on what paper he put his signature. In view of such deposition of the D.W.2, the learned Advocate submits that the court committed an error of law in basing its finding as to service of summons upon the deposition of D.W.2. The learned Advocate also submits that the petitioner has proved his case by examining witnesses. He submits that P.W. 2 Golam Hossain duly corroborated the statement of P.W. 1 the petitioner that P.W. 2 told him that the opposite parties drove out the laborers of the petitioner from the disputed land on 23.6.1982. The learned Munsif while rejecting the application under Order 9 Rule 13 did not at all take into consideration those facts in arriving at a finding as to whether the service or summons was duly served upon the petitioner and the learned court also failed to give a finding as to whether the petitioner was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing before the court at the time of hearing of the Misc. Case No. 342 of 1980 and thereby committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice. Mr. Amirul Kabir Chowdhury the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties faintly submitted that as the learned court on consideration of evidence on record came to a finding that summons was duly served, the order impugned was a legal order and should not be set aside.

4. From reading the Judgment of the Court below and the record I find that the petitioner has successfully proved by adducing evidence that he came to know about the ex-pane order on 23.6.1982. I also find on examining the process server's report that the summons was served by hanging on the alleged refusal by the petitioner to sign the acknowledgment. But surprisingly from the deposition of D.W. 2 Kabir Ahmed it is found that he could not say who were the persons present at the time of delivering the summons by the process-server and who were the attesting witnesses and what was the paper on which he put his signature. Taking into consideration these aspects of the statements of D.W. 2 and deposition of P.W. 1 and P.W. 2, I have no hesitation in holding that no summons was served upon the petitioner and it was shown to have been served by hanging falsely without there being any attempt to deliver the same to the petitioner. In this view of the matter, I cannot accept finding of the learned court below that the summons was duly served upon the petitioner. From perusal of the record it is also found that the process server who served the summons by hanging has not been examined. But Or. 5 R. 19 C.P.C. enjoins a duty upon the court to examine the process-server where the summons is returned under R. 17 C.P.C. and the return has not been verified by the affidavit of servicing officer.  Rule 19 also speaks that the Court may make such further inquiry in the matter and shall either declare that the summons has been duly served or order such service as it thinks fit. In view of the provisions of R. 19 of Order 5 C.P.C. it can easily be held that where the summons is returned under R. 17 it is mandatory on the part of the Court to examine the process server on oath and to declare that the summons has been duly served. Unless these requirements of law are satisfied it cannot be held that the summons was duly served. From perusal of the record of the court below I am unable to find that those requirements of law have been fulfilled in this case. In that view of the matter, I hold that there being no service of summons on the petitioner the ex-parte decree passed by the court below is liable to be set aside.
	
5. For the aforesaid reasons, I allow the Miscellaneous case No. 81 of 1983 and set aside the ex-parte decree dated 10.4 .1982 passed by the learned Munsif, Cox's Bazar in Miscellaneous case No. 342 of 1980 of the said Court. The petitioner is directed to pay a sum of Tk. 250/- to the pre-emptor-opposite party by way of costs. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. No order as to costs. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. A. M. Mahmudur Rahman, J: This rule at the instance of the petitioners calls in question the order dated 28.3.1985 of the learned Munsif, First Court, Sadar, Chittagong dismissing the Other Execution Case No. 23 of 1984 filed by the petitioners.

2. The petitioners, the landlords of the suit premises, instituted Other Suit No. 172 of 1976 in the Court of Munsif aforesaid against the tenant, Sukhendu Bikash Das, father of the opposite-parties Nos. 1-4 and husband of opposite party No.5, for his eviction from the suit premises on the allegations that the tenant defaulted in payment of rent and the landlord required the premises for bona fide use and occupation. Sukhandu contested the suit denying the allegations made in the plaint by filing written statement. The trial court decreed the suit for eviction and for recovery of Tk. 190/- as compensation by its decree dated 30.11.78. The defendant's appeal being Other Appeal No. 31 of 1979 against that decree was dismissed by the Subordinate Judge, First Court, Chittagong. Against the decree of the Subordinate Judge the Rule obtained by the defendant Sukhendu Bikash in Civil Revision No. 274 of 1983 was also discharged on hearing by an order of this Court on the 2nd January, 1985. After the discharge of the Rule by the High Court Division the petitioners put the decree in execution in the Other Execution Case No. 23 of 1984.

3. During pendency of the said Execution Case the defendant died leaving behind the opposite-parties herein as his only heirs and legal representatives. The said legal representatives were substituted in the said Execution Case at the instance of the petitioners. Thereafter the opposite parties filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the executing Court for dismissing the execution case on the ground that the right of tenancy was personal right and not being heritable the Execution Case was not maintainable against the opposite parties on the death of the judgment-debtor. The petitioners contested the application by filing written objection. They contended that application under section 151 of the Code of Civil procedure was not maintainable as there is an alternative remedy provided in Civil Procedure Code for challenging the order granting substitution of the opposite-parties in place of Sukhendu Bikash Das. Secondly, opposite parties were rightly substituted as on the death of the defendant being his legal representatives and as such the Execution Case was maintainable against them.

4. The learned Munsif, however, dismissed the Execution Case holding that the right of tenancy in respect of the suit premises was a. personal right and not heritable on the death of the judgment-debtor. Being of the view he also vacated the order of substitution and observed that the decree became infructuous on the death of the tenant, the petitioners were to institute a fresh suit against the opposite-parties herein for their eviction from the suit premises. The learned Munsif relied upon the case of Abdus Sattar & others Vs. Suresh Chandra Das & ors., 32 D.L.R. (A.D) 170; Abdul Latif and another Vs. Abdul Mannaf and others, (1982) 2 B.C.R.(A.D) 428 and Md. Abdus Salam Chowdhury Vs. Jamini Ranjan Das and ors. in Civil Revision No. 756 of 1981 decided on 6th May, 1982, a photostat copy of a certified copy of the judgment in Civil Revision No. 756 of 1981 was placed before me by the learned Advocate for the opposite parties.

5. The learned Advocate for the petitioners very strenuously argued that he decision reported in 32 DLR (AD) 170 although held that the tenancy at will creates a personal relation between the original landlord and the tenant and is terminable by death of either party yet in the present case the Execution Case against the opposite party Nos. 1-5 will not be defeated merely on the ground of death of the judgdebtor during. Pendency of the case as the point mint which requires consideration by this Court in the instant case was not mooted and decided in the aforesaid decision. Mr. Shafiqur Rahman further argued that a executing Court cannot go beyond the decree and in this case as the decree was put into execution by. The tenant during his life time, the executing Court should not have entertained the application for dismissal of the Execution Case.

6. Mr.Jvloqbul Ahmed on the other hand submitted. relying on the decisions referred to above that on the death of Sukhendu Bikash Das the tenancy was determined as the same was in the nature of personal right and not heritable and as such the opposite parties are not bound by the decree and the execution case is liable. to be dismissed against his clients and it was rightly dismissed by the trial court.

<u>7. Now let us revert to the question: Whether a decree obtained by a landlord against his tenant and put into execution by him is executable or not against his heirs on his death during the pendency of the execution case? To answer this question it would be necessary first to examine certain provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure and the Premises Rent Control Ordinance before we enter into the discussion of the decisions referred to above: Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman placed before me section 2(11) and section 50 of the Code of Civil Procedure and section 2(9) of the Premises Rent Control OrdiNance, 1963. According to the definition as given in section 2(11) of the Code a legal representative means a person who in law represents the estate of a deceased person and includes any person who inter- meddles with the estate of the deceased. Section 50 of the Code provides that where a judgment- debtor dies before the decree has been fully satisfied, the holder of the decree may apply to the Court which passed it to execute the same against the legal representative of the deceased. Section 2(9) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 that tenant means any person by whom, or on whose account rent it payable for any premises and includes a legal representative as defined in the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 and a person continuing in possession afar the determination of a tenancy in his favour. It appears from the definition of tenant as given in section 2(9) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 that the expression "Tenant" includes a legal representative as defined in the Civil Procedure Code. The present opposite parties being heirs of Sukhendu Bikash Das are, in my opinion, his legal representatives within the meaning of section 2(11) C.P.C. as they represent the estate of their predecessor-in-interest, Sukhendu Bikash Das. Now let us consider some of the decisions on this point. In the case of Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee and others Vs. Haracharan Singh, 1934 Lah. Addision, J. in delivering the judgment of the Division Bench has observed as follows :-</u>

<u>"The definition of legal representative in S.2(11) Civil Procedure Code, is very wide. It  means a person who in law represents the estate of a deceased person and includes any person who intermeddles with the estate of the deceased."</u>

8. In the case of Amarchand  another V. Parmanand and others, 1934 All 474 a Division Bench, of the Allahabad High Court presided over by Sulaiman; C.J. held:

"It is only after a suit has been instituted that the Civil Procedure Code comes into operation. It follows that the definition of the expression" "legal representative," to be found in the Civil Procedure Code, is meant only for the purpose of the Code and not as a general statement of a substantive rule of law."

9. In view of the definition of legal representative as given in section 2(9) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance and on the strength of the judicial pronouncements made in 1934 Lah 1 and 1934 All 474 I am led to hold that definition of legal representative as contemplated in section 2(11) of the Civil Procedure Code shall be given a wide meaning to include the heirs of a deceased tenant who died during the pendency of an Execution Case started in pursuance of a decree for eviction of the tenant from, the suit premises for the limited purpose for execution of the decree obtained against the legal representatives of the-tenant, This matter may be viewed from another angle. The opposite-parties are in possession of the suit premises since. The time of their predecessor-in-interest, Sukhendu Bikash Das, on the basis of the lease created in his favour. But on his death the opus  rites are continuing in possession the premises in suit but not on the basis of any lease. But even then their possession can not be said to be a possession of trespassers and such possession of the opposite parties herein, in my opinion, would not be unconscionable toehold as possession of the tenants by sufferance. This view taken by me gets support from the following observation made in 32 DLR (AD) 170.

<u>"Since some interest is created, even though personal, by monthly tenancy, which may not  be, to borrow an English concept, an estate in favour of the tenant, nevertheless the heirs or successors-in-interest of a tenant in occupation of the premises on his death do not become trespassers, because neither their predecessor nor they entered the premises wrongfully, and so their continuance in the premises will be that of a tenant by sufferance, to borrow again another English concept".'</u>

10. As in this case the decree was put into execution against the defendant and on his death as the opposite parties who are in possession of the premises in question, the Execution Case is legally enforceable against them as they are tenants by sufferance. In the case of Abdus Sattar Vs. Mohiuddin & ors. 38 DLR (AD) 97 it has been held that the heirs of the deceased tenant who continue to stay in the premises arc held to be tenants by holding over and were under legal obligation to restore possession to the landlord. Now let us consider the decision reported in (1982) 2 B.C.R (AD) 428. In (1982) BCR (AD) 428 it has been held that as tenancy cease to exist on the tenant's death the heirs of the decease; tenant do not inherit the tenancy and as such they arc not entitled to restitution. The principle of law lair down in this case can hardly be disputed. The facts of this case are different from the facts of theistic case and the question which is posed before me is al together different from the one considered in that case. The decision of that case rests on the question of restitution of the premises to, the legal heirs on termination of tenancy on the death of the tenant. II view of the facts and the question that fell for deter monition in that case being all together different from the present one the decision has no direct bear of in the instant case before us.

<u>11. The views expressed in Civil Revision No. 756 of 1981 by Syed Muhammad Hussain, J. that a fresh suit against the heirs of the deceased tenant who are actually living in the suit premises is to be filed for their eviction did not at all receive any consideration of section 2(11), section 50 of the Code of Civil Procedure and section 2(9) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963. It seems to me that at the bar no argument was also advanced before the learned Judge relying upon the aforesaid provisions of law as is done in the present case and as such the learned Judge had little occasion to consider all these aspects of the law. However, in view of my discussions above on the question, with due deference, I am unable to accept the, view expressed by S.M. Hussain, J.</u>

12. Mr Shafiqur Rahman further argued that an executing Court cannot go beyond the decree and in the case as the decree was passed against the tenant Sukhendu Bikash Das during his life time and the decree not being a nullity the executing Court wrongly entertained the application under section 151 of the Code for dismissal of the Execution Case arid dismissed the same illegally. He referred the case of Baliram Hari Vs. Mukinda Kisan, 1951 Nagpur 145 wherein it has been held that executing Court cannot question a decree and it is its duty to execute the decree as it is and not to go beyond it. The principle of law in this respect is well-settled. But in view of the question that falls for our determination we are not called upon to decide this issue in this case before us.

13. The trial Judge also fell into error in dismissing the execution case invoking inherent jurisdiction under section 151 C.P.C. inasmuch as for dismissing the execution case as on the ground the decree being nullity and infructuous on the death of the tenant an independent suit lies and thus there being an alternative remedy provided for in the Code itself the exercise of power under section 151 C.P.C. on the part of the learned Munsif in dismissing the execution case is unwarranted in law.

14. For the reasons stated above, I hold that the there Execution Case No. 23 of 1984 pending in the our of Munsif First Court, is maintainable-against the opposite-parties. Accordingly, I set aside the impugned order. The execution Case No. 23 of 1984 pending in the court of the Munsif shall proceed.

15. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The parties are to bear their own costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Mohammad Fazlul Karim, J.: This Rule Nisi was issued on an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the Peoples' Republic of Bangladesh calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 15.4.89 (Annexure I to the petition) passed by the Court of Settlement, Bangladesh Abandoned Buildings, Dhaka in Case No. 423 of 1988 (Ka 48, Block F, Mohammadpur, Dhaka) maintaining the inclusion of Holding No. 6A/7, Block F, Joint Quarter, Mohammadpur, Dhaka belonging to the petitioner in the list of abandoned property dismissing the aforesaid case should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 
	
	2. The petitioner, Mohammad Haider Ali Fakir has filed this application asserting as the rightful owner in occupation of the said holding with a semi-pucca structure thereon by virtue of an agreement to purchase from Ali Mohammad Khan, the original allottee of the Government of erstwhile East Pakistan allotted on 25.10.62 followed by delivery of possession on 13.12.62. Mr. Khan received Taka 9,000.00 as earnest money out of total consideration of Taka 10,000.00 and delivered vacant possession of the house and executed a deed of agreement for sale on 19.5.71 in favour of the petitioner with the stipulation to execute and register the sale deed on compliance with the formalities for the purpose. Due to failure to obtain the kabala, the petitioner filed a suit for specific performance of contract being Title Suit No. 555 of 1974 in the Court of 1st Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against Ali Mohammad Khan and the Ministry of Public Works as the defendants which was decreed ex parte on 10.12.76. On execution of the said decree, the petitioner obtained a sale deed executed and registered through the Court on payment of balance consideration money in Title Execution Case No. 10 of 1977 on 10.8.77. The petitioner has been in continuous possession of the case house since purchase on payment of Municipal Tax, electricity and Was a bills. The Government conducted a house to house survey in respect of the case holding on 9.2.84 and found the petitioner in possession on the basis of the said agreement and consequent decree of the civil Court but to the utter surprise of the petitioner he was served with the notice dated 8.2.86 issued by the respondent No. 1, Ministry of Works to surrender possession of the case holding or to show cause against such surrender within 7 days from the service thereof treating the same as an abandoned property. Respondent No. 1 published the case holding in 'Ka' list in the official Gazette (Extraordinary) dated 23rd September, 1986. The petitioner thereafter moved the Court of Settlement for exclusion of the holding from the list of abandoned property and the same was numbered as Case No. 423/88 (Ka 48, Block F, Mohammadpur, Dhaka) The Court of Settlement by its judgment and order dated 15.4.89 dismissed the case and maintained the inclusion of the holding in the list of abandoned property. Thus being aggrieved the petitioner moved this Court and obtained this Rule and operation of the impugned judgment and order was stayed till hearing of the Rule. 

	3. The respondent No. 1 filed affidavit-in-opposition denying the allegations made in the petition stating, inter alia, that the original lessee never executed a deed of agreement for sale of the case property on 19.5.71 nor received any earnest money but the petitioner has created the same by forging the signature of the original lessee in order to grab the case property and obtained the ex parte decree by practising fraud upon the Court. The petitioner has been in unauthorised and illegal occupation of the case property. That the said sale of the house was hit by Article 6 of President's Order 16 of 1972 as no permission for sale of the holding was obtained from the Government. During the war of liberation the original lessee left Bangladesh with the members of his family and after liberation his wherea bouts were not known and as such the property has vested in the Government as abandoned property. The Court of Settlement compared the signature of the original lessee in the original lease deed with the signature in the deed of agreement and arrived at a finding of fact that the agreement was created by forging the signature of the original lessee. 

	4. Mr. Khademul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, has placed the petition and the affidavit-in-opposition together with the Annexures and submitted that the respondents acted without lawful authority in treating the property as an abandoned property in the absence of any formation of the opinion by the Government, that the absence of the original lessee from Bangladesh was for the purpose prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh and in the absence of any such opinion the property cannot be treated as abandoned property and relied on the case of Bangladesh Vs. Messrs. ATJ Industries Limited and others, 28 DLR (AD) 120. Mr. Chowdhury next submitted that the plaintiff being in possession in the case holding since the deed of agreement for sale dated 19.5.71 on payment o the part of the consideration and subsequently his title was perfected by getting a kabala executed and registered through the Court on 10.8.77 on the basis of decree passed in Title Suit No. 555 of 1974, the Court of Settlement acted illegally in holding that the transaction is hit by Article 6 of the President's Order 16 of 1972 and the decree is binding on the Government until it is set aside by a court of competent jurisdiction and the decree stands against the Government and referred to the decision in the case of Rahela Khatoon Vs. Chairman, Court of Settlement reported in 45 DLR 5. Mr. Chowdhury also submitted that in view of his possession in the case land on the basis of the deed of agreement dated 19.5.71 and subsequent notice dated 8.2.86 issued by the respondent No. 1 either to vacate or to show cause why vacant possession shall not be taken or to show cause against such surrender within the period fixed, the respondent acted illegally in publishing the case holding in the 'ka' list of the abandoned building under the provisions of section 5(1) of the Bangladesh Abandoned Building (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. LIV of 1985) and as such the very lisping of the property as abandoned property has been made illegally and without lawful authority Mr. Chowdhury next submitted that in view of the decree for specific performance of contract on scrutinizing the documents, namely the agreement for sale, the Court of Settlement acted illegally in going behind the decree maintaining the inclusion of the property in the list of abandoned property and arriving at a finding that the signature is forged and the agreement is an ante-dated one. 

	5. Mr. Md. Saidur Rahman, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing with Mr. Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, has submitted that the formation of opinion that the absence of the owner of the house from Bangladesh is prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh is required only when the original owner himself comes before the Court challenging the declaration of the property as abandoned property. The Court of Settlement arrived at a finding that the whereabouts were not known and as such the property was rightly declared as abandoned property and included in the official Gazette. The learned Assistant Attorney-General further submitted that classifying the property either in 'ka' list of the abandoned building the possession has been taken as abandoned property under the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 or in 'kha' list of the building in respect of which notice for surrendering or taking possession as abandoned property under the said order has been issued do not change the character of the property of the abandoned property as has been contemplated in section 5(1) (a) (b) of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985.

	6. As regards the ex parte decree in the suit for specific performance of contract and the consequent execution and registration of title deed in favour of the petitioner, the learned Assistant Attorney- General submitted that the said transfer is hit by Article 6 of President's Order 16 of 1972 and as such the character of the property remained unaltered/ unchanged even after the said decree of the civil Court not answering the description as has been contemplated under proviso (a) to sub-section 1 of section 5 of the said Ordinance. The learned Assistant Attorney-General has referred to the unreported decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Hosne-Ara Begum Vs. Chairman, the Court of Settlement and others in CPSL Appeal No. 290 of 1990. 

	7. Abandoned property has been defined in Article 2(1) of the President's Order 16/72 which reads as follows: 
	"(1)" "abandoned property" means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property including- 
	(i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh; 
	(ii) any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 (Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972), but does not include- 
	(a) Any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh; 
	(b) any property which is in the possession or under the control of the Government under any law for the time being in force. 

	8. In the case Government of Bangladesh Vs Messrs ATJ Industries Limited and others reported in 28 DLR (AD) 120 it has been held that: 

	"The defining part denotes property owned by a person who is either not present in Bangladesh, or whose whereabouts are not known, or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property. A question may arise whether the three sub-clauses are disjunctive or conjunctive. We think they have been used disjunctively and there is no need to construe them conjunctively." 

	Then comes the inclusive definition. In the inclusive definition is included two categories of property, first is the property owned by a person who is a citizen of a State which after 25th day of March, 1971 either is at war or engaged in military operation against Bangladesh; the second is the property taken over by Government under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1971. So far as the inclusion clause is concerned both the categories of properties come within the meaning of the definition of "abandoned property". 

	Then is the exclusion clause the first question which arises is whether the exclusion clause also qualifies the inclusion clause. Except for the fact that the exclusion clause follows the inclusion clause, there is nothing in the grammatical construction of the whole clause to indicate that it qualifies the inclusion clause. Exclusion clause contemplates two categories of property. The first is the property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. The second is the property which is in possession or under the control of the Government under any law in force for the time being. The second part of this exclusion clause needs no classification for the purpose of this appeal. The first part of the exclusion clause is not only an exception but it qualifies the definition clause and this qualification is such that it is implicit with the definition and an integral part of it. Definition clause cannot be conceived without this implicit qualification. What then is the qualification? The sub-clause says that if the residence of the owner of a property outside Bangladesh is, in the opinion of the Government, for a purpose not prejudicial to the interest of the State, then the property is not an abandoned property. In this sub-clause the condition is such that the operation of the definition clause will come into effect only when the Government has formed its opinion. The definition clause with inclusion and exclusion clauses have been so framed that we do not find any other reasonable construction to bestow on entire clause of Article 2(1) than we have given. On the formation of opinion of the Government the definition clause comes into operation, but once opinion has been formed the law takes effect from 28.2.72, the day President's Order No. 16 of 1972 was promulgated. The Government is to form its opinion on the events as they stood on 28.2.72." 

	9. The aforesaid definition clause was again reiterated in a recent decision in the case of Government of Bangladesh Vs. Mirza Shahab Ispahani reported in 40 DLR (AD) 116. 

	10. In the cited decision the owner was claiming before the Court that the property is not an abandoned property and in such circumstances of the case the question was whether the owner was residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which in the opinion of the Government is prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh or not. The sub-clause says that if the owner of the property is residing outside for any purpose the Government is obliged under the law to form an opinion that his absence from Bangladesh was prejudiced to the interest of Bangladesh in order to bring his property within the mischief of an abandoned property. 

	11. But in the instant case the whereabouts of the original owner/allottee by the Govt. were not known on the date when the President's Order 16/72 was promulgated and as such by the defining part of the definition clause the property owned by the person whose whereabouts were not known would bring the property within the mischief of abandoned property in Article 2(1) of President's Order 16/72. So the 1st part of exclusion clause providing for formation of opinion by the Government has no application in the instant case. 

	12. It appears that section 5(1), publication of lists of buildings, has classified the building as either (a) a list of buildings the possession of which has been taken as abandoned property under the President's Order; or (b) a list of buildings in respect of which notice for surrendering or taking possession as abandoned property under the said order have been issued, and no other consequence has been profiled for listing the building either in (a) without taking over possession or in (b) to section 5(1) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 but by section 5(2) of the said Ordinance it has been provided that the list published under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have vested in the Government as such. 

	13. So from the above, it cannot be said that mere listing the case property in 'Ka' list, the possession of which, according to the petitioner, is him, do not make any difference as regard the character of the case land as an abandoned property. The petitioner also could not rebut the said presumption by adducing any evidence before the Court of Settlement which is clear from the finding of the Court below, inter alia that the domicile certificate, non-option certificate; citizenship certificate and reliable evidence of nationality of Bangladesh of the original allottee, who is an immigrant are not forthcoming in the records. The petitioner Could not show or there is no material to show that the possession of the said land has not been taken pursuant to notice to surrender dated 8.2.86 prior to publication in the official Gazette dated 23.9.86. The Court of Settlement passed an order for taking over the possession of the case holding by evicting the present occupant on the basis of assertion of the petitioner in his application under section 7 of the Ordinance, 

	14. As regards the submission regarding the decree for specific performance of contract, the provision (a) to sub-section (1) of section 5 contemplates that no such list treating the property as abandoned property shall include any building in respect of which any decree or order has been passed at any time before the publication of the list in the official Gazette, by any Court declaring the building not to be an abandoned property not to have vested in the Government under the President's Order or declaring the possession by the government of the building as an abandoned property under that order to be illegal or invalid or directing the Government or any officer or authority subordinate to it to return, restore or transfer the building to any person. 

	15. In the instant case the petitioner has obtained an ex parte decree for specific performance of contract against the original order on 10.12.76 but the said decree has nothing to do with the character of the property as abandoned property and does not answer the description contemplated in proviso (a) so as to exclude the suit property from the list of abandoned property under the said Ordinance. 

	16. In an unreported case referred to above (CPSLA. No. 290 of 1990) our Appellate Division in a similar case has observed that: 

	"The ex parte decree and the miscellaneous case are valueless under the circumstances." 
	As such the decision referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner reported in 45 DLR 5 is of no avail to him. Moreover, the provision of proviso (a) to section 5(1) was not referred to or considered in the said .decision, 

	17. We have perused the deed of agreement (Annexure 'B') which does not speak that delivery of possession was ever given to the petitioner but in the deed executed through the Court, (annexed as 'C' to the petition) it was stated that : 

“উক্ত মূল্যের টাকার মধ্যে বিগত ১৯.৫.৭১ ইং তারিখে বায়না বাবদ মং ৯,০০০/- (নয় হাজার) টাকা নগদ বুঝিয়া পাইয়া দলিল গ্রহিতা বরাবরে তপছিল বর্ণিত সম্পত্তির দখল ছাড়িয়া দিয়া উক্ত তারিখেই দলিলগ্রহিতার বরাবরে এক খন্ড বায়নাপত্র দলিল সম্পাদন করিয়া দেয়।”

	18. So it is very clear that the assertion of the petitioner as regards the delivery of possession as made out in the plaint and consequent registration of the deed with the said averment through the court were wrong and the petitioner was. not put into possession by the lessee in the case land but it appears from the notice dated 8.2.86 under section 7 of President's Order 16/72 that he is in unauthorised possession of the case holding and as such the Court of Settlement as well has rightly ordered for taking delivery of possession by evicting the petitioner therefrom on the finding that the transfer pursuant to the alleged deed of agreement and the title deed executed and registered through the Court are in violation of Article 6 of President's Order 16/72. 

	19. The Court of Settlement arrived at the findings of fact on consideration of the materialon record that the whereabouts of the original allottee (vendor of the petitioner) were not known and on comparison of the signatures of the lessee (vendor of the petitioner) in the affidavit; application for allotment of a holding and lease deed executed between the lessee and the Govt. do not tally with that of the alleged original bainanama which is a got up one on the face of it, and as such rightly left the decree, which is valueless, out of consideration. 

	20. In the aforesaid premises, we are of the opinion that the property has been declared as an abandoned property under the provisions of President's Order 16/72 and the petitioner has failed to show that the inclusion in the official Gazette was without lawful authority. We have no reason to interfere with the impugned decision as the Court of Settlement did not commit any error or did not exceed its jurisdiction in passing the impugned decision. 	

	In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. 

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule is against an order of the learned District Judge, Chittagong restoring Partition Suit No. 560 of 1983 of the Court of Munsif, Banshkhali on setting aside an ex-parte preliminary decree. 

2. The petitioners No. 1-17 instituted Partition suit No. 16 of 1973 in the Court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Satkania against the opposite party Nos. 1-3 and others. The plaint having been rejected by the trial court an appeal was taken to the District Judge and the appellate Court remanded the suit to the trial Court for amendment of the plaint. After the remand the defendants filed an objection to valuation of the suit and the value of the suit was determined at Tk. 2,700/-. As, against that order the revisional case No. 92 of 1979 was preferred to the Court of District Judge, Chittagong who allowed the revision case with the direction to re-assess the valuation of the suit on the basis of the documents. Subsequently, due to change of territorial jurisdiction of the Court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Satkania, the suit was transferred to the Court of Munsif, Bashkhali who received on 16.11.83 the record of the case. The date of hearing was notified in the notice Board. The suit on transfer was re-numbered as Partition Suit No. 560 of 1983. The learned Munsif after several adjournments of the hearing of the suit posted the same for peremptory hearing on 27.12.1983 and passed an ex-parte preliminary decree in absence of the opposite parties Nos. 1-3. A final decree was also passed and possession was delivered to the petitioners No. 1-24. Against the final decree Partition Appeal No. 407 of 1984 is pending before the Court of District Judge. 

3. The opposite parties No. 1-3 before me filed Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 1984 on 29.5.1984 under Order 9 rule 13 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte preliminary decree of the Court of Munsif, Bashkhali alleging, interlaia, that they were not aware of the- transmission of the record of the suit after hearing the valuation matter by the appellant Court as the learned Advocate and his clerk did not inform about the transmission of the record from the court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Satkania and they were under bona fide belief that they would be informed about the hearing of the suit by the learned Advocate and his clerk. On 14.5.1984 when the petitioner NO.4 disclosed about the ex parte decree to the witnesses the opposite parties No. 1-3 filed Miscellaneous Case No.88 of 1984 on 16.5. 1984 having enquired about the suit and knowing about the ex parte decree. The petitioner Nos. 1-17 contested the ground of limitation and defect of parties. They further alleged that the ex parte decree was passed in presence of the opposite-parties Nos. 1-3 on 27.12.1983 and the case was filed to harass them. 

4. The learned Munsif dismissed the Miscellaneous Case on contest holding that the opposite parties Nos. 1-3 were not prevented by sufficient cause the case was barred by limitation and for want of an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act for condo nation of delay. 

5. The Miscellaneous Appeal No. 308 of 1985 of the opposite-parties against that order was allowed restoring the suit by the impugned order dated 27.9.1986 passed by the learned District Judge. 

6. Mr. Nurul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the petitioners first, urged that provisions of Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure are not attracted in the instant case inasmuch as there are specific provisions provided in the Code for the remedy and there being three alternative remedies available to the opposite-parties namely by way an application under Order 9, rule 13 for setting aside the ex parte decree, an appeal against the ex parte decree and an independent suit for declaration that the ex parte decree was bad and illegal the lower appellate court acted illegally in invoking the inherent jurisdiction under Section 151 of the Code in passing the impugned order. He further urged that the lower appellate court wrongly following the decision in the case of Master Abdul Aziz Vs. Abani Mohan Kukuherjee and others reported in 30 DLR (SC), 221 passed the impugned order. He referred me to the following observation of their Lordships. 

"What has been held in the above cases is that the Court has an inherent power under Section 151 of the Code to set aside its order passed under a misapprehension of facts when true facts are brought to light and that the Court has also power under the aforesaid Section 151 of the Code to vacate an order obtained by misleading the Court and practicing fraud upon it." 

7. He submitted that from the above observation it appears that there was misrepresentation in obtaining the order in that case but in the instant case no such misrepresentation or fraud was practiced upon the court by the petitioners in obtaining the ex parte decree. The submission seemingly seems to have force. Mr. Fazlul Karim, on the other hand, submitted that the petitioners did not disclose to the trial Court that an order was passed by the appellate Court regarding the re-assessment of the valuation of the suit and the petitioners upon such suppression obtained the ex parte decree. He further submitted that as no notice was given by the Court regarding transfer of the suit the ex parte decree was liable to be set aside. He placed reliance in support of his contention upon the case of Hiralal and others Vs. State and Bihar, 1968 Pat. 439. In that case 3 cases were pending before the District Judge, Arrah. The said cases subsequently were transferred to the court of Subordinate Judge for disposal. But the court did not notify the fact of transfer of the case to the parties or their pleaders. It was held that in cases of transfer made by the court Suo motu notice of transfer must be given to the parties or their lawyers. 

8. In my opinion want of notice of transfer of the suit is a sufficient ground for the opposite parties Nos. 1-3 in this case for not appearing at the time when the suit was called on for hearing by the learned Munsif, In the case of Ram Sukul Pathak Vs. Kesho Prashand Singh 1918 Pat., 341, it was held by the learned Chief Justice who delivered the judgment of the report that; 

"It seems to me that it would be desirable in these cases where an order of transfer is made that notice should be given in every case to the parties or their representatives. I find a passage in the judgment of J wale Prasad. J., which deals with this point and with which I entirely agree. He says: 

"In my mind such an important order as the transfer of a case from one court to another should invariably be communicated to the persons concerned and in token of such communication the signature of the parties or their pleaders should be obtained and when the signatures are not obtained the order-sheet should show that the information has been communicated". 

9. From the facts of this case before one it appears that there was order by the appellate court on remand to reassess the valuation of the suit by the trial Court on the basis of the documents already put in the trial Court and it was within knowledge of the petitioners as they were present in the trial Court when the ex parte decree was passed and as such it was their duty to bring to the knowledge of the Court that the suit was not valued in terms of the remand order of the lower appellate court. Withholding of such material fact from the knowledge of Court was deliberate and willful omission on the part of the petitioners and, in my opinion, such act tantamount to practising fraud upon the court in obtaining an ex parte decree in this case. The petitioners did conceal this from the trial Court at the time when the ex-part decree was made in order to obtain advantage of ex parte decree. Had they brought this fact to notice of the court it certainly ought not to have made the ex parte decree rather it would have proceeded to reasses the valuation in accordance with the direction of the court of appeal. The contention of the learned Advocate that the lower appellate court wrongly applied the principle of law enunciated in the case of A. Aziz is not tenable. It is true, when alternative remedy is provided in the Code a party is not entitled to invoke the provisions of section 151 of the Code. Section 351, however, can be invoked to, set at naught an order obtained from a court by practising fraud, by misleading it and where it passes an order or a decree upon misapprehension of the facts. I hold that such willful concealment on the part of the petitioners is a sufficient ground to invoke the provision of section 151 of the Code to set at naught the ex parte decree. 

10. Now let me consider the contention that the application under Order 9 rule 13 read with Section 151 of Code admittedly being barred by limitation and there being no application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act the Court below ought not be have condoned the delay and passed the impugned order. According to article 164 of the Limitation Ad the period of limitation for setting aside a decree passed ex parte is thirty days from the date. of decree or where summons was not duly served, thirty days from the date of knowledge of the decree. Prior to 18.5.1967 Section 5 of the Limitation Act was not applicable to a proceeding under Order 9 rule 13. But by amendment made on 18.5.1967 Section 5 has been made applicable to such proceeding. In this respect the case of Khorshed Ali Chowdhury Vs. The People's Republic of Bangladesh, 29 DLR 376 may be referred to. In the instant case no separte application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act was filed along with the application under Order 9 rule 13 read with Section 151 of the Code. Therefore, the question that falls for determination is : Where no application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act is filed whether the Court is competent to set aside an ex parte decree merely on the basis of an application under Order 9 rule 13 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure? From a close reading of Section 5, it seems to me, that the court can condone the delay without such application provided the parties seeking relief satisfy the court that there was sufficient cause for not filing the application within time. Whether there was sufficient cause or not has to be gathered by the Court itself before whom such application is made from materials on record. In this case the reasons for delay have been duly stated by the opposite-parties in their application for setting aside the ex parte decree and in support of their case witnesses were also examined and evidences were led. From reading of the language of Section 5 of the Limitation Act I do not find that it enjoins upon a party filing an application under Order 9, rule 13 read with Section 151 of the Code to file a formal application under Section 5 of the said Act. In this case the panics having had duly stated the reasons for delay and as both the parties having had led evidence in support of their respective cases there could be no better or other reasons which could be stated in an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act and as such a formal application under Section 5 was not a must. It is also evident from record that there was no notice given by the court at Bashkhali to the opposite parties No. 1-3 regarding arrival of the records of the suit from Satkania which on transfer was re-numbered as partition suit No. 560 of 1984. In that event how can it be possible for them to know that the suit filed in the court of Munsif, Satkania was re-numbered as partition suit No. 560 of 1984 of the Court of Banshkhali without such notice from the Court? Taking this aspect into consideration, I am constrained to hold that there was sufficient cause for the opposite parties for not appearing at the time when the suit was called on for hearing and the delay in filing the application was sufficiently explained. The word" sufficient" cause should be construed liberally in order to advance the cause of substantial justice and not to shut out a litigant from the door of justice. A doctrinaire approach should be avoided because the court is to construe a provision of law for advancement of justice and not to retard it. A litigant should not- be deprived of the benefit to which he is otherwise entitled in law. As the court below found sufficient cause on consideration of the materials placed before it, it passed the impugned order., In the case of Mr. Kulsoomun Nissa and another Vs. Noor Mohammad alias Sultan Haider and another 1936 All 666, the learned Chief justice expressed himself in the following manner: 

" The first ground on which the appeal has been dismissed by the lower appellate Court is that the plaintiffs had not made any formal application for an extension of time under Section 5, Limigation Act, and that, therefore, their appeal against Hakim Shyam Sundar Lal was beyond time. In our opinion the Court below has erred in exercising its discretion in this matter". 

11. In the case of Firm Kaura Mal Vs. Firm Mathra Dass the Punjab High Court, 1959 Punj. 648 following 1930 All.  666 observed: Merely because there was no written application filed by the appellant was hardly sufficient ground for refusing him the relief, if he was otherwise entitled to it. 

"The language of Section 5 of the Limitation Act does not provide that an application in writing must be filed before relief under the said provision can be granted." 

12. The view taken by their Lordships in the above cases has also been followed by our High Court Division in the case of Chowdhury Saifuddin Ahmed Vs. Sharnsuddin and others, 40 D.L.R., 10. That is a case directly on the point before me as there was not an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act. The trial Court dismissed the application filed for setting aside the ex parte decree on the ground that no application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act was filed for condo nation of delay. His Lordship Mustafa Kamal, J. following the decisions in the cases of Ms. Kulsoomun Nissa and Firm Kaura Mal observed: 

"though as matter of prudence and Procedure a separate application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act is always desirable, no harm has been done in the present case as in the main application under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure the appellant has sought to explain the reasons of his delay in filing the miscellaneous case". 

13. Being in respectful agreement with his Lordship I hold that mere absence of a formal application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act in the present case is no bar to the grant of the relief sought for by an application under Order 9 rule 13 read with section 151 of the Code where in the said application all the facts constituting the delay are duly stated which are required to be stated in an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act on consideration of which the court is able to condone the delay. 

14. Mr. N.I. Chowdhury, submitted further that the petitioners Nos. 18-24 who got saham should have been made opposite parties in the application and non-impleading them was defect of parties. He relied upon the decision in the case of Apil and other Vs. Ayatullah Pramanik and others, 6 D.L.R.  461. According to Order 9, rule 14 no decree shall be set aside unless notice of the application for setting aside the decree is served upon the opposite parties. In this case notices were served upon the plaintiffs and there was substantial compliance with the requirement of Order 9, rule 14 of the Code. On the other hand on the strength of Apil Bibi I hold that the plaintiffs- petitioners who got the ex parte decree are the opposite-parties within the meaning of Order 9 rule 14 of the Code as in the said decision it has been held that the plaintiffs in partition suit arc the opposite-panics within the meaning of Order 9 rule 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Therefore the decision does not help the learned Advocate. It is also urged that the Miscellaneous Case not having been decided in presence of petitioners Nos. 18-24 they have suffered loss. I do not find force in the contention. The suit being restored, in my opinion, they arc not to be debared from claiming the saham given and restoration of the suit does not prejudice them. It appears that the plea of defect of parties was taken in the written objection but no issue was framed on it by the trial Court nor the petitioners did press for framing the issue on the defect of parties. The petitioners also did not raise this point before the lower appellate Court. 

15. Objection as to defect of parties has to be taken at the earliest time and after framing issues it should not be entertained. If not so taken, it shall be deemed to have been waived. In that view of the matter I hold that the petitioners also by their conduct waived the plea of defect of parties. The aforesaid view finds support from the decisions in the cases of Gurucharan Jena Vs. Satya Narayan Jew Thakur and others, 1971 Ori. 15; Parameswaran Vs. Shangaran, 14 Mad. 489. Vithabal vs. Pandu, 26 Born. 301., Khirsingti Vs. Brijlal 1949 Nag. 314 and in the case of Chandra Kanta Goswami Vs. Ram Nohiqi Debi and others 1956 Cal. 577. Therefore, the contention that the Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 1984 suffers from defect of parties has no force and cannot be allowed at this stage. 

16. In this respect it is pertinent to observe that while granting an application for restoration of a suit on setting aside an ex parte decree the court is to allow the application upon such terms as to cost. As no cost has been awarded by the lower appellate court in this case, I direct the opposite-parties Nos. 1-3 to pay cost of Tk. 250/- to the petitioners. The court of Munsif, Bashkhali is also directed to communicate to the parties concerned about the transfer of the suit to that court and fix a date for hearing of the suit. 

17. In the result, the Rule is discharged with the aforesaid observations. There will be no order as to costs. 

Let the records of the lower Courts be sent down at once. 

End.

full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed. J.- In this appeal by special leave the question for determination is whether the provision for restitution as contained in section 144 of the Code or Civil Procedure, briefly the 'Code', is applicable to an order in a pre-emption case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 1950.

2. Facts of the case, so far necessary for disposal of this appeal, are that the respondent filed an application for pre-emption of a hind sold to the appellant by his co-sharer, and obtained an ex-parte order dated 7 March, 1975 allowing the pre-emption, and in pursuance of that order took delivery of possession of the land. But the order of pre-emption was ultimately set aside by the High Court Division in revision by an order dated 8 February, 1978 and pre-emption case was restored to tile and it is now pending before the trial court, namely, 3rd Court of Munsif at Comilla. The appellant-preempted filed in the meantime, an application under section 144 of the Code claiming restoration of possession of the land to him in view of the fact that the order for pre-emption has been set aside. The trial court rejected the application for restitution whereupon an appeal being Misc. Appeal No. 154 of 1978, was preferred before the District Judge. The learned Subordinate Judge who heard the appeal, took the view that provision for restitution under section 144 of the Code is applicable to an order In a pre-emption case and accordingly allowed the appeal as well as the application under section 144 and ordered that possession of the land be restored to the pre-emption-appellant, The pre-emptor challenged this order of restitution by a revisional application before the High Court Division and the latter by the impugned order dated 7 July, 1981 set aside the order of restitution observing that .an order in a pre-emption case not being a decree within the meaning of section 2 of the Civil Procedure Code, provision for restitution under section 144 is not applicable to such and order,

3. Mr. Zillul Huq, learned Counsel for the appellant, has contended firstly that though an order for pre-emption is not a decree, it has got the force of a decree and secondly, that even if the provision of section 144 of the Civil Procedure Code is not applicable to an order in a pre-emption case, still restitution may" be available under section 151 of the Code ill exercise of the inherent power of the court to pass any order at its discretion to meet the ends of justice. In support of these contentions he has referred to a number of cases mainly of Indian Jurisdiction particularly the cases of Wahid Vs. Zobedha, AIR 1952. Nag 190; Maharaj Sasikanta Vs. Jam Baksh-53 CLJ. 49; Rai Charan Vs. Debi Prasad, 26 C.W.N. 408; Ramanath Karmakar Vs. Sheikh Ahsanulla 34 C.W.N. 746 and Naren Vs. Benode 54 C.W.N. 896. Mr. Shaukat Ali Khan. learned Counsel appearing for the respondent has contended, on the other hand that in the absence of any specific provision for restitution on reversal of an 'order' as distinguished from a 'decree' restitution cannot be allowed by any court at its direction or in exercise of its inherent power.

<u>4. 'Restitution' simply means restoration of something to a person from which it was taken away earlier under an erroneous judgment of a court. Question of restitution arises when the erroneous judgment of the court is varied reversed or set aside. Section 144 of the Code which provides for restitution says that restitution thereunder is available when a decree is varied or reversed. It is silent as to whether restitution is available when an order is varied, reversed or set aside. But the principle of restitution is that on the reversal of a judgment an obligation is created for a party who had received the benefit of the erroneous judgment to make restitution to the other party what he had lost and that it is also for the court to see that ends of justice is not frustrated. The Court may place the parties in the position which they would have occupied but for the erroneous judgment. Considering from this angle it is quite legitimate to argue why the broad principle of restitution as provided in section 144 should not be applicable in the case of reversal of an erroneous order by which a person had been deprived possession of his property in a civil proceeding which ends with an order having the force of a decree.</u>

<u>5. In English law as to restitution, no distinction is found .to have been made between order, judgment and decree. In Halsbury's Laws of England law of restitution has been enunciated as: "Where a wrongful or irregular execution has been set aside or where a judgment or order has been reversed after execution thereon has taken place, restitution will be made to the successful party. The order setting aside the execution or reversing the judgment or order should provide for this; and if it does execution may issue upon it in the ordinary course. If the order does not so provide, another order may be made, or a writ called a writ of restitution be issued commanding the judgment creditor to restore the property or pay over the proceeds of sale." The Judicial" Committee of the Privy Council while examining the question of restitution under section 44 of the Civil Procedure Code in "Jai Berham Vs Kadernath AIR 1922 (PC) 269, has observed that it is the duty of the court to place parties in the position which they would have occupied but for the wrong decree and went further to hold that the duty of the court to grant restitution arises ever outside the provisions of section 144. Their Lordships observed: "Nor indeed does this duty arise merely under this said section. It is inherent in the general jurisdiction of the court to act rightly and fairly according to the circumstances towards all the parties involved."</u>

<u>6. It appears that following this decision of the Privy Council different High Courts of the Sub-continent allowed restitution in the case of reversal of orders in exercise of their discretion under section 151 of the Cope. I need not refer to aII the cases cited by Mr. Zillul Huq in this connection but brief reference may be made to some of them. In the case of Wahid VS Zobeda, AIR 1952 Nag. 190, the appellant father of two minor sons, was directed to pay maintenance of his minor sons to their mother on an application under section 10 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1887; maintenance was accordingly paid but after a few years that order was reversed whereupon he prayed for recovery of the money already paid invoking section 144 of the Code. The High Court held that section 144 of the Code was not attracted since the order reversed was not a decree within the meaning of section 2 of the Code but nevertheless observed that recovery of the money was permissible under section 151 of the Code in exercise of the court's inherent power to meet the ends of justice. The Court pointed out the distinction between restitution: under section 144 and that under section 151 in that section 144 is mandatory whereas section 151 is purely discretionary. In Maharaj Sasikanta Vs. Jalil Baksh 53, CLJ, 49, sale of a jote in execution of a riot decree was .set aside on an application under Order 21, rule 92 of the Code whereupon all application was made claiming restitution which was allowed in exercise of inherent power of the Court under section 151 of the Code. In the case of Rai Charan Vs. Debi Prasad 26, C.W.N. 408 restitution was claimed by way of recovery of the money paid to the mortgagee auction-purchaser and it was held by the High Court that it was competent to the executing court to make an order of restitution with a view to secure to complete justice between the parties concerned even if the case does not come within the terms of section 144."</u>

<u>7. In the instant case the High Court Division concentrated its whole attention on section 144 of the Code and observed that "apart from section 144 of the Civil Procedure Code there is no other provision in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and for that matter in any other law for the restitution of an property in view of the variation of any order made by any Appellate Court". The High Court Division referred to the definition of a decree under section 2 of the Code and has observed that since an order of pre-emption is an appealable order it stands excluded from the definition of a decree whether restitution is available under section 151 was not considered by the High Court Division in this case. The underlying principle of restitution is that when a person is deprived of some right or property by an erroneous judgment, order or decree then in the event of the reversal of that judgment, order or decree, he may become entitled to restitution of his right or property and that it is the duty of the court to see that the ends of justice be met Such restoration becomes all the more necessary if the erroneous judgment or order has caused injury to the person deprived of his property. If any law specifically provides for restitution, such as section 144 of the Code, restitution must be granted by the court under this section its term being mandatory. But this section is not exhaustive; it only defines the procedure for restitution in the case of a reversal of a decree. In the case of reversal of an order the same remedy should be given by the Court in the exercise of its inherent power under section 151 C.P.C. The inherent power of the Court should be exercised at its discretion, according to the merit of each case. This discretionary power cannot be exercised when restoration, if allowed, will run counter to the interests of justice. The view taken by the learned Subordinate Judge that "section 144. Civil Procedure Code connotes an order" is not correct since an order for pre-emption is not a decree. This order may have the force of a decree but it is not included in section 144. That is why probably the word 'order' 'has been inserted in this section by an amendment in India in C.P C. But the High Court Division's view that no restitution is available in the case of reversal of an order of pre-emption is not supportable either. The order, of the Subordinate Judge allowing the restitution is treated as one having been passed under section 151 of the Code. Subject to this modification the appeal is allowed, the order of the High Court Division is set aside and that of the Subordinate Judge is restored.</u>

There will be no order as to costs.

End.
