This Civil Revision No. 1086 of 1992 and Civil Revision No. 1087 of 1992 arising out of the same judgment have been heard together and are being disposed of by this judgment.

2. This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff-appellant petitioners was directed against the judgment and decree dated 16.4.94 and 22.4.92 respectively passed by the Subordinate Judge, Commercial Court, Barisal in Title Appeal No. 115 of 1990 affirming the judgment and decree dated 26.5.90 and 6.6.90 respectively passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Barisal in Title Suit No. 395 of 1984.

3. The short facts necessary for the disposal of this Rule may be stated as follows:

Babu Tufan Das, the predecessor of the plaintiff appellant-petitioner being plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 235 of 1981 in the Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge) 2nd court at Barisal against the defendant-opposite party for khan possession by evicting the defendant from the suit but as described in the schedule to the plaint and subsequently on transfer of the suit to the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Barisal, it was renumbered as Title Suit No. 395 of 1984. The case of the plaintiff is that the plaintiff is the owner of 0.09 decimal of land of RS plot No. 2048 by pattan taken in 1359 BS from the previous owner Sukumar Sen and others. This land was wrongly recorded in the khatian in the name of the previous owner and so, the plaintiff Tufan Das filed a suit being Title Suit No. 555 of 1958 against the said previous owner for declaration of this title in the suit land and the suit was decreed on 15.7.59 and then the plaintiff Tufan Das got his name recorded in the khatian and paid rent and taxes as usual and thus the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land. That the defendant opposite party No. 1 is the younger brother of the plaintiff and that the defendant had no house of his own in the town and on his prayer, the plaintiff allowed the defendant to stay in the northern bhiti Gulpata hut measuring 8 x 5 Banga in 1976 and since then the defendant has been residing therein temporarily in the suit hut. That subsequently plaintiff petitioner wanted to make a pucca construction on his own land and for that purpose the plaintiff asked the defendant opposite party to vacate his Gulpata hut but that the defendant refused to vacate the hut and, as such, the plaintiff-petitioner instituted the aforesaid title suit for khas possession.

4. After 5 years of plaintiffs Title Suit No. 235 of 1981(renumbered as Title Suit No. 395 of 1984), the defendant-opposite party as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 19 of 1986 against this petitioner as defendant for declaration of his title in 8 annas share of the total suit property of 0.09 decimals of land and also for a declaration that the decree dated 15.7.59 passed in Title Suit No. 555 of 1958 is fraudulent, collusive, void and not binding upon the opposite party. The claim of the opposite party in his Title Suit No. 19 of 1986 is that the petitioner and the opposite party being full-brothers and that the petitioner being the eldest brother, both of them jointly took settlement of the disputed land from the previous owner but that the petitioner fraudulently instituted Title Suit No. 555 of 1958 claiming his sole interest in the land in question and obtained a fraudulent collusive decree on 15.7.59. The learned Assistant Judge held analogous trial of both the suits and decided both the suits by one judgment. After hearing the parties, the learned Assistant Judge, dismissed the suit for eviction brought by the plaintiff-petitioner and decreed the suit of the opposite party for declaration of his title in 8 annas share vide his judgment and decree dated 26.5.90 and 6.6.90 respectively.

5. Against that judgment and decree dated 26.5.90 and 6.6.90 respectively, the petitioner filed two separate Appeals Nos. 115 of 1990 and 116 of 1990 in the Court of learned District Judge, Barisal. Both the appeals were heard by the Subordinate judge, Commercial Court, Barisal. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing the parties, dismissed both appeals by one judgment and confirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court vide his judgment and decree dated 16.4.92 and 22.4.92 respectively.

6. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, the appellants as petitioners have preferred these two revisional applications under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the two Rules being CR No. 1086 of 1992 and CR 1087 of 1992.

7. Mr. Shamsul Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant-petitioners, has submitted that the opposite party failed to prove his case of joint settlement in his Title Suit No. 19 of 1986 and that he could not also prove by any evidence that he took the settlement of the suit land along with his brother the petitioner but that both the courts below by misreading the facts and evidence, decided both the suits in favour of the opposite party and thus this decision of the learned Subordinate Judge has caused a failure of justice to the plaintiff-petitioners.

8. Mr. Mihir Kanti Majumder, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant opposite party, has, on the other hand, submitted that the plaintiffs case was that defendant opposite party being his own younger brother was his licensee in the suit hut since 1976 but that his witnesses have said in their deposition that defendant has been possessing the suit hut since 1359 BS and that both the courts below after proper appreciation and discussion of all the evidence clearly came to the finding that the defendant-opposite party has been possessing the suit hut since much before the alleged licence-possession of 1976 and under such facts and circumstances, the learned courts below have rightly and correctly decided both the suits in favour of defendant-opposite party.

9. By a perusal of the impugned judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge, it appears that the plaintiff petitioner's case is that he alone took settlement of 0.09 decimal of land of plot No. 1533 of CS Khatian No. 859 from the original owner Kiran Bala Das and others in 1359 BS but defendant opposite party's case, on the other hand, was that Kiran and others granted settlement of this 0.09 decimal of land to both Tufan Das and Kala Chand Das in 13th Falgoon 1359 BS but that none of the parties filed any paper to show the claim of the respective settlement. From this fact it appears that the alleged settlement was an oral settlement and, as such, that was a matter for decision by oral evidence.

10. It appears from the impugned judgment that after discussion of all the evidences of the case, both the courts below have come to a concurrent finding that both the brothers have been possessing the suit land in equal share by constructing respective huts therein since 1359 BS. They have come to a further finding that the plaintiff-petitioner could not prove his claim of the opposite party being his licensee in respect of the suit hut only.

11. Mr. Shamsul Alam, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioners, submits that the plaintiff-petitioner subsequently filed a Title Suit No. 555 of 1958 against the original owner and got the decree and then got his name recorded in SA Khatian by filing Misc. Case under section 54 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and then paid rent to the Government regularly and that all these papers have been marked as exhibits in the suit but that the learned courts below did not consider these facts of the case.

12. In this respect, Mr. Mihir Kanti Majumder, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, has contended that these are the subsequent papers and that these papers and the rent receipts cannot create any title in favour of the plaintiff- petitioner, nor can it take away the defendant opposite party's right, title from the suit land.

13. It appears that the learned trial Court have discussed the facts of the case more elaborately with reference to the evidence and the legal presumption and came to the finding that both the brothers took settlement and both of them paid salami money of Taka six hundred to the landlord by selling that paternal land to Halima Khatun. The trial Court further found from the evidence of PWs and DWs that both brothers, Tufan Das and Kala Chand Das have been living in the suit property in their respective separate huts since 37/38 years with their family and that the decree obtained by Tufan Das in Title Suit No. 555 of 1958 was an ex parte and collusive decree and this had been done by elder brother Tufan Das to deprive the younger brother Kala Chand Das from the suit property. The learned Subordinate Judge also came to the conclusion that the learned trial Court has rightly come to this decision.

<u>14. Mr. Shamsul Alam next argued that the defendant's suit No. 19 of 1986 in the form of simple declaration without a prayer for partition' in respect of unspecified undivided property was not maintainable but yet the learned courts below by misreading the provision of law have erroneously decreed that suit. In support of his argument, the learned Advocate referred to a decision in the case of Tayeb Ali Vs. Abdul Khaleque and others reported in 43 DLR (AD) 87.</u>

<u>Their Lordships in that case observed as under:</u>

<u>"The suit being one for declaration of title to an unspecified share of an undivided plot of land on the basis of gift and there being no evidence that the donor thereof was in exclusive possession at any time is not maintainable without a prayer for partition."</u>

<u>15. Mr. Mihir Kanti Majumder, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, in this respect argued that the case referred to above was a case, for declaration of title filed by the plaintiff on the basis of a transfer by gift and that his donor's exclusive possession therein was not proved at all, but that the instant case before us is not a case of title on the basis of purchase of gift but that it is a case of original co-ownership and the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 19 of 1986 is admittedly in joint possession of the suit property and, as such, the nature of the present case is quite different from the case referred to above. In this connection, Mr. Mihir Kanti Majumder referred to a decision in the case of Joy Narain Sen Ukil Vs. Srikanta and others reported in AIR 1922 (Cal) 8 wherein it has been held that:</u>

<u>"Where a plaintiff is in joint possession of immovable property, whether such possession be actual possession of his share of the whole or actual possession of part coupled with constructive possession of the remainder, he is entitled to maintain a suit for declaratory relief with a view to remove a cloud on his title created by the act of the defendant disputing his share; in a suit so framed declaration of title is all that plaintiff needs and he is consequently not called upon to ask for consequential relief by way of partition."</u>

<u>Mr. Mihir Kanti Majumder argued that it has been established by evidence that the opposite party is a co-owner in joint possession of the suit property comprising 0.09 decimal of land and, as such, the suit in the form of declaration of his title in respect of his share in this 0.09 decimal being clouded by his brother will be maintainable.</u>

16. It appears that in the instant case the opposite party being plaintiff filed his Title Suit No. 19 of 1986 for simple declaration of title in respect of 8 anna share in the suit property comprising 0.09 decimal of land. Admittedly, the total suit land is 0.09 decimal and both the brothers are jointly living therein, therefore, it is not an unspecified land but that it is quite a specified piece of 0.09 decimal of land, part of which is in exclusive physical possession of the younger brother since 37/38 years as has been found by both the courts below. So, in the facts and circumstances of the instant case before us, the principle laid down in the cited case of AIR, 1922 (Cal) at page 8 appears to be applicable. I, therefore, find that the defendant's case being suit No. 19 of 1986 will be maintainable in this form and that the learned courts below have correctly come to their conclusion.

17. Mr. Shamsul Alam referred to another decision in the case of Erjan Ali Vs. Joyrial Abedin Mia reported in 35 DLR (AD) 216 wherein their Lordships observed in the following:

"Rent receipts are evidence of possession, and may be used as collateral evidence of title. Mr Alam contends that the plaintiff petitioner paid rent of the suit land to the government and received dakhil as which are exhibit 8 series but that the defendant opposite party could not produce a piece of dakhila showing his payment of any rent or taxes. Mr. Alam argued that these rent receipts have presumptive value towards the petitioner's possession and title in whole of the suit property.

<u>18. In this connection, Mr. MihirKanti Majumder contends that defendant-opposite party being found to be in joint possession of the suit property with his elder brother Tufan Das, the payment of rent by Tufan Das can be presumed to be payment of joint rent and that Tufan Das at best can claim rateable amount of rent from the defendant-opposite party, but for that joint ownership, of the defendant opposite party shall not be extinguished. It appears that the instant case is a case of co-ownership, and joint possession has been established by evidence and, as such, the instant case before us is different in nature and the payment of rent by the plaintiff-petitioner alone for a joint property will not go to change the character of joint ownership and joint possession of both the brothers.</u>

19. Mr. Mihir Kanti Majumder argued that both the courts below elaborately discussed all the facts and evidence of the case and came to a concurrent finding of facts based on evidence on record and as such this court in revisional jurisdiction has little scope to interfere with the concurrent finding of facts arrived at by both the courts below. In support of his contention the learned Advocate cited a decision in the case of Shambhu Nath Poddar Vs. Bangladesh Railway and ors reported in 43 DLR (AD) 82 wherein it has been held by their Lordships as under:

"A revisional court acts beyond its jurisdiction in setting aside concurrent finding of fact when there is no misreading and mis-appreciation of the evidence on record."

Admittedly, the petitioner and the opposite party of the instant case are two brothers. Admittedly, both the brothers are living in the suitland of 0.09 decimal of land in two separate huts on the basis of a pattan from the original owners. Both the courts below discussed all the facts, circumstances and the evidences on record quite elaborately and correctly together with presumptive circumstances of the case and came to a concurrent finding of fact that both the brothers have been living in this 0.09 decimals of land in their respective separate huts since 1359 BS entering therein at a time and thus the learned courts found that both the brothers have got title and possession in the suit property. I do not find any misreading or mis-appreciation of the evidence by any of the courts below. I find that the learned Subordinate Judge has correctly and properly discussed and appreciated the facts, circumstances and the evidence of both the cases and come to the conclusion on the basis of the materials on record. I do not find anything wrong in his finding of facts.

20. Considering all the above facts and circumstances, I am of the opinion that the learned Subordinate Judge has not committed any error of law nor caused any failure of justice by passing the impugned judgment. I, therefore, find, that the impugned judgment does not call for any interference by this court.

In view of the above, both the Rules are discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Mozammel Hoque J: This Company Appeal under section 202 of the Companies Act, 1913 is directed against the judgment and order dated 27.11.86 passed by Mr Justice Latifur Rahman in Company Matter No. 29 of 1982 directing liquidation of the appellant-company under sections 162 and 163 read with section 166 of the Companies Act.

2. The facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of the appeal are, that the Agrani Bank as petitioner (which we will refer to as petitioner Bank) filed an application for winding up the respondent-appellant (which we will refer to as company) under sections 162 and 163 read with section 166 of the Companies Act before the Company Court alleging, inter alia, that the petitioner bank was a Nationalized concern and has been carrying on business throughout the country. The appellant-company was a private limited company having its registered office at 82, Motijheel Commercial Area and factory at Fatulla, Dhaka. The company opened and operated account under several headings in the local office of the petitioner-Bank since pre-liberation days and enjoyed cash credit facilities by hypothecation, pledge of goods, etc. After liberation of Bangladesh, the company was taken over by the Government and placed under the management of Bangladesh Fertilizer, Chemical and Pharmaceutical Corporation now Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation. After taking over, it was run and managed by the aforesaid corporation and ultimately the abandoned shares were sold to the original Bangladeshi Share-holders/ Directors and then it was released on 21.8.76 and possession was handed over to its original owners, namely, Share-holders/Directors. The company took over possession of all its assets and liabilities including pre-liberation liabilities. In a meeting of the company the Board of Directors acknowledged the company's liabilities including those of the petitioner-Bank for the period prior to the release of the unit. There are long standing liabilities of the company to the petitioner-Bank. In spite of notices, requests and demands for adjustment of the loan, the company, though on several occasions made promises and assurance, did not take any step for adjustment of the loans. When notice was issued, the liability of the company to the petitioner-Bank stood at Tk. 30,69,606.92 on 28.7.82. But when the petitioner filed application before the Company Court, the Out-standing dues were shown at Tk. 39,41,371.12 as stood on 14.10.82.

3. It was the further case of the petitioner-Bank that the goods pledged would value at Tk. 3,79,500/-. In spite of demands, the company had not secured the liability and it appears that it had no capacity to adjust the liability and repay the loan with interest. The company had failed and was neglecting to pay its debts on demand and, in fact, it was unable to repay the debts. Since the company was unable to repay its debts to the petitioner-Bank, the company is liable to suffer liquidation under law. The petitioner-Bank prayed for winding up the company as it failed to pay the loan of Tk. 39,41,371.12 as stood on 14.10.82.

4. The company appeared before the Court, contested the aforesaid application of the petitioner-Bank and denied its liability and the allegations made in the application by filing affidavit-in-opposition. It is their case that the industrial enterprise has been taken over as abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and thereafter it was placed tinder the statutory corporation by President's Order No. 27 of 1972. It was their further case that the goods were pledged and the petitioner-Bank was in custody of those goods worth Tk. 3,79,500/- and the petitioner-Bank did not allow the company to have its goods and sell those at the appropriate time at appropriate value for liquidating its debts. Due to the fault of the petitioner-Bank, the company had to suffer loss and damage estimated at about Tk. 30,00,000/-. The market value of the raw materials held by the petitioner-Bank amounted to Tk. 3,79,500/-. It is their further cast that if the loss of Tk. 30,00,000/-is adjusted against the claim of the petitioner-Bank, the outstanding dues would remain only at a few lakh Taka. It is stated by the company that the liability as regards interest during the period from the date of taking over till the date of release are not the legal liabilities of the company and the maximum penal rate of interest should not be charged against the company. If the value of the goods pledged, the damage caused by the action of the petitioner-bank and the interests charged upon the company for the whole period of unrest and for the period it was under the corporation are taken up together and adjusted, then there will be no liability of the company to the petitioner-Bank. Since the company had counter-claim for damages for non-delivery of the goods on cash payment in time and there were disputed claims, an application under sections 162 and 163 of the Companies Act is not maintainable.

5. By annexure-"X" of the affidavit-in-opposition of the company, it was shown that after the company was released, the company paid Tk. 12.92 lacs as against Tk. 9.19 lacs which shows that the company paid Tk. 3.73 lacs in excess of the value.

6. The petitioner-Bank filed affidavit-in-reply to the aforesaid affidavit-in-opposition of the company. In fact, it re-iterated its claim as made in the application. It further denied the claim of the company allegedly Tk. 30,00,000/- stating that it was an imaginary claim and there is no evidence to show the aforesaid alleged liability of the petitioner-Bank to the company. It was further stated that they charged penal interest in view of circular of Bangladesh Bank dated 25.1.79.

7. The company filed a further affidavit-in-opposition on 19.11.86 stating that the title deeds of land measuring 13 bighas in Kashimpur mouza were deposited with Agrani Bank, Local Office, Motijheel as collateral security against loan given to the company. It was their further case that the existing value of the aforesaid 13 bighas of land would be Tk. 45 lacs approximately. In another affidavit-in-position which was filed in Court on 13.2.86 by the company, it appears that the interests during the period of turmoil in 1971 and after nationalization stood at Tk. 14,25,702/- and if the aforesaid amount of interests is deducted from the total claim, then all the liabilities stood fully secured and as such the petitioner-Bank is not entitled to go for a winding up proceeding.

8. During the hearing of the aforesaid matter before the Company Court, another alleged creditor, namely, Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation (BCIC) appeared and filed an affidavit before the Court on 10.7.85 alleging that the aforesaid company was liable to it for an amount of Tk. 59,46,131.03 and for the aforesaid amount, the BCIC had already filed Money Suit No. 40 of 1980 and Money Suit No. 244 of 1982. It is their case that on liquidation its loan should be adjusted out of the sale-proceeds of the property of the company. Against the aforesaid affidavit of BCIC, the company also filed an affidavit-in-opposition disputing its liability.

9. Another creditor Bangladesh Shilpa Bank also filed an affidavit before the Company Court on 17.3.83 and claimed that the company was liable to it for an amount of Tk. 72,58,914.09. It was their case that it should not be liquidated. Alternatively it prayed that if it is liquidated, then their dues being first charge should be satisfied first. The Shilpa Bank also filed a case being Miscellaneous Case No. 107 of 1979, subsequently renumbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 50 of 1984 iii the Commercial Court, Dhaka, claiming the above amount. Ultimately, on 28.6.86 the Shilpa Bank got a decree for Tk. 20,30,793.46. Against the aforesaid decree both the petitioner-Bank and the Company filed two miscellaneous appeals in this Court which are pending for hearing.

10. After perusing the materials on record and hearing the learned Advocates of the parties, the learned Company Judge (Latifur Rahman, J.) passed the judgment on 27.11.86 allowing the application of the petitioner-Bank and directing the company, namely, the Bangladesh Tyres Ltd. to be wound up. The Official Receiver was also appointed as Liquidator who was directed to take over charge of the company forthwith with all its assets, liabilities and records. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment of the learned Company Judge, the Bangladesh Tyres Ltd., the appellant-company, preferred the present appeal.

11. Before going into the merit of the appeal, let us first consider the claims of the Shilpa Bank and the BCIC. It is on record that BCIC had already filed two suits against the appellant-company and those were pending in Court at the relevant time. Since the BCIC had already gone before the Court in order to establish its claim, it is not proper for us to make any comment or say anything about it in this judgment. In the similar way, we have seen that the Shilpa Bank also filed a miscellaneous case against the appellant-company and obtained a decree as stated above, and both the parties filed two separate appeals in this Court against the aforesaid decree. So, we are reluctant to make any comment or consider about the alleged claim of the Shilpa Bank in this appeal. In order to dispose of the present appeal, we may rely and use the relevant statements of facts which have been produced before this Court by submitting affidavits by the BCIC and the Shilpa Bank. But mere reliance on such statements in this judgment will not prejudice any of the parties in their respective suits and appeals.

<u>12. Dr. M Zahir, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, submits that the present application under sections 162 and 163 of the Companies Act is not maintainable in view of the fact that there was counter-claim of Tk. 30,00,000/- by the appellant-company. It is his case that if the amount of Tk. 30,00,000/-, value of the goods pledged and the security given to the petitioner-bank are taken up together, in fact, there would be no liability. We are unable to accept the first contention of Dr. Zahir in view of the fact that this counter-claim of Tk. 30,00,000/- for damage has not been proved by any evidence on record. It is just an allegation made in the counter-affidavit and no evidence has been placed before the Court in support of such counter-claim. In this view of the matter we are unable to accept the counter-claim of Tk. 30,00,000/-.</u>

13. Dr. Zahir next submits that as there is a bonafide dispute about the claim over the whole matter and unless and until the claim is settled in between the parties, an application under sections 162 and 163 of the Companies Act is not maintainable. We will see later on what is the bonafide dispute over claim in between the parties.

<u>14. Let us now consider the claim of the petitioner-Bank amounting to Tk. 39,41,371.12 as stood on 14.10.82. Dr. Zahir submits that the interests amounting to Tk. 14,25,702.00 in total charged against the company for the period of turmoil and for the period from the date of taking over of the company till the date of release cannot be legally charged. To allow such interest is absolutely a discretion of the Court. Petitioner-Bank is not entitled to claim such interests for such abnormal period as a matter of right. Further, during the aforesaid period the Share-holders/Directors of the company had no do-main and control over the management of the company. In a word, during that period the Share-holders/ Directors had legal disabilities over the affairs of the company and as such they should not be made bound to pay interests for such period. Although the Share-holders/Directors took over the company with all its assets and liabilities at the time of release of the company in their favour, it means legal and compulsive liability. The interests in question can not be treated as compulsive liability. Dr. Zahir tried to strengthen his above argument relying upon the case of M/s. MM Ispahani Ltd. Vs. Sonali Bank, 37 DLR (AD) 1. In the above case the question of payment of interest for the period over which the Share-holders/Directors of a taken-over company like the present one came up for consideration of their Lordships. After considering the matter in details their Lordships observed as follows:</u>

<u>"64. In principle, what appears from section 34 CPC itself is that the Court is not bound by what is provided in the contract itself, the matter of awarding interest being completely within its discretion. So, in a case involving the award of interest on any dues outstanding against the debtor, the Court is free to award interest at such rate as it may think fit. Ordinarily, that means if all that has happened to the lot of the appellant company were not there and the case would have been like any other loan transaction in normal circumstances, there would have been no objection to award interest on such principles. In the very extra-ordinary circumstances of the case without interfering with the principles enunciated by the aforesaid decisions as mentioned by the learned Counsel for the respondent Bank, we arc reluctant to award any interest at all not only from the date of filing the suit till the date of the decree but for the entire period beginning from 13.12.71 to the date of the decree. The reason being the unmerited deprivation of the appellant company to enjoy riot only his property and business rights but also utilization of the loan obtained from the Bank and the security offered against the loan by the company. It is true that the Government has ultimately returned the appellant company to its former directors but even then excepting the amount of nearly Taka one crore which the administrator deposited in the company's account in 1972, neither any sum by way of compensation nor the equivalent amount of jute stocks were returned to the company. In this view of the matter we arc reluctant to award any interest on the dues outstanding on 13.12.71 for the aforesaid period.</u>

<u>"68. The next question comes as to whether the Court will grant any interest on this amount for the period beginning from 13.12.71 to filing of the suit on 29.11.74. As the company came under total disability in the matter of operating its business as well as the Bank accounts for no fault of its own, it can legitimately ask for not granting any interest on the aforesaid outstanding clues for this period. It has been seen that the Bank also did not take any steps for clarifying its position regarding the repayment of the loan either from the company or from the Government during this period which it ought to have. We are, therefore, not in favour of awarding any interest for this period."</u>

<u>15. Relying upon the above decision of the Appellate Division we find substance in the above contention of Dr. Zahir and hold that the petitioner-Bank is not entitled to claim as a matter of right the above interest which stood at Tk. 14,25,702/-. We are of the view that due to the situation beyond control as stated above and in the interest of justice and equity, the Share-holders and Directors of the company shall not be made liable to pay the above interest. If the above interests namely, Tk. 14 lacs and odd is deducted from total claim of Tk. 39,41,371.12, the claim comes to Tk. 25 lacs and odd. At the relevant time admittedly the goods pledged were worth Tk. 3 lacs and odd and if this amount is deducted, then the claim of the petitioner-Bank comes to Tk. 21 lacs and odd approximately.</u>

16. Dr. Zahir then submits that if the debt of the bank can be shown secured, the prayer for winding up of the company cannot be entertained. In order to consider this submission of Dr. Zahir, it is required to examine the provisions of sections 162 and 163 of the Companies Act which run as follows:"

162. A company may be wound up by the Court—(i) if the company has by special resolution resolved that the company be wound up by the Court;

(ii) if default is made in filing the statutory report or in holding the statutory meeting;

(iii) if the company does not commence its business within a year from its incorporation, or suspends its business for a whole year;

(iv) if the number of members is reduced in the case of a private company, below two or, in the case of any other company, below seven;

(v) if the company is unable to pay its debts;

(vi) if the Court is of opinion that it is just and equitable that the company should be wound up.

163,—(1) A company shall be deemed to be unable to pay its debts—

(i) if a creditor, by assignment or otherwise, to whom the company is indebted in a sum exceeding five hundred (Taka) then due, has served on the company, (by causing same to be delivered by registered post or otherwise) at its registered office, a demand under his hand requiring the company to pay the sum so due and the Company has for three weeks thereafter neglected to pay the sum or to secure or compound for it to the reasonable satisfaction of the creditor; or

(ii) if execution or other process issued on a decree or order of any Court in favour of a creditor of the company is returned unsatisfied in whole or in part; or

(iii) if it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that the company is unable to pay its debts, and, in determining whether a company is unable to pay its debts, the Court shall take into account the contingent and prospective liabilities of the company.

17. Section 162 stipulates that a company may be wound up if the company is "unable to pay" its debts. In the present case, the petitioner-Bank is relying upon this provision is section 162(v) of the Companies Act for winding up of the company. Now, inability clause "unable to pay" has been defined in section 163. From section 163, it appears that if demand is made and within three weeks thereafter if the company neglects to pay the sum or to secure or compound for it to the reasonable satisfaction of the creditor, in that case it will amount to "unable to pay" for the company.

18. Now, let us see whether the company is unable to pay the debts or the debts have been secured to the satisfaction of the petitioner-Bank. As we have stated above if the amount of interest and the value of the goods pledged to the petitioner-Bank are taken up together and deducted, then the liability would come to Tk. 21 lacs and odd, at the relevant time. In the further affidavit of the company filed in Court on 19.11.86, it has been stated that the title deeds of lands measuring 13 bighas in Kashimpur mouza had been deposited with Agrani Bank, Local Office, Motijheel as collateral security for the company and the value would be approximately Tk. 45 lacs. On behalf of the petitioner-Bank an affidavit was Red on 16.8.88 and in that affidavit, there was assertion that there was a talk of compromise and some terms and conditions were laid down. In one of the terms, it was stated that the appellant-company shall not sell any property of the company or its sister concern which were mortgaged with the bank till liquidation of the entire liabilities of the borrower Company with the bank. There was no denial on behalf of the petitioner-Bank that the collateral security as stated above had been given to the bank. Now, Dr. Zahir submits that if the collateral security along with the value of the lands of the company where the factory is situated and the value of the machineries were taken up together, then it appears that the debts or liabilities to the bank are fully secured, and as the debt is secured on property of the company, the application for winding up under sections 162 and 163 of the Companies Act cannot be maintained. We find substance in the above contention of Dr. Zahir. At the time of hearing of the case, on our query, Mr. Siddique, the learned Advocate appearing for the Bangladesh Shilpa Bank, has disclosed that the factory of the company is situated at Fatullah and this company has got about eight bighas of land on which the factory is situated. Today, an application has been filed on behalf of the Bangladesh Shilpa Bank stating that the machineries of the factory and the lands at Fatullah Industrial Zone had been hypothecated to the Shilpa Bank. Dr. Zahir submits that the value of the eight bighas of land in Fatullah Industrial Zone together with the value of the machineries would be about Taka several crores and arc sufficient security to the out-standing dues of the petitioner-Bank. He further submits that although the Shilpa Bank has got the first charge over the above property, even then the claim of the petitioner-Bank would be satisfied by the company's property even after satisfying the first charge of the Shilpa Bank. From the facts and circumstances as well as the materials on record, we are of the view that the outstanding dues of the petitioner-Bank, as stated above, had been sufficiently secured when the application under sections 162 and 163 of the Companies Act had been filed before the Court and for that reason no winding up of the company is, at all, warranted.

<u>19. What is the legal liability of the company may be determined in a regular suit where the claim and counter-claim may be agitated and decided. Even after having regular decree in a money suit, the petitioner-Bank may be entitled to go for an winding-up proceeding if the company fails to pay the decretal amount. At this stage we are unable to hold that the company is legally unable to pay its debts or it is bankrupt and for this reason the loan cannot be satisfied and liquidation proceeding has been the appropriate proceeding in order to satisfy the debts of the petitioner-Bank.</u>

<u>20. Dr. Zahir has referred to the case of Bengal Luxmi Cotton Mills Ltd. and others Vs. Mahaluxmi Cotton Mills Ltd. and others, reported in AIR 1955 (Cal) 273 in order to support his contention that when a bonafide dispute over the claim is made by the company, winding up proceeding on such bonafide dispute of claim is not an appropriate legal proceeding. In that case similar question arose and a Division Bench consisting of Chakravartti CJ and SR Das Gupta J, after discussing the matter in details, observed as follows:</u>

<u>"(4) The case cited does not support the whole contention of the learned Advocate-General. As the decision was relied on as having modified the statement of law, as contained in Buckley, it will be convenient to read the statement at the present stage. It runs as follows:</u>

<u>"A winding up petition is not legitimate means of seeking to enforce payment of a debt which is 'bonafide' disputed by the company. A petition presented ostensibly for a winding-up order but really to exercise pressure will be dis-missed and under circumstances may be stigmatized as a scandalous abuse of the process of the Court. Some years ago petitions founded on disputed debt were directed to stand over till the debt was established by action. If, however, there was no reason to believe that the debt, if established, would be paid, the petition was dismissed.</u>

<u>The modern practice has been to dismiss such petitions. But, of course, if the debt is not disputed on some substantial ground, the Court may decide it on the petition and make the order".</u>

<u>(See "Buckley on the Companies Act." Twelfth Ed. P 452).</u>

<u>(5) In the case cited the passage was quoted from the 11th Ed. of Buckley, pp. 356, 357 and in quoting it, the learned Master of the Rules observed that the law and practice in regard to such matters have been stated in the passage "with sufficient accuracy."</u>

<u>(6) In order to appreciate the passage correctly, it may be useful to recall what the position is as to making a winding-up order against a company on the ground of its inability to pay its debts. The basis of such an order is that the company has ceased to be commercially solvent and, accordingly, it is fit and proper in the interest of the creditors and share-holders not to allow it to function further as a company. When there has been a failure to pay a debt in accordance with a statutory notice of demand, insolvency is to be presumed, but it may also be proved in otherwise. The basis of a winding-up order on the ground of company's inability to pay its debts is, however, always insolvency.</u>

<u>(7) Read in the light of that principle, the true meaning of Buckley's summary of the English decisions appears to me to be this; when a company has failed to pay a debt, but it appears that the failure occurred, not because the company was unable to pay, but because it disputed the liability on a substantial ground and there is nothing to show that if the dispute is decided against the company, it will not or will be unable to pay the debt, there is not present proof of insolvency and therefore no sufficient basis for making a winding-up order. In such a case, the winding-up Court will only sec if the grounds on which the liability is disputed are substantial and if the dispute is in that sense bonafide. If it finds the issue in favour of the company, it will ordinarily not proceed further and decide the dispute itself and determine whether or not a debt exists and has become payable.</u>

<u>In such a case, the Court will either dismiss the petition for winding-up or keep it pending till the creditor has established his claim in a regular action. The principle on which the Court will forbear from deciding the dispute and making a winding-up in case it decides it against the company, is that winding-up proceedings are not intended to be exploited as a normal alternative to the ordinary mode of debt-realisation and that it is more convenient that claims should be investigated and decided in a regular action."</u>

21. The principle laid down in the aforesaid judgment, we find, has got application in the facts and circumstances of the present case inasmuch as bonafide dispute over the claim of the petitioner-Bank very much exists in the present case.

<u>22. A limited company is a juristic person created under a statute. It also lives, runs and functions under the provisions of the statute and its death warrant can also be issued under the same statute. In our opinion it is the duty of the Court to save and protect the life of such a person as far as practicable and the death warrant in the form of winding up should be sparingly issued in exceptional circumstances. To the last minute effort must be made to save a company from liquidation.</u>

<u>23. We have gone through the judgment of the learned Company Judge. From the judgment, it appears that his Lordship simply incorporated the alleged claims made by the different creditors. But, unfortunately, he has not considered in details the existing assets and liabilities of the company, the alleged interests claimed and other circumstances and materials to see as to whether the company was actually unable to repay the loan or the debts have been secured. His Lordship has found that the appellant company has no bonafide defence and the debt is not, in fact, disputed as the bank papers filed in this case show that the denial of the debt is not based on any substantial ground. We are unable to persuade our-selves to accept the. above sweeping finding of the learned Company Judge in view of our discussions made above, and as such the judgment impugned in this appeal cannot he sustained in law.</u>

24. In the result, this appeal is allowed and the judgment and order passed by the learned Company Judge on 27.11.86 is hereby set aside. The application of the petitioner-bank under sections 162 and 163 read with section 166 of the Companies Act is hereby rejected. The Liquidator is directed to hand over possession of the factory and all assets and properties to the company including accounts at once.

There will be no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Altaf Hossein, J.—This application under section 115 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and decree dated 16.6.79 passed by the teamed Additional District Judge, Special Court II, Dacca in Title Appeal No. 103 of 1978 affirming the judgment and decree dated 8.5.1978 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dacca in Title suit No. 197 of 1977 of his court.

2. Facts of the case, in brief am as follows: The opposite party No. 1 here as plaintiff filed Title suit No. 197 of 1977 in the 4th Court of the Subordinate Judge Dacca for a declaration that the decree dated 20.9.1972 passed in Title suit No. 35 of 1971 of the 3rd Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dacca in respect of the suit property was void, illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff and also for a declaration that the Kabala obtained through court in execution of the decree of the aforesaid title suit was null and void. The case of the plaintiff was that the suit property along with other properties belonged to 3 brothers Nibaran Chandra Mitra, Abinash Chandra Mitre and Satish Chandra Mitre by purchase. On an amicable partition among the brothers, Abinash Chandra got the suit property and died thereafter leaving behind three sons Santi Priya, Chitta Priya and Snehamoy the present opposite parties 3 to 5 as heirs. The opposite parties 3 to 5 transferred the suit property to plaintiff by a deed of exchange registered on 30.5.63 through their attorney Syed Amir Ali. Opposite party No. 1 filed Title suit No. 35 of 1971 in the 3rd Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dacca against opposite parties 3 to 6 for specific performance of contract in respect of the suit property and got an ex party decree and thereafter by putting the decree in execution got a kabala executed through court. The plaintiff thereafter filed Title suit No. 197 of 1977 for declaration as aforesaid on the allegation that the defendant No. 12 had obtained the decree by fraudulent suppression of processes and has thereafter obtained a kabala through court in execution by practicing fraud upon the court.

3. The suit was contested by the petitioners here who were defendants 2 and 3 in this suit. The defendant No. 2 claimed to purchase from defendant No. 1. Defendant No. 3 is the husband of defeating No. 2. The suit was contested by denying all material allegations of the plaint. The case of the defence was in short that the plaintiff had no title to the suit property as claimed by her and no locus standi to file the suit. It was contended that the deed of exchange on the strength of which the plaintiff claimed title in the suit property was fraudulent and without consideration. It was averred that processes were duly served and they were not suppressed and the ex party decree was obtained in due course of law and the kabala was executed and registered though court in accordance with the law.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the cases of the respective parties and the evidence on record decreed the suit. In appeal, the learned Additional District Judge affirmed the judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge. Being aggrieved the defendants 2 and 3 who were the appellants before the Appellate Court have filed this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

5. Mr. Nizamuddin Haider with Mr. Jane Alam and Mr. A.B.M. Abbasuddin Ahmed, learned Advocates appeared in support of the Rule and Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, Mr. Nurul Huq, Mr. Mahmudul Islam and Mr. Khairul Hoq appeared to oppose the Rule. Mr. M.A, Wahab, Assistant Attorney-General appeared on behalf of the Government of Bangladesh who is opposite-party No. 8.

6. The main grievance of Mr. Haider, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, is that the learned Appellate court as also the learned trial court have failed to give decisions on two issues relating to the title of the plaintiffs in the suit land and her locus standi though evidence was adduced in relation to these issues and that the courts below hay not considered material evidences produced by the defendants in support of their case relating to those issues. He has made other grievances also but in view of the order that we propose to make in the case we do not consider it necessary to state those grievances.

7. It appears from the record of the title suit that on the petition of the defendant. No. 2 filed on 15.6.1977 two additional issues were framed to the following effect, namely :-

"(a) Has the plaintiff her claimed title to the suit property ?

(b) Has the plaintiff locaus standi to file the suit" ?

8. Though the petition was objected to, the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the defendants' prayer for framing of these additional issues. The judgment of the learned trial court, however, shows that these two additional issues were not incorporated in the judgment and there has been no findings on these issues. In appeal, the defendants 2 and 3 appellants agitated the learned appellate court to make findings on these issues and additional evidence was also adduced before the learned appellate court but the judgment of the learned appellate court shows that the learned Appellate Court also did not give his findings on these issues. Order 20, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides as follows.

"5. Court to state its decision on each issue. In suits in which issues have been framed, the court shall state its finding or decision, with the reasons thereof upon each separate issue unless the finding upon any one or more of the issues is sufficient for the decision of the suit".

Failure of the learned trial court to state its finding or decision on these additional issues framed on the prayer of the defendants petitioners is, therefore, a contravention of the provision of rule 5 of Order 20, C.P.C. and is an error. of law apparent on the face of the record. Failure of the learned Appellate Court to consider this defect in the judgment of the trial court which was canvassed before it and its further failure to record fin-dings on these issues even though additional evidence was taken is also an error of law apparent on the face of the record.

9. Confronted with this situation, Mr. B. N. Chowdhury the learned Advocate for the opposite parties has contended that though the learned trial court and the learned appellate court did not take up these issues specifically for decision, they have in fact, decided these issues. We have gone through the judgment of the learned trial court and it appears that he has observed that in the present suit as it has been framed there is no scope for going to the matter relating to the question of title. "We have not been able to appreciate the logic of the trial court when an issue on title had specifically been framed. There was also no scope for the learned Additional District Judge to avoid giving a decision in the matter which he appears to have done. The learned Additional District Judge has observed that in the suit, he was required to see whether the plaintiff had locus-standi to file the suit and by referring practically only to the documents of exchange, he came to the conclusion that the plaintiff had locus-standi. He did not consider the case of the defence that the plaintiff had no properties in Murshidabad with which the properties of the Mitras in Bangladesh were alleged to have been exchanged and the evidence filed on the side of the defence in support of their contention that the plaintiff had no properties at Murshidabad. He has only gone into the matter superficially. This was a suit for declaration that a decree passed against some third parties in a suit in which the plaintiff was not a party was void and without jurisdiction and the locus stated on which the plaintiff relied was that she owned the properties by exchange. Before the plaintiff can he given a declaration under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act she had to prove before the court that she had the legal character or the right to property she claimed and unless the plaintiff could prove such legal character or right to property, she could not be given any declaratory relief. In view of the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, we are of the opinion that since the plaintiff’s entitlement to maintain the suit was based on the ownership of the property she claimed, the question of title of the plaintiff was directly and substantially in issue in the suit and without deciding this issue the plaintiff could not have been given any relief under section 43 of the Specific Relief Act which she prayed for. A decision on the issue of title would also decide her locus steal to file the suit. In the circumstances, the trial court has committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record not only in not incorporating these additional issues framed at the instance of the defendants specifically in the judgment and stating his decision thereon but also in holding that in the suit before him there was no scope to go deep into the matter. It is true that the finding of the trial court that the suit was maintainable without a prayer for declaration of title cannot be found fault with but that does not mean that in a suit of the present nature the question of title cannot be gone into deep and that even on the face of specific issues framed in the suit. It also appears from the appellate judgment that the learned appellate court was of the view that it was not a suit for declaration of title and it was enough if the plaintiff has been able to make out a prima facie case that he has right, title and interest in the disputed property, we find no basis for the proposition that in a suit of the present nature, it was enough if the plaintiff could make out a prima facie case that he has right, title and interest in the suit property. The learned appellate court failed to consider that the learned trial court has failed to state his findings and decision on the additional issues framed and has failed to consider the defence case and the evidence adduced before the trial court as also the additional evidence adduced before him to substantiate the defence case that the deed of exchange was fraudulent and without consideration. We refrain from making any comment on the worth of the evidence that were adduced by the parties in support of the title claimed by the plaintiff or in negativing the title of the plaintiff lest this should prejudice the rehearing which we propose to order in this case. Mr. Chowdhury has contended that the learned appellate court has found that the plaintiff has title in the suit property. We have already observed that the learned appellate Court merely concerned itself in finding a prima facie title and on the face of what the learned appellate court has itself observed on the judgment. Mr. Chowdhury cannot be heard to say that the learned Appellate Court has found title in plaintiff. Mr. Chowdhury could not place before as any decision to prove his alternative contention that a prima facie title in a suit of this nature was, enough.

<u>10. Mr. Chowdhury, has, however, taken up an alternative line of argument. He has contended that when an order is obtained from the court by practicing fraud upon the court the Court has inherent power to vacate that order mom. He has relief upon the case laws reported in 20 DLR (Dacca) 937 (Abel Kalam Rahmatallah vs. Md. Ashique) and A.LR. 1948 Nagpur 52 (Ballabhdas Lachminarayan Mahethwari vs. Sobhaji Kesharesingh and another.) Both these cases relate to the question of the inherent power of the court to set aside a sale held in an execution proceeding on the ground of fraud practiced upon the court. In 20 D.L.R. case, it was held that where auction sale has been procured by practicing fraud on court, the executing court in case like this does not become functus officio even where the auction sale has been confirmed, sale certificate issued and possession delivered, but under its inherent powers under section 151 Court is competent to set aside the sale. The decision of the Nagpur case is also to similar effect. It was held that the practice of fraud on the court is a serious matter and it renders void everything which is founded on such fraud. It is not only within the powers but it is the duty of the court to take notice of such fraud when detected or brought to its notice. The court cannot permit a party guilty of a fraud on the court to enjoy what it has secured thereby. The facts of the two reported decisions are however, of somewhat exceptional nature with which the facts of the present case has no semblance. Besides in the 20 D.L.R. case the court had held that the court had not become focus officio. But so far as the case before as is concerned, we are of the opinion that once the court has passed an ex parte decree, it becomes functus officio and it is beyond the powers of the court to exercise its inherent jurisdiction to set aside the decree on detecting fraud. In such case, the remedy of an aggrieved person lies in the specific provisions of the C.P.C. as, for example, in filing an application under Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C. or an appeal or in a separate suit for setting aside the decree on grounds of fraud, as has in fact been done in this case. The inherent powers of the court. cannot be invoked. We are of the firm opinion that so far as the ex parte decree is concerned the court has no power to vacate it and set it aside even on detection of fraud at a subsequent stage. The next question is whether the order passed in the execution case alleged to be obtained fraudulently is liable to be declared void. Mr. Chowdhury has contended that as required by P.O. 142 of 1972, an affidavit was filed by an officer of the court on the basis of an affidavit filed by defendant No. 1 Wares Ali and Wares An had sworn a false affidavit to the effect that the Mitras were Bangladeshi nationals though it was evident that they are Indian nationals. What has happened in this case is that on the basis of an affidavit which is alleged to be false, the court, it is stated, has directed its officer to swear an affidavit before the Registrar and on the basis of that the Registrar has registered the document. The case has, therefore, traveled far beyond the hands of the Court and the court has no longer any seisin over the matter. If any fraud has been practiced, it has been practiced in the matter of registration and the court obviously exercises no inherent power to set aside and vacate the registration done by the Registrar. Besides, even for getting a declaration that the registration was null and void for contravention of the provision of P.O. 142 of 1972, a party seeking the declaration must prove his legal character or right to property and if this has not been proved, he cannot get a declaration under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. In this view of the matter, even for getting a declaration that the transfer was null and void being hit by the provisions of P.O. 142 of 1972, the plaintiff has to prove her legal character or right to property. The contention of the learned Advocate that the ex parte decree and the sale-document having been brought about by practicing fraud on the court, the court has inherent jurisdiction to set aside the decree as well as the sale is not, therefore, tenable. Forbearance by the courts below to decide issues framed compels us to remand the suit for a rehearing and we are of the opinion that the case should be remanded to the trial court for a rehearing of the suit and for stating its findings and decisions on all issues including the two additional issues framed at the instance of the defendants on 15.6.77.</u>

11. The Rule is, therefore, made absolute. The judgments and decrees of the courts below are set aside ad the suit is sent back on remand to the trial court for a rehearing in accordance with law and in the light of the observations made above on the evidence already on record and on such further evidence as the parties may choose to adduce. The additional evidence adduced before the appellate court may be adduced afresh before the trial court, if the parties so desire. In the circumstances of the case, we make no order as to costs.

Abdul Wadud Chowdhury, J.- I agree.

End.

full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J: This First Miscellaneous Appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 12.9.83 passed by Mr. Anisul Hoque  Choudhury, District Judge, Dhaka in Miscellaneous case No.104 of 1983, arising out of Miscellaneous Appeal No. 248 of 1983.

2. The plaintiff-appellant filed Title Suit No. 363 of 1983 in the 1st Court of Munsif. Dhaka on 6.7.83 for permanent injunction against the respondents. On the same day he filed an application under Order 39, rule I C P C. for temporary injunction till the disposal of the suit as well as an order of ad-interim injunction and status quo. The learned Munsif issued notice upon the respondent No 1. Dhaka Municipal Corporation to show cause why the order of temporary injunction shall not be granted but refused the prayer of ad interim injunction. On 14.7.83 the plaintiff-appellant filed another application for passing an order of temporary injunction or status quo against the defendant No. 1 Dhaka Municipal Corporation but the prayer was rejected on the same date. On 18.7.83 the plaintiff filed a similar application which was also rejected by the learned Munsif on the same day on the ground that the defendants have already appeared and a date has been fixed for filing written objection. So the petition for temporary injunction or status quo cannot be considered at that stage.

3. The plaintiff appellant, it appears, without waiting for the defendants to file their written objection and without waiting for the bearing of the temporary injunction matter, preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 248 of 1083 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka against the order dated 18.7.83 passed by the learned Munsif rejecting the plaintiff's fresh application for an order of temporary injunction or status quo. Mr. Mahmudul Amin Choudhury, the learned District Judge, Dhaka disposed of the said Miscellaneous Appeal after hearing the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 Dhaka Municipal Corporation and by his judgment and order dated 10.8.83 allowed the appeal and directed both the parties to maintain status quo for 2 months from 10 8.83 and the trial Court was directed to dispose of the suit within 2 months from the date of receipt of the records from the Court of the District Judge. The defendants were also directed to file their written statement within 20 days from the date of receipt of the records from the Court of the District Judge.

4. 10 days after passing of the aforesaid order by Mr. Mahmudul Amin Choudhury, District Judge, Dhaka, the defendant No 1 Dhaka Municipal Corporation preferred an application for review under Order 47. rule 1 CPC. of the judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka on 10.8.83 in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 248 of 1983. The application for review was numbered as Misc. Case No 104 of 1983. In the mean. while Mr. Mahmudul Amin Choudhury was transferred from Dhaka and Mr. Choudhury was appointed the District Judge-in-Charge, Dhaka who issued notice upon the plaintiff appellant under Rule 4. Sub-rule (2), proviso (a) of the Order 47 fixing 7.9.83 for hearing of the application for review. The plaintiff-appellant filed a written objection .Against the application for review. The matter was heard subsequently by the learned successor District Judge, Dhaka, namely. Mr. Anisul Hoque Choudhury who by his judgment and order dated 12.9.83 allowed the application for review and dismissed the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 248 of 1983 and affirmed the order of the learned Munsif dated 18.7.83.

5. Thereafter the plaintiff-appellant preferred this First Miscellaneous Appeal against the aforesaid judgment aria order of the learned District Judge, Dhaka dated 12 9.83 passed in Misc. Case No. 104 of 1983.

6. The short facts of the case are that the plaintiff Al-haj Md. Ruhul Amin styling himself tithe General Secretary, Fish, Meat and Vegetable Market Shopkeepers Association (Government Vegetable. Markets filed the aforesaid Suit on the averments inter alia, that the plaintiff-Association is a registered Association bearing the Registration No. E.B. 757 in the year 1953 consisting of 283 members who have got pucca or semi-pucca shops, stalls and establishments in the premises of New Market Kacha Bazar Area, Police Station Dhanmondi, District Dhaka since 1953, The members of the plaintiff Association have been running their business as allottees under the defendant No. 2, the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development. The said defendant No. 2 have been realising rents from the members of the plaintiff. Association regularly. The defendant No. 1 the Dhaka Municipal Corporation issued letters to the members of the plaintiff. Association informing that the said defendant had taken the charge of management and realisation of rents of all Government markets situated in the New Market. The defendant No. 1 asked them to furnish copies of allotment letters, agreements, if any, papers showing transfer of possession, receipts showing last payment of rent and 3 attested copies of passport size photographs of the allottees and also to pay arrear rents to the defendant No. 1. The defendant No. 2 have not informed the members of the plaintiff Association that the Government bad transferred the right of management and realisation of rents to the defendant No. 1. The defendant No. 1 has now taken steps to abruptly demolish the structure of all the shops and establishments of the members of the plaintiff-Association and has invited sealed tenders from contractors for construction of a new project named as Kitchen Market on the site of the allotted shops of the members of the plaintiff-Association the plaintiff contended that the defendant No. 1 has no right to demolish the existing structures belonging to the Government without providing them with alternative arrangement for running their shops and establishments and without giving them allotments in the proposed new building. The plaintiff prayed for a decree of permanent injunction against the defendants restraining them permanently from demolishing the pucca and semi-pucca shops and establishments of the members of the plaintiff-Association lying and situated in the Fish, Meat, Vegetable Government New Market, Dhaka and from removing the plaintiff- association and its members from the said Market. The application for temporary injunction was also to the same effect.

7. As already stated the defendant-respondents were given time by the learned Munsif to file written objection against the plaintiff's prayer for temporary injunction. but before they had any opportunity to file any written objection the plaintiff filed 2 successive fresh application for temporary injunction and status quo, and when the last such application was rejected on 18.7.81 on the ground that the defendants has already appeared and a date has been fixed for filing written objection, the plaintiff did not wait for the hearing of the temporary injunction matter in the Court of the learned Munsif and preferred an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 248 of 1983 before the then learned District Judge, Dhaka Mr. Mahmudul Amin Chowdhury. It is in the said Court of the learned District Judge, Dhaka that the defendant No. I Dhaka Municipal Corporation got the first opportunity to tile a written objection against the plaintiff's prayer for temporary injunction and status quo. The Municipal Corporation specifically stated in Paragraph 5 of its written objection that the application for temporary injunction is barred by Martial Law Order No 40 of 1982. The defendant No. 1 also stated as per order of the Chief Martial Law Administrator contained in his Memorandum No. 7002/4-CIV-I dated 8.7.82 all Government markets were handed over to the defendant No. 1 Dhaka Municipal Corporation which order was subsequently endorsed by the Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development. The Dhaka Municipal Corporation took over possession of those markets from the Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development on 6.2.82. and 13.2.82. While transferring the Government New Market as also other markets of the Dhaka City to the Dhaka Municipal Corporation the Government properly demarcated the transferred area in a site plan and also furnished a list of allottees with outstanding arraignments in respect of each shop of all the markets including the Government New Market. The members of the plaintiff-Association were merely licencees for a specified period the terms of which had long ago expired and the said licences had not been renewed. The Dhaka Municipal Corporation took the stand that the members of the plaintiff Association are no longer allottees under the Government as the entire New Market complex had been transferred to the Dhaka Municipal Corporation and as the said Corporation had been realising rents for the shops and stalls since 1.7.87. As per direction of the Chief Martial Law Administrator the Dhaka Municipal Corporation has undertaken a massive plan for constructing a multistoried modern Fish. Meat and Vegetable Market by demolishing the existing 2 kacha tin sheds out of 7 tin sheds and the Meat and Fish block. For that purpose the shopkeepers of these blocks were invited to a discussion in the matter. They gladly accepted the plan of the Municipal Corporation and expressed a desire to get an assurance that after the construction of the proposed multistoried market they would be provided with shops therein. They also assured that they would shift their business temporarily is the alternative site provided by the Municipal Corporation in the New Market complex. Accordingly the Corporation issued a letter dated 21.7.83 to all the shopkeepers individually numbering 117 to temporarily shift their shops to a place shown to them within the vicinity of the New Market Complex which is very close to the remaining 5 tin sheds presently not affected by the development plan. They were further intimated by the same letter that they would be provided with shops in the proposed market building after its construction. In Martial Law Order 40 of 1982 "any corporation" is disjunctive from "'other body or authority". Since any corporation also includes a Corporation established by or under any law, I hold that the Martial Law Order No. 40 of 1982 applies to a development plan undertaken by the respondent-Dhaka Municipal Corporation.</u>
