22. Having thus found that the respondent Corporation had some grounds for being aggrieved by the judgment and order of the learned predecessor District Judge, there now remains the question as to whether the respondent-Corporation has chosen the right procedure and the right forum for redress of their grievance.

Order 47, rules 1 and 2 C.P.C. provide as follows:-

"1. (1) Any person considering himself aggrieved—

(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is allowed, but from which no appeal has been preferred.

(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is allowed, or

(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of Small Causes, and who, from the discovery of new and important matter or evidence which, after the exercise of due diligence, was not within his knowledge or could not be produced by him at the time when, the decree was passed or order made, or on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, or for any other sufficient reason desires to obtain a review of the decree passed or order made against him, may apply for a review of judgment to the Court which passed the decree or made the order.

(2)....................

2. An application for review of a decree or order of a Court, not being a (the High Court Division). upon some ground other than the discovery of such new and important matter or evidence as is referred to in rule 1 or the existence of a clerical or arithmetical mistake or error apparent on the face of the decree, shall be made only to the Judge who passed the decree or made the order sought to be reviewed: but any such application may, if the Judge who passed the decree or made the order has ordered notice to issue under rule 4, sub-rule (2), proviso (a), be disposed of by his successor."

<u>23. It is well settled that the right of review of a judgment is a substantive right and the scope, extent, manner and forum of review are circumscribed by the provisions of the statute which confer on the litigants the right of review. If one forgets for the moment the existence of Order 47, rule 2, it will be obvious from a reading of Order 47, rule 1 that the right of review has been conceded on some limited grounds and the broad forum for review of a judgment lies "to the Court which passed a decree or made the order". If the legislature has stopped there, and had not provided for rule 2, it would have been easy to conclude that the forum for review of a judgment would be the Court which passed the decree or made the order, irrespective of whether the Judge who passed the decree or made the order or his successor entertained the review. As a matter of fact India has omitted Order 43, rule 2 by the Civil Procedure Code (Amendment Act, 1956 and the position in India today after the omission of rule 2 is that a review lies before the Court which passed the decree or made the order on any of the grounds mentioned in rule 1. It does not matter any more in India whether the Judge who entertained the review is the original Judge or the successor Judge.</u>

<u>24. Rule 2 however has qualified the application of rule I as far as the ground and forum for review are concerned If the ground for review is the discovery of such new and important matter or evidence as is referred to in rule 1 or the existence of a clerical or arithmetical mistake or error apparent on the face of the decree, then the review will lie to the Judge who passed the decree or made the order as well as to his successor in office. Review on these grounds are entertainable and disposable by the Court which passed the decree or made the order. The presence or absence of the original Judge who passed the decree or made the order is immaterial. But if an application for review of a decree or order is made on any other ground, then rule provides that the said application "shall he made only to the Judge who passed the decree or made the order sought to be reviewed." So it is the ground of review which makes all the difference in the forum for review. If however, the Judge who passed the decree or made the order has ordered notice to issue under rule 1, sub-rule (2) proviso (a), the application for review may be disposed of by his successor.</u>

<u>25. The difference between rules 1 and 2 is obvious on more than one point. Whereas the ground for review mentioned in rule I may be, among others, "error apparent on the face of the record," "the ground for review in rule 2 may he among others 4'the existence of a clerical or arithmetical mistake or error apparent on the face of the decree " "Record" is a wider term than "decree." Record" include; judgment, decree, pleadings, evidence, exhibits, but "decree" means precisely that which is defined in section 2(2) C.P.C. Again "error apparent on the face of the record" is a much wider term than the words "clerical or arithmetical mistake or error apparent on the face of the decree." Whereas in Rule 1 the application for review can be made "to the Court which passed the decree or made the order", in rule 2 except on the grounds stated in the rule itself, the application for review shall he made only to the judge who passed the decree or made the order sought to he reviewed."</u>

26. Order 47 rules 1 and 2 have existed in the Statute Book since 1908 and in the same form in the earlier Civil Procedure Codes as well. During nearly 75 years of its existence rule 2 has been noticed in the various jurisdictions of this Subcontinent. I am informed by both sides, however, that there is no decision on rule 2 in our superior Courts. At one stage I asked the learned Additional Attorney General and the learned Advocate for the appellant to give their opinion as to whether it would be adviseable to refer this matter to the learned Chief Justice for constitution of a larger Bench in order to decide more authoritatively whether a successor Judge can review the Judgment of the predecessor judge on the ground of an error of law apparent on the face of the judgment. As the learned Additional Attorney General expressed his anxiety in favour of disposal of this matter as expeditiously as possible. I refrain from taking dim course and am proceeding to dispose of the point in the light of arguments advanced from the Bar.

27. Order 47, rules 1 and 2 are reproductions of sections 623 and 624 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1882. Section 623 was identical to Order 47, rule 1 and Section 624 was identical to Order 47, rule 2. As early as on April 17 18S5 it was held in the case of Sarangapani Vs. Narayanasarni. ILR 8 (Mad) 567, by a Division Bench of the Madras High Court that section 624 of the Civil Procedure Code 1882 must be read as a proviso to section 623. Therefore, when a Court had been abolished and its business transferred to a Court presided over by an another judge, such judge should not entertain an application for review of judgment except in the case. provided for by section 624. The necessity of keeping the forum for review in tact in terms of the grounds of review, was therefore a long felt necessity.

However, that is past history. As far as the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 is concerned, there are no dearth of decisions all over the sub-continent as to what is the true import and meaning of rule 2. To proceed chronologically.

28. In the case of Baliram Piraji Dearao Vs. Yeshwanta M. G Mt. Tulshi, AIR 1924 (Nagpur. 190, a single Bench of the Nagpur High Court held that if there is a mistake or error apparent on the face of the "record" such as is referred to in Order 47, rule 1, the application for review cannot he entertained by the successor judge. As the present case is not of a clerical mistake apparent on the face of the decree referred to in Order 47, rule 2, the successor judge had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for review. It is to be noticed that the very entertainment of a review not covered by the grounds in Rule 2 affects the jurisdiction itself. It is not a mere matter of procedure.

29 In the case of Thommil Pudia Malikal Kathyumma Vs. Thommil Pudia Malikkal Muhammad Kutty and others, A.1 R. 1926 (Madras) 1083, a learned Single Judge of the Madras High Court held that in terms of Rule 2 review petition on the ground of an accidental slip it entertainable before the successor of the judge who disposed of the case. This decision has been cited by Mr. Mahmudul Islam to show that the forum for review is not an incidental provision inserted in rule 2 but a provision of such importance that the superior Courts of nearly all jurisdictions in the sub-continent have laid great emphasis on it.

30. In the case of Maulvi Abdul Jabbar Palwan Vs. Azizur Azizur Rahman Mea, A.l.R. 1937 (Cal.), Nasim Ali, J. delivering the judgment of a Division Bench case observed as follows "The ground for review is this: that at the time when the order sought to be reviewed was made, the District Judge, the pleaders of the parties, as well as the parties themselves, were not aware of the existence of s. 12, Act of 1920; on account of this ignorance of law the decree. holder's application was not entertained by the District Judge and consequently this is an error of law apparent on the face of the record. R. 2, O. 47 lays down that an application for review upon some ground other than the existence of a clerical or arithmetical mistake apparent on the face of the record, shall be made only to the judge who made the order. If the mistake is clerical or arithmetical the application can be made to his successor. The application for review by the decree-bolder on the ground that there is mistake of law on the face of the record could not therefore be entertained by the successor of the judge who made the order. The application for review must therefore be rejected as not maintainable in law."

31. In the case of Kaluram Ramchandra Vs Nandalal Gulapchand, AI R. 1949 (Nagpur) 298 it was observed as follows :—

"(8) This is a ground on which review is permitted by O. 47, r. 1 Civil P.C. . That rule sets out other grounds also on which an application for review of judgment or order could be made and it lays down that review application must be made to the Court which passed the decree or made the order. This means that review application lies to the same Court and not to any other Court even though it may be a Court of concurrent or higher jurisdiction or an appellate or revisional Court. At the time when the application for review comes to be made the Presiding Judge of the Court may be the same Judge who passed the decree or order or there may be his successor Rule 2 of Or. 47 therefore provides whether or not the successor of the Judge, though in the same Court, can entertain review application. Rule 2 has thus to be read as a proviso to R. 1. According to R. 2, if the application for review is on one of these grounds, namely, (1) discovery of a new and important matter or evidence as is referred to in R. 1 or (ii) the existence of a clerical or arithmetical mistake or error apparent on the face of the decree, it may be made to the successor of the judge but an application for review on any grounds other than these two, on which an application would be permissible by R. 1 must be made to the Judge who passed the decree or order and cannot be made to his successor. (9) In the present the review is sought on the ground of mistake or error on the face of the record and not on the ground of a clerical or arithmetical mistake or error on the face of the decree. Therefore, according to R. 2 of Or. 47, the application should have been made to the Judge, Shree Chiplonkar, who made the decree."

32. In the case of Ramdayal Vs. Kailshi, A.I R. 1950 (Allahabad) 160 Malik, C.J. in a Division Bench case observes as follows :-

"The only ground for review which was pressed before the lower Court was that the Judge whose decree was sought to be reviewed bad not taken into consideration a document which was already on the record. The allegation that a Judge did not take into consideration a piece of evidence which was on the record cannot be said to be a "clerical or arithmetical mistake or error apparent on the face of the decree" In R. 1(1) of Or. 47 Civil P.C., the words used are "some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record" while in R. 2 the words used are "clerical or arithmetical mistake or error apparent on face of the decree".  Instead of the words. 'on the face of the record in sub-rule (1) of rule 1 of Or.47, the words in r. 2 of Or.47 are 'on are the face of the decree. We cannot assume that the legislature used the words in two rules in the same sense. The word 'decree' is defined in the Code and it means "the formal expression of adjudication which, so far as regards the Court expressing it conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit and may be either preliminary or final", while the word, 'judgment', has been defined as 'the statement given by the Judge of the grounds of a decree or order.' The word, 'record' in rule 1 or Order 47, Civil P,C., would clearly include the judgment, the decree and the other papers on the record, while the word 'decree' in R. 7, cannot include the judgment or the other papers on the record."

<u>33. It is therefore well settled that except for discovery of new and important matter or evidence as is referred to in rule 1 or the existence of a clerical or arithmetical mistake or error apparent on the face of the decree an application for review can only be made to the judge who passed the decree or made the order sought to be reviewed. Mr. Mahmudul Islam submits that in the present case the predecessor District Judge has passed no decree and therefore there can be no question of existence of a clerical or arithmetical mistake or error apparent on the face of the Decree. If the predecessor District Judge had made an error apparent on the face of the judgment, as the respondent-Corporation claims, then in terms of rule 2 the application for review could only have been preferred before him and him only. If the predecessor District Judge bad at least issued the notice, then the successor District Judge could have disposed of the review application. But the notice in the present case was issued by the District Judge-in-Charge.</u>

34. The learned Additional Attorney Qeneral submits that the successor Judge can entertain application for review if there is an error apparent on the face of the decree not only for a clerical or arithmetical mistake but also for an error of law apparent on the face of the decree. He has submitted the case of Ram Baksh Vs. Mt. Rafeswari Kunwar. A 1.R. 1948 (Allahabad) 213, a Division Bench decision, in support of his contention. The short facts of the case are that a Civil suit was filed by the respondent for a declaration that the order of the District Judge directing a refund of the decretal amount deposited was illegal and without jurisdiction. The suit was dismissed but ultimately in a Letters Patent Appeal the High Court observed that no declaration of the type sought for could be given and further observed that the order of the District Judge directing a refund of the decretal amount was manifestly wrong and the proper remedy against it was to apply for a review petition explaining the delay. In the meantime the District Judge who passed the original order of refund of the decretal amount was transferred and a new District Judge held the office. The Reviewing Judge allowed the application. It was contended before the High Court that there was an error, if any, of law on the face of the decree and therefore such an error is not an error contemplated by either rule 1 or rule 2 of Order 47. It was held that the error committed by the predecessor Judge was an error of law apparent on the face of the decree and it is reviewable under Order 47, rule 2 by the successor Judge.

<u>35. I fail to see how this case helps the learned Additional Attorney General. The order of the predecessor District Judge directing a refund of the decretal amount was a part of the decree passed by him. Whether an error of law or a mere clerical or arithmetical error apparent on the face of the decree can be reviewed by the successor Judge is not the point in issue in the present case. No decree has been passed by the predecessor District Judge in the present case. The point in the issue in the present case is whether a successor judge can review an error of law apparent on the face of the judgment passed by his predecessor.</u>

36. The next case relied upon by the learned Additional Attorney General is the case of Vasant Jaiwantrao Mahajan Vs. Tukaram Mohadaji Patil, AIR 1960 (Bom) 485 It has been held in this case that where a relevant provision of law this instance Order 9. rule 13 Proviso 1 as not been considered at the time of passing an order, such an order can be reviewed, if necessary, by the Judge who passes that order or by his successor But as already stated rule 2 of Order 47 has been omitted in 1950 in India. A judge who passes a decree or makes an order can himself or his successor may review the decree or order on the grounds stated in Order 47, rule 1 in India after the said amendment. This case therefore, is no authority for the proposition that the successor Judge can review the judgment of his predecessor Judge if there is an error of law apparent on the face of the judgment.

37. The learned Additional Attorney General has next contended that if the successor Judge issues the notice under rule 4, sub rule (2), proviso (a), and if thereafter he disposes of the review petition, then that is a substantial compliance of rule 2. He argues that in rule 2 the successor Judge suffers from no disability in disposing of an application for review if the Judge who passed the decree or made the order has ordered notice to issue under rule 4, sub-rule (2), Proviso (a). It is his contention that once the predecessor Judge issues the notice of review to the opposite party, his role is practically over and the successor Judge can review the decree or order on any of the grounds specified in Order 47, rule I. From this, the learned Additional Attorney General submits that if the predecessor Judge cannot issue the notice under rule 4, sub-rule (2), Proviso (a) for any reason then that is a mere irregularity. If his successor in office issues the notice and disposes of the review application then that is substantial compliance with the provisions of Rule 2.

38. It is very difficult to sustain the contention of the learned Additional Attorney General. If the successor Judge can issue the notice and dispose of the application for review g, on grounds not covered by rule 2, then Rule 2 becomes completely nugatory. This rule will practically be obliterated from the statute hook if such interpretation is accepted. Moreover, the submission of the learned Additional Attorney General is against the weight of authority. In the case of Shamser Ali Vs. Jagannath and others, 17 C W.N. 103, an application for review of an order of a District Judge upon a ground other than the discovery of new or important matter or evidence or the existence of a clerical or arithmetical error on the face' of the decree was, owing to the absence of the District Judge, received by the Subordinate Judge who registered it and directed notices to issue to the opposite party. Later on, the District Judge returned and various orders relating to the postponement of the review application and analogous matters were passed by him. Be-fore the application could be heard on merits the District Judge unfortunately died. His successor took up the matter and allowed the application for review. It was held that the order allowing the review was in contravention of rule 2 of Order 47 and should be set aside. This was a decision of a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court comprised of Mookerjee, J. and Beachcroft, J Their Lordships held as follows:—

"It has been argued on behalf of the respondent that as the Judge was absent from the. District, it was competent to the Subordinate Judge, who was in charge of the duties of his office, to receive the application and issue notice thereupon under r. 4. sub. r. 2, proviso (a) of Or. 47. This contention is clearly unfounded. The policy of the Legislature is that, in matters of this description, the application shod be received and considered by the Judge who made the original order. It was never intended that the application should be considered by his successor or by some person in charge of the duties of his office. If this view were not accepted, the result would be that practically an appeal would be beard- against the original order by the successor in office of the Judge who passed the order."

39. In the instant case the predecessor District Judge was transferred and the application for review was filed before the District Judge-in-Charge. He issued notice to the plaintiff opposite party under rule 4, sub-rule (2), proviso (a) of Order 47. After the appointment of a regular District Judge, the successor District Judge disposed of the application for review on a ground which is not covered by rule 2 of Order 47. I hold therefore that the successor District Judge acted without jurisdiction in disposing of the application for review.

<u>40. The learned Additional Attorney General however has advanced another argument which is not to be found in any of the decisions earlier dealt with. He submits that if an application for review is disposed of by a successor Judge on the grounds not allowable under Rule 2, no consequence has been provided for in Rule 2 itself. As no consequence has been provided for Rule 2 should be construed to be merely directory in nature and not mandatory at all. He submits that it is a settled proposition of law that when the legislature does not provide for any adverse consequence for non-fulfillment of a provision of law then that provision has always been regarded as directory and not mandatory. He has cited the cases of Montreal Street Railway Co. Vs. Normandin, 1917 A.C. 170 t P.C.) , Biswanath Khemka Vs. Emperor, A.I. R. 1945 (F.C. 67. State of U.P. Vs. Manbodhan Lal Srivastava, A.I R. 1957 (SC.) 912 and the case of Mozammel Haque Vs. the State, B.C.R. 1983 (H.C.D.), to which I was a party, in support of his contention. The cases cited by the learned Additional Attorney General do not seem to have any relevance to the matter under consideration. The question whether a certain provision in a statute imposing a duty on a public body or authority is mandatory or directory is not the issue before this Court. That was the issue before the Courts in the decisions cited by the learned Additional Attorney General. In the long line of decisions cited above it has been made abundantly clear that if an application for review not covered by the grounds mentioned in rule 2 is disposed of by the successor Judge then the assumption of jurisdiction by the successor Judge is illegal. The consequence of an illegal assumption of jurisdiction need not be spelt out in black and white in a statute.</u>

<u>The decision will fail for want of jurisdiction. It is as simple as that. In the result the appeals allowed but without any order as to costs. The judgment and order of the reviewing Judge in Miscellaneous Case No. 104 of 1983 is set aside.</u>

<u>41. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant has filed an application under section 151 C.P.C. stating that the predecessor District Judge had passed an order of status quo to be effective for only 2 months from 10.8.83 which will expire on 10.10.83, i.e , within 11 days. He had also directed the learned Munsif to dispose of the main suit within 2 months from the late of receipt of the record from his Court. If both these time-limits are not extended in the interest of justice, the plaintiff-appellant will be seriously prejudiced and will Suffer irreparable loss and injury. He has also submitted that the suit could not be disposed of owing to no fault or latches of the plaintiff, but because some time was consumed in the disposal of the review petition, and the present First Miscellaneous Appeal.</u>

42. The learned Additional Attorney General has strongly opposed this prayer on the simple ground that the respondent Corporation urgently needs the completion of the development plan that it has undertaken. He also submits that the plaintiff-appellant has not preferred any appeal or has not submitted any application in any other forum for extension of time. Therefore any prayers now for extension of time is incompetent.

<u>43. Martial Law Order No. 40 of 1982 is an existing law on injunction and no Colin can ignore it. But it must also be remembered that in Clause 4 (1) of the schedule added at the end of the Proclamation of the 24th March, 1982 by Proclamation Order No. 1 of 1982, dated 11.4.82, it has been provided that the High Court Division of the Supreme Court shall have such jurisdiction as is or may be conferred on it by law. This schedule is as much a part of the Martial Law of the country as the Martial Law Order No. 40 of 1982. Under sec. 3 of Civil Procedure Code, which confers jurisdiction on the High Court Division, the District Court is subordinate to the High Court Division. If the High Court Division finds that the Court of Munsif could not execute the order of the District Judge owing to factors beyond its control it becomes an unavoidable duty on the part of the High Court Division, exercising jurisdiction in accordance with law over the District Court, to help it execute the orders of its higher Court. Therefore simply on the ground, and not on any other ground whatsoever, that the learned Munsif could not carry out the order of the learned District Judge for reasons beyond his control, I direct that the order of status quo be extended to one month and 20 days further from 10.10.83. This direction however will take effect from 10.10.83 but shall not take effect if any Court higher than the District Judge, Dhaka grants a stay of operation of the judgment and order of the predecessor District Judge in the meantime or thereafter. The learned Munsif is directed to dispose of the suit within the extended period. Let the records be sent back immediately by special messenger.</u>

End.

Civil Revision No. 4000 of 1991 (Dhaka)
Civil Revision No. 46 of 1990 (Sylhet) and Civil Order No. 851 of 1989
lawyer:
Mr. AKM Faiz, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner 
Mr. Azizur Rahman Chowdhury with Mr. Md. Abdul Mannan, Advocates ----- For Opposite Party No.1
parties:
Altaf Ahmed ----- Petitioner
Vs
Moinuddin Zaigirdar and another ----- Opposite Partes
full_judgment:
Bimalendu Bikash Roy Chowdhury, J: This Rule is directed against an order of the executing court refusing to stay further proceedings for execution of a decree for eviction of a monthly tenant from certain shop premises. The prayer for stay was made by the petitioner on the ground that the decree under execution had been challenged in a suit before the senior Assistant Judge, Sylhet, Regard being had to the facts of the case the executing court took a view that it was no longer open to the petitioner to ask for stay of the execution proceedings. In order to determine the correctness of the view it will be necessary to make a brief statement of facts.

2. One Taib Ali, who happens to be the father of the petitioner, was a monthly tenant in the said shop premises under the opposite party. In 1973 the opposite party as plaintiff brought a suit being Title Suit No. 140 of 1973 in the court of the Munsif, Sadar, Sylhet for eviction of the monthly tenant from the premises. Taib Ali contested the suit, but it was decreed by the trial Court. The decree was, however, set aside in appeal. On further appeal to the High Court Division the appellate decree was set aside and the Judgment and the decree of the trial Court was restored. Taib Ali then prayed for special leave to appeal to the Appellate Division which was refused on 28.5.89.

<u>3. In the meantime the decree holder opposite party put the decree into execution in Title Execution No. 2 of 1989 in the court of Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Sylhet. The present petitioner filed an application before the executing court on 10.6.89 praying for stay of further proceeding of the Execution Case till the hearing or Title Suit No. 174 of 1989 filed by him in the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sylhet on or about 4.6.89. It was claimed in suit that he purchased the disputed property on 30.5.89 from some of its owners. and a decree in Title Suit No. 140 of 1973 was not binding on him. The prayer for stay was opposed by the decree holder on the plea that the petitioner had been set up by the Judgment-debtor, only to deprive the decree holder of the fruits of his decree. The executing court after a hearing rejected the prayer of the petitioner on 28.8.89. The unsuccessful petitioner then preferred a revisional application before a vacation Bench of the High Court Division at Sylhet and obtained an order dated 11.10.89 in Civil Order No. 851 of 1959, staying further proceeding of the execution case till the hearing of the substantive revisional application after the re-opening. The decree holder, however, made a prayer for vacating the said stay order and a Single Bench of this Court, by an order dated 21.3.90, allowed the prayer on the following view:</u>

<u>"It is submitted by Mr. Azizur Rahman Chowdhury, the learned Advocate on behalf of the opposite party that although the opposite party got the decree for eviction of the tenant as far back in 1976 and the decree for eviction was affirmed by this court, The decree holder opposite party has been deprived of the fruits of the litigation at the instance of the 3rd party being the son of the judgment-debtor.</u>

<u>Since the petitioner took no step for hearing of the revisional application and instead obtained an order of stay of the execution case without moving the revisional application, the order of stay granted by this court should be vacated. In that view of the matter the order of stay of the execution of Title Execution Case No.2 of 1989 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Sylhet granted by this court on 11. 10 89 and subsequently extended is hereby vacated."</u>

<u>The petitioner thereafter made no effort to get the revisional application heard. He filed a fresh petition before the executing court and renewed his prayer for stay of the execution proceeding. By the impugned order dated 15.5.90 the executing court rejected the said application on the view that it was no longer open to the petitioner to maintain a fresh application for stay on the self-same facts. In my opinion the order suffers from no error of law for the following reasons: Firstly, the petitioner being a third party to the decree has no locus standito maintain an application for stay of the execution proceeding, and secondly, the facts of the case do not also warrant an exercise of the discretionary power of the Court to make an order of stay.</u>

4. The Rule is, accordingly, discharged. Regard being had to the facts of the case I, however direct the petitioner to pay a sum of Taka 510.00 as costs to the opposite party.

Civil Order No. 851 of 1989 I find no merit in this application which is, accordingly, summarily rejected.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the order dated 10.12.84 passed by the Additional District Judge 2nd Court, Dhaka in Misc. Appeal No. 154 of 1984 allowing the appeal ex parte and setting aside the order of dismissal dated 4.1.84 passed in Misc. Case No. 9 of 1983 and also setting aside the decree dated 20.1.83 passed in Title Suit No. 290 of 1980, 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka and restoring the title Suit to its file and number would not be set aside.

2. The defendant opposite party No. 1 filed an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside decree dated 20.1.83 passed in Title Suit No. 290 of 1980 of the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge Dhaka. In the suit the defendant opposite party No. 1 entered appearance on getting summons and filed written statement but ultimately refrained from contesting the suit as a result the suit was decreed ex parte on 20.1.83. The application filed by the defendant No. 1 having been entertained the opposite party No. 1 was required to issue notice upon the opposite party Nos. 3 and 4 by post and for the same to be put in postal requisites on 11.12.83. The opposite party No. 1 having not complied with the said order 4.1.84 was fixed for putting in the postal requisites as a last chance. On 4.1.84 the defendant opposite party No. 1 having failed to put in the postal requisite in compliance of the Court's order, the Misc. Case No. 9 of 1983 was dismissed for default. Against the said order dated 4.1.84 passed in the said Misc. Case, the opposite party No. 1 preferred appeal before the learned District Judge. Dhaka which was submitted as Miscellaneous Appeal No. 154 of 1984. The said appeal was allowed by the learned District Judge ex parte in the absence of the petitioner and the order of dismissal dated 4.1.84 passed in Misc. Case No. 9 of 1983 was set aside and simultaneously the ex pane decree passed in Title Suit No. 290 of 1980 was also set aside and the suit was restored to its file and number. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and order the petitioner obtained the instant rule.

3. It is submitted that the summons were fraudulently suppressed and it was shown to have been served on the defendant petitioner collusively and the opposite party No. 1 managed to obtain the ex parte judgment and order on 10.12.84 in the appeal to the detriment of the petitioner.

4. Mr. Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the appeal was not maintainable in the form and manner it was filed, that no appeal lies as the application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was dismissed for default at a very earlier stage for non-filing of the requisite and not at the stage when it was ready for hearing and in that view of the matter the learned appellate Court committed an error of law in his decision in allowing the same which has occasioned a failure of justice and for that matter the judgment and order is required to be set aside. By way of elucidating the point the learned Advocate submits that the appeal having been dismissed for default for non-filing of the postal costs at the stage when the case was not ready for hearing the order of dismissal should be deemed to be an order under Order 9 rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure and as such not appealable and therefore learned court should have dismissed the appeal on the ground of maintainability."

5. Mr. SB Berua, appearing for the opposite party No. 1, submits that the order having been passed by the court-in the Misc. Case on an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure the provision of Order 9 rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure has no manner of application in the case. The language of Order 9 rule 2 runs as follows:

"Where on the day so fixed it is found that the summons has not been served upon the defendant in consequence of the failure of the plaintiff to pay the court-fee or postal charges (if any) chargeable for such service, the Court may make an order that the suit be dismissed:

Provided that no such order shall be made although the summon has not been served upon the defendant, if on the day fixed for him to appear and answer he attends in person or by agent when he is allowed to appear by agent."

6. It is agreed on behalf of the petitioner that the provision which is applicable in respect of the suits as mentioned in the rule also applies in respect of proceeding according to section 141 of the Code. The argument of the learned Advocate is of no sub-stance as the procedure laid down in Order 9 rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure specifically mentions about the suits.

7. The next point Mr. Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits is that Order 43 rule 1(d) provides for an appeal against the judgment and order passed in such a proceeding which is contested, or at least in a matter which is ripe for hearing, and not in respect of an order which is passed at the initial stage as was done in the present case. Mr. Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed further submits that there is a difference between an order of dismissal passed for non-filing of the requisite at an early stage and the order passed at a later stage and therefore, dismissal of a case at an early stage of the proceeding for non-filing of the requisite remedy by way of appeal is not available.

<u>8. It is contended by Mr. SB Barua, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1 that an order of dismissal for default under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure is appealable under Order 43 rule 1(d) of the Code no matter whether the order is passed at the earlier or later stage. In the case of Abdul Majid Talukder Vs. Abdur Rob Talukder reported in 32 DLR page 57 the following principle is laid down:</u>

<u>"The expression 'rejected' is wide enough to include a dismissal for default under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Accordingly, such an order is appealable". It is further held:</u>

<u>"The distinction sought to be made between the word 'rejected' and the order 'dismissed' appears to be a distinction without a difference. The words 'rejected', 'struck of', 'closed', 'recorded' and 'dismissed' have similar import, but differently used with reference to the facts and circumstances of each case and there is no distinction between them in substance".</u>

<u>9. In the case of Md. Hashim Khan Vs. Major Fazal Elahi Khan reported in PLD 1959 Quetta I. a distinction to the general rule was sought to be made by a single judge who held:</u>

<u>"The word 'rejected' implies an order on merits while the word 'dismissed' implies an order passed not on merits, but on account of non-appearance of a party."</u>

<u>10. This distinction which was sought to be made in the above noted case has been resolved in a number of cases of this court. The principle laid down by Ibrahim, J in the case of Abdur Rahman Maji and another Vs. Abdul Wadud Mia and another reported in 2 PLD (Dacca) 287 has been consistently followed in many cases and also in the case of Abdul Majid Talukder Vs. Abdur Rob Talukder reported in 32 DLR page 57 wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>"We are in respectful agreement with the opinion of Ibrahim, J. in the case of Abdur Rahman Maji (Supra) In our view, a defaulter whose application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been dismissed for default has a lawful remedy in an appeal under Order 43 rule 1(d). The expression 'rejected' is wide enough to include a dismissal for default under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Accordingly, we hold that such an order is appealable".</u>

<u>11. Since the statute provides remedy to the aggrieved person against whom application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been dismissed for default, whatever might be the stage of passing the order in the Miscellaneous Case I am quite in agreement with the decisions quoted above and find that the appeal arising out of the order of dismissal of the proceeding under Order 9 rule 13 Code of Civil Procedure is maintainable.</u>

12. Mr. Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, next submits that the Misc. Case having been dismissed for default on 4.1.84 for not filing the requisites, the case was not ready and as such in the appeal the Miscellaneous Case could not have been disposed of on merit and in that view of the matter, the learned court committed an error of law in his decision in setting aside the ex parse decree dated 20.1.83 passed in Title Suit No. 290 of 1980 while disposing up the appeal and thus has exceeded his jurisdiction vested in him.

13. From the facts stated in the judgment of the court below it is found that the notice issued upon opposite party No. 2 and 2(a) was awaiting report and before the submission of the same the order of dismissal of the misc. case was passed by the Subordinate Judge for non-filing of the requisite.

<u>14. The learned Subordinate Judge having passed the order dismissing the Misc. Case at the stage while the case was not ready for hearing as regard service it is held that the learned Court of appeal below committed an error of law in setting aside the order of the Subordinate Judge passed on 4.1.84 in the Misc. Case. Now it is to be seen whether the Court of appeal below was justified in setting aside the ex parte decree passed on 21.1.83 in Title Suit No. 290 of 1980 while setting aside the order of dismissal passed in Miscellaneous Case. As the Misc. Case No. 9 of 1983 was dismissed for non-filing of requisites without entering into the merits as to whether the defendant failed to appear and contest the suit after receipt of the summons in the suit or the defendant was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing and contesting the suit the appellate Court below committed error of law and exceeded his jurisdiction in setting aside the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 290 of 1980 and in that view of the matter the order of setting aside the ex parte decree and restoration of the Title Suit No. 290 of 1980 to its original file can not be sustained.</u>

<u>15. In the result, the rule is made absolute. The judgment and order of the appellate Court passed on 10.12.84 in Misc. Appeal No. 154 of 1984 is hereby set aside. The order dated 4.1.84 dismissing the misc. case for default is also hereby set aside and the case No. 9 of 83 is sent back to the Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka for hearing on merit after giving opportunity to the parties.</u>

There will, however, be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Wahidul Momin Chowdhury, Advocate ----- For the Petitioners. 
Shahidul Islam Chowdhury, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Rabia Khatun and another ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh,represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Satkhira and others
  ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioners was directed against the judgment and decree dated 10.5.92 and 17.5.92 respectively passed by the District Judge, Satkhira in Title Appeal No. 155 of 1990 reversing those dated 29.5.90 and 5.6.90 respectively passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Satkhira in Title Suit No. 222 of 1987.

2. The short facts necessary for the disposal of this Rule may be stated as follows:

The petitioners as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 222 of 1987 in the court of Assistant Judge, Satkhira for declaration of their right, title and interest in 6.50 acres of suit land described in the schedule to the plaint and for a declaration that the suit property is not a vested or non-resident property and the treating of the property as vested property is illegal, void and fraudulent and for a further declaration that the property is not affected by the order dated 10.12.85 in VP Case Nos. 88, 89 and 84 arising out of VP case Nos. 410 and 418 of 1983. The case of the plaintiffs is, that the plaintiff-petitioner No. 1 and her husband Omed Ali Gazi have been owning and possessing the suit properties of Mouza Kathamda and Dadbanga of the District of Satkhira by way of exchange deed dated 26.6.1964 with the admitted owners Shippada Das and others and subsequently by way of auction purchase held on 17.7.78 and confirmed on 17.9.98. The plaintiffs exchanged their own properties of 24 Parganas in India with the suit properties of the original owners, Although the exchange deed of the plaintiffs property was registered in Calcutta on 26.6.64 yet the plaintiff's deed of exchange could not be registered in Bangladesh due to some legal impediments against transfer of properties of minority community. Thereafter the plaintiffs mutated their names in the SA Khatian and have been possessing the same in their exclusive and actual physical possession on payment of rent to the government and then the plaintiff-petitioners amalgamated and consolidated all the khatian lands into one SA Khatian No. 172 by settlement case No.46 of 1980-81. Plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land with the knowledge of all and the government without any objection from any quarter. The plaintiffs constructed dwelling huts in some portion of the suit land and cut tank in other portion and cultivating the remaining portion. That one Nurul Islam in connivance with the staff of defendant-opposite party No. 2 created a lease of the suit land in his name treating the property as vested and non-resident property in VP Case Nos. 410 and 418 of 1983. The suit property had never been treated as vested property since the plaintiff's possession from 1964 but abruptly for the first time in 1983 defendant No.2 started VP case Nos. 410 and 418 of 1983 and created a lease in favour of opposite party Nos. 7 and 8. The plaintiffs have been owning and possessing the suit land and the defendants have no right, title or possession in the suit land, Hence, the suit for the aforesaid declarations.

3. The defendant Nos. 1 to 4 and 5 to 7 contested the suit by filing two separate written statements stating, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable that the plaintiffs have no right title in the suit land nor have any cause of action for the suit. The further case of the defendants in that the original owner of the suit land, Shippada Das and others had left for India and permanently resided there and the property was listed as vested and non-resident property and thereafter, it was leased out to one Shamsur Rahman, Nazrul Islam and Abdul Mazid by way of granting DCR in their favour in VP Misc. case Nos. 410, 418 of 1983-84 and that the lessees have been possessing the suit land. The exchange deed of the plaintiffs is collusive and that the plaintiffs created 20 certificate cases collusively by practising fraud and then purchased the same in collusion with others. The sale proclamation was not duly published and the sale money was not satisfactory and hence, the Thana Revenue Officer cancelled the auction-sale and that the amalgamation of the land in one khatian has also been cancelled. So, the plaintiffs are not entitled to get any relief in this suit.

4. After hearing both the parties and considering the facts and evidence adduced by both the parties, the learned Assistant Judge decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs vide his judgment and decree dated 2.9.90 and 5.6.90 respectively. Against that judgment and decree, the defendants filed an appeal being Title Appeal No. 155 of 1990 in the court of the District Judge, Satkhira. The learned Dist. Judge after hearing both the parties, allowed the appeal and set side the judgment and decree of the learned Assistant Judge vide his judgment and decree dated 10.5.92 and 17.5.92 respectively.

5. Being highly dissatisfied with and aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the learned District Judge, the plaintiffs as petitioners have moved this court under section 115 of the CPC and obtained the present Rule.

6. Mr. Wahidul Momin Chowdhury, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioners, has submitted that the learned Assistant Judge after considering the facts, evidence and the position of the matter had rightly decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs but the learned District Judge by misreading the relevant laws and the facts and evidence of the case, has erroneously reversed the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge and dismissed the plaintiffs suit and thereby occasioned a failure of justice to the plaintiffs. The learned advocate further argued that the learned District Judge is not justified in holding that the suit property has vested in the government as enemy and non-resident property in spite of the fact that the plaintiffs have entered in the suit land in 1964 by way of exchange with the original owners and that the suit property was never treated as vested and non-resident property since after 1964 till 1983 when the government started a VP case.

7. Mr. Shahidul Alam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant- opposite parties, has, on the other hand, submitted that the suit property was listed as enemy property in the census list of 1966 to 1968 and thereafter, the enemy property authority had leased out the land in favour of opposite party Nos. 6 to 8 and granted DCR in their favour and that they have been possessing the suit land. Mr. Shahidul Alam Chowdhury further argued that the original owner Ship Pada Das and others left Bangladesh and so the government rightly treated the suit land as enemy property which was subsequently vested in the government as non-resident property and, as such, the learned District Judge is justified in dismissing the plaintiffs suit.

8. From the facts of the case, it appears that the plaintiffs have sought for declarations in respect of the suit land on three grounds, that they have got the suit property by way of exchange by an un-registered exchange deed executed by the original owner Ship Pada Das and others in 1964 in exchange of their own property in India and since then they have been possessing the land. The second Claim of plaintiffs is, that they have purchased the suit land in auction-sale from the government in certificate cases and after auction-purchase they have mutated their names in the record of rights. The third claim of the plaintiffs is that they have been possessing the suit land since 1964 for more than 12 years and thus they have acquired title by adverse possession.

9. From the submission of Mr. Shahidul Alam Chowdhury, the learned advocate for the defendant-opposite parties, it appears that the exchange as claimed by the plaintiffs is not true and that the exchange Misc. case as started by the plaintiffs was dismissed and that the suit property was listed as enemy property in the census list of 1966-68. Mr. Shahidul Alam Chowdhury further argued that the opposite party Nos. 6 to 8 have taken lease of the properties as enemy property and have been possessing the same and thus the Government have been managing and possessing the suit property through their lessees.

10. Mr. Wahidul Momin Chowdhury, the learned advocate for the plaintiff-petitioners, on the other hand, has shown me a paper in the record wherein the concerned Tahsildar of the area had submitted a report to the certificate officer stating that the suit property was not an enemy property whereupon the certificate case No. 400 of 1977-78 was started about which we shall discuss later on. From VP Case Nos. 410 and 418 of 1983-84 as filed before the trial Court which was not marked as exhibit, it appears that on 23.2.84 the SDO of Satkhira stated in his first order that Md. Shamsur Rahman, Nazrul Islam and Abdul Mazid Sarder prayed for early lease of the suit properties for the year 1390 BS and it appears from the proposal of the VP Tahsilder that the suit property was listed as vested property but was not leased out to anybody till today.

11. From the above order of the VP Custodian, the SDO of Satkhira, it appears that the suit property was never leased out to anybody from 1964, the date of plaintiffs' claim of entry, till 23.2.84. Mr. Shahidul Alam Chowdhury could not show as to who was in possession on behalf of the government during the period from 1964 till 23.2.84 except the statement that the government was in possession. But the fact remains that the government acts through some persons but it appears that there was none to perform the act of possession of the suit property on behalf of the government.

12. Mr. Shahidul Alam Chowdhury next argued that when the plaintiff-petitioners filed a petition before the ADC (Rev) praying for releasing the suit property from the vested property as was treated in VP case Nos. 410 and 418 of 1983, then it came to the notice of the government about the facts of the suit properties and then the vested property custodian started VP case and granted lease. It has been observed in the impugned judgment of the learned District Judge also that when the plaintiffs filed the petition praying for releasing the suit properties from the list of vested properties, then it came to the notice of the ADC (Rev) that the suit property was illegally auction-sold in the name of the auction purchaser and was mutated in his name and then the ADC passed the order for cancellation of the said auction-sale.

13. From the above facts and submissions and from the observation of the learned District Judge, it appears that the vested property authority had no connection with the suit property from 1964 till 1983 nor managed or possessed the suit land at all. By cutting a DCR dated 23.5.84 as it appears from the last order of the VP Case Nos. 410 and 418 of 1983, no lease right can be created in favour of anybody. This order of the VP authority passed in VP Case Nos. 410 and 418 of 1983 dated 23.4.83 and the above facts and circumstances of the case, will go to show that the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land from 1964.

14. About the plaintiffs claim of exchange of the suit property with the original owner, Ship Pada Das and others, Mr. Shahidul Alam Chowdhury submits that the plaintiffs filed an exchange case which was dismissed and so the plaintiffs could not register the exchange deed and, as such, the plaintiffs cannot claim the suit land by way of any exchange. In this respect, Mr. Wahidul Momin Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-petitioners, has submitted that the plaintiffs filed an exchange case which is still pending. It appears from the judgment of the learned District Judge that the learned GP made a submission before him that the plaintiffs' exchange case was still pending before the Divisional Commissioner. Wahidul Momin Chowdhury next submits that the plaintiffs have filed 58 rent receipts showing payment of rent to the government in respect of the suit property since 1965. It appears from these exhibited rent receipts -that the plaintiffs started paying rent for the suit properties from 1965 and continued to pay rent. So it appears that in spite of exchange being not regularised till today, the plaintiffs have been paying the rent of the suit land to the government as per dakhilas, exhibit 8 series. All these dakhilas appear to be another continuous evidence of possession of the plaintiffs in respect of the suit land. It this connection, Mr. Wahidul Momin Chowdhury referred to a decision in the case of Naresh Chandra Nandi Vs. Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and others reported in 28 DLR 437. In has been observed by their Lordships in that case thus:

"Before an (enemy) property is declared to be in unlawful possession of a person the latter must be served with notice to the effect that he is in unlawful possession of the property in question and ask him to show cause why he should not be ejected and upon hearing him, if he appears, that order of ejecting him is to be passed. Without such notice the order passed against him will not be a valid order."

Their Lordships further observed as under:

"Before settlement, the respondent No. 2 is to take possession of the land from the petitioner who is admittedly in possession of the land. Unless the possession is taken from the petitioner the Respondent No. 2 will have no power to settle the land to any person."

<u>15. Although the facts of the suit land of the instant case came to the notice of the ADC (Rev) from the application filed by the petitioners in 1983 to get the suit land released from the VP List as has been done by the authority in VP Case Nos. 410 and 418 of 1983, yet the Vested Property Authority did not serve any notice asking the plaintiffs to vacate the possession of the suit property before granting the lease in favour of opposite party Nos. 6 to 8 vide a DCR dated 23.5.84 nor did the authority take possession of the land before granting the lease. Under such circumstances, it appears that the lease granted in favour of the opposite party Nos. 6 to 8 is nothing but a paper transaction only.</u>

16. It appears that the plaintiffs next claim of the suit land is an auction purchase vide some certificate cases for arrears of rent.

17. Mr. Shahidul Alarn Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for defendant-opposite party, argued that the plaintiffs claim of possession and payment of rent from 1964 till today will show that there was no arrear of rent and, as such, it will appear that the alleged auction-sale was a fraudulent and collusive auction-sale made in favour of the plaintiff-petitioner and immediately after knowing about the matter, the authority had cancelled the auction and so the plaintiffs did not acquire any title by auction purchase. In this connection, Mr. Wahidul Momin Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioners, has, submitted that the plaintiffs have purchased the suit land in auction held by the government certificate officer and if there was any collusion or fraud, it will be a fraud between the government officer and the plaintiff-petitioners and, as such, the government authority, being a party to that fraud, could not take any advantage of their own fraud. By a reading of the certificate case of 1978 it appears that it was suddenly put to auction sale showing an arrear of a small amount only. Under such circumstances, some element of collusion and fraud appears to be there in the auction sale and that there was also an order directing cancellation of that auction sale.

<u>18. The plaintiffs next claim is a claim of title by adverse possession. It appears from the record that an exchange deed was executed and registered by the plaintiffs in favour of the original owners of the suit land in 24 Parganas. But it appears that the alleged exchange deed in favour of the plaintiffs executed in 1964 in respect of the suit land has not yet been registered and that on the basis of that unregistered deed of exchange, the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land since 1964 till today. It has been argued on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioners that the plaintiffs have acquired title by such continuous adverse possession. In this connection, Mr. Wahidul Momin Chowdhury has cited a decision in the case of Mir Laik Ali Vs. Standard Vacuum Oil Company (ESSO) and Abdur Razzak. reported in 16 DLR (SC) 287. It has been observed by their Lordships in that case as under:</u>

<u>"Where there is an invalid transfer in favour of a person and he holds possession of the property transferred as transferee, his possession is in his own right and adverse to the transferor. If he continues in possession of immovable property for more than twelve years he will acquire an indefeasible title"</u>

<u>19. The learned Advocate further referred to a decision in the case of Momtazuddin Ahmed Chowdhury Vs. Deputy Commissioner & Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property, Comilla reported in 20 DLR 375. It has been held by their Lordships in that case in the following:</u>

<u>"A person who is in possession of a property of an enemy by virtue of an agreement either of tenancy or of purchase cannot be termed as an illegal or unauthorised occupier and, as such, cannot be asked to quit the property and hand over possession thereof to the Custodian of Enemy Property."</u>

20. From the facts and evidences of this case and nature of rent receipts showing payment of rent of the suit land to the government, it appears that the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land from 1964 on the basis of an unregistered deed of exchange. The alleged lessee of the vested property, Mr. Abdul Mazid as DW 5 has stated in his deposition that he did not file any power and. that he was not possessing the suit property and that the PWs have also said in their deposition that the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit property. It appears that the learned Assistant Judge has discussed all these evidence thoroughly and found that the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land. The learned District Judge in his impugned judgment has observed that "no right is created by adverse possession for less than 60 years against the government and that the plaintiffs did not complete 60 years possession against the government from the date of their alleged exchange" In this connection, Mr. Wahidul Momin Chowdhury, the learned advocate for the plaintiff-petitioners, has argued that the plaintiffs adverse possession was not against the government but that it was a case of adverse possession on the basis of un-registered deed of exchange against the original owners since 1964 before the government claim of enemy property. It is true that the plaintiffs, as it appears from the facts and evidences, have been possessing the suit land from 1964 adversely to the original owners and others and not against the government. The government was not in the picture until 1983. In view of the fact that the government did not have any connection with the suit land till 1983, when they allegedly granted a lease in favour of some persons, the opposite party nos. 6 to 8, who also did not get any possession till today, I am of the opinion that the learned District Judge is not correct in making such a proposition in respect of adverse possession of the suit land. The learned District Judge could not properly appreciate .the fact and law relating to adverse possession in respect of the suit land.

21. Mr. Shahidul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite party, argued that the plaintiffs have not prayed in the prayer portion of the plaint for any declaration on the basis of adverse possession. But it appears from 'Ka' prayer in paragraph 8 of the plaint that the plaintiffs have prayed for a declaration of their title in respect of the suit property as described in schedule 'Kha' on the basis of the statements of their claims as made in the plaint. Mr. Wahidul Momin Chowdhury has showed me paragraph 4 of the plaint wherein they have made a Claim that the plaintiffs are entitled to get the decree on the basis of adverse possession for more than 12 years peacefully and continuously. Thus, it appears that the plaintiffs have made a full claim of declaration of title on the basis of their peaceful and continuous adverse possession for more than 12 years.

22. By a perusal of the judgment of the learned trial Court and the impugned judgment of the learned lower appellate Court, it appears that both the courts below found possession of the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs. From the facts and circumstances of the case as discussed above, it will also appear that the plaintiffs have been continuously possessing the suit properties from 1964 till today and thus they have acquired a title to the suit land by adverse possession.

23. In view of what has been discussed above, I am of the opinion that the impugned judgment passed by the learned District Judge is not based on correctly or properly appreciated facts and evidence on record and hence I find that the learned District Judge has committed an error of law resulting in an error in his decision by passing the impugned judgment which has caused a failure of justice to the plaintiffs-petitioners. The impugned judgment, therefore, calls for interference by this court.

24. In view of the above, the Rule is made absolute and that the impugned judgment and decree are hereby set aside and those of the trial Court are restored. There will be no order as to costs.

Send down the LC records to the court concerned at once.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioner is against judgment and decree dated 24.2.88 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Bhola in Title Appeal No. 11 of 1986 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 21.12.85 passed by the Munsif, Borhanuddin Upazila in Title Suit No. 163 of 1984.

2. Short question involved in this Rule is whether Court of appeal below was justified in holding that plaintiff-petitioner has no locus standi for declaring decree passed in an earlier Title Suit No. 26 of 1977 in which he was not a party and no relief was granted against him as not binding on him and in setting aside the decree of the trial Court on such erroneous view.

3. In this case admittedly defendant-opposite party No. 1 was appointed temporary Nikah Registerar on 1.11.75 under Rule 5(1) of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Rules, 1974 and his appointment was cancelled by Memo dated 10.1.77. Admittedly, the said memo cancelling his temporary licence was declared illegal and the defendant-opposite party Nos. 2-5 were restrained from interfering with the work of the opposite party No. 1 as Nikah Registrar and giving effect to the said order of cancellation. It is true that in the said suit filed on 21.1.77 plaintiff-petitioner was not added as a defendant but he was appointed permanent Nikah Registrar on 10.9.81 under Rule 5 (4) of the said Rules. Petitioner filed Title Suit No. 107 of 1983 subsequently re-numbered as Title Suit No. 163 of 1984 challenging the said decree as he was directed by the Deputy Commissioner, Bhola to take steps for setting aside the said decree. Though the Court of appeal below observed that the petitioner was appointed perm anent Nikah Registrar after the temporary injunction passed in Title Suit No. 26 of 1977 was vacated and as such the decree in the said suit became infructuous but set aside the decree of the trial Court on an erroneous view that the petitioner had no locus standi and cause of action for filing the suit as no relief was sought against him in Title Suit No. 26 of 1977.

3. It appears from the copy of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 26 of 1977 that defendant-opposite party Nos. 2-5 were restrained by an order of perpetual injunction from interfering with the work of the opposite party No. 1 as Nikah Registrar and giving effect to the order dated 10.1.77 cancelling his temporary licence.

<u>4. It is true that a Nikah Registrar is appointed under Rule 5(1) of the said Rules "on purely temporary basis until a Nikah Registrar is licensed by the Government on regular basis." So the said decree passed in Title Suit No. 26 of 1977 is contrary to the said Rule. Hence observation of the Court of appeal below that with the appointment of plaintiff-petitioner as permanent Nikah Registrar decree passed in Title Suit No. 26 of 1977 has become infructuous is correct interpretation of law. But so long a decree remains un-challenged even if it is illegal that may create complications and is binding upon the parties. It has already been noticed that the plaintiff-petitioner was compelled to file the suit as he was directed by the Deputy Commissioner, Bhola to take steps against the decree passed in Title Suit No. 26 of 1977. Undoubtedly, the said decree has been adversely affecting the petitioner and interfering with his functioning as a Nikah Registrar. In that view of the matter, Court of appeal below was not justified to set aside judgment and decree of the trial Court on the view that the petitioner was not a necessary party in the earlier suit and no relief was sought against him. When a decree adversely affects a person not a party to the same he may file a suit for declaring the same not binding on him and get the same set aside if found illegal as in the present case.</u>

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree are set aside and those of the trial Court restored.

End.
