full_judgment:
This rule calls in question the legality and propriety of the impugned Order No. 63 dated 20.7.85 passed by Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Khulna in Title Execution Case No. 16. of 1977 staying further proceedings of the Execution Case till the disposal of Title Suit No. 239 of 1985 of the said court. 

2. Facts giving rise to this provisional application may briefly be stated thus: Plaintiff-decree holder petitioner filed partition suit being Title Suit No. 336 of 1970 in the court of Subordinate. Judge Khulna impleading opposite party as defendants Summons were served on the defendant-opposite parties duly. Most of the defendants reside in the same homestead and the female co-sharer resides at some other homestead with their husbands. Although defendant-opposite received summons and were in the know of the filing of partition suit, they did not appear in the suit purposely with ulterior motive of causing harassment and so willfully allowed suit to be decreed exported on 5.9.72 in the preliminary form. Thereafter plaintiff-petitioner filed application for final decree in Title Suit No. 336/70 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Khulna. An Advocate Commissioner on being appointed by court went upon the land and measured it and prepared field book and map and thereafter submitted report in court on 30-4-74. No objection was raised against the report of Advocate Commissioner and accordingly preliminary decree dated 5.9.70 was made final on 26.7.74 and the Commissioner's report, case map, field book etc were made part of the decree. 

3. In the meantime Sk. Abul Hasanat, predecessor-in-interest of opposite party No. 2(a) to 2(m) and Aftabuddin opposite party No.2 filed an application under Order 9 Rule 13, C.P.C. for setting aside the exparte decree dated 5.9.72 being Misc. Case No. 100/74 on the ground of non-service of summons. Petitioner filed objection and contested the Misc. Case alleging that the summons and registered card were duly served on the opposite party and that allegation of suppression of summons was false and frivolous. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence adduced by the parties dismissed the Misc. Case by his judgment and order dated 29.3.75 holding that summons were duly served (vide judgment Annexure-"D'). Being aggrieved by this order of dismissal opposite party filed an appeal being Misc. Appeal No. 186 of 1975 in the Court of learned District Judge, Khulna and the said appeal was dismissed on contest on 3.9.76 (vide judgment Annexure- 'E'). 

4. Thereafter defendant No.1 now dead and his full sister opposite party No.12 filed another rehearing case under Order 9 rule 13, C.P.C. (Misc. Case No. 139 of 1977), for setting aside the ex-parte decree dated 5.9.72 passed in Title suit No. 336 of 1970 of the court of Subordinate Judge. This Misc. Case was dismissed for default on 8.11.80 (vide Annexure-F'). In the meantime petitioners filed Title Execution Case No. 16 of 1977 for getting delivery of possession of the land allotted to them on the basis of final decree dated 26.7.74. The aforesaid opposite party being un-successful in the two aforesaid re- hearing cases, set up their another brother opposite party No.3, Sk. Mostafa and through him filed Title Suit No. 339 of 1985 in the court of learned Subordinate Judge, Khulna to have ex-parte decree and final decree dated 5.9.72 and 26.7.74 respectively passed in Title Suit No. 336 of 1970 of the said Court set aside. This suit was filed only on 20.7.85. In this suit it is alleged that there was no service of summons and summons were suppressed. The plaint of the suit is Annexure- 'A'. On the same day opposite party filed a petition under Section 151, C.P.c. for getting further proceeding in Title Execution Case No. 16 of 1976 stayed (vide Annexure- 'R'). The learned Subordinate Judge by his order dated 20.7.85 passed the impugned order staying further proceeding of said execution case. Being aggrieved by the order of stay, plaintiff petitioners moved the provisional jurisdiction of this Court and obtained the Rule. 

5. No affidavit-in-opposition has been filed by the opposite party controverting the averment made in the application supported by affidavit but it is submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge passed the impugned order staying further proceedings of the Title Execution case no. 16 of 1977 in exercise of his inherent power under Section 151, C.P.C. and as such it docs not call for any interference. 

6. Mr. Sk. Razzaque Ali, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, has submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge in passing the impugned order of stay, illegally and improperly exercised his inherent power under section 151, C.P.C. which resulted in miscarriage of justice and that the impugned order dated 20.7.85 being a non-speaking order cannot be sustained in law and that the learned Subordinate Judge did not apply his judicial mind to ascertain if facts of the case warrant application of 'Section 151, C.P.C. to secure the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of court. The learned Counsel continued to urge that object of filing sub-sequent Title Suit No. 239/85 is malafide device to stay execution proceeding and thereby to deprive the plaintiff-petitioner of the fruit of hard earned decree and in such circumstances the stay order deserves to be vacated. The learned Counsel further submitted that in case opposite parties succeeds in his suit, he can obtain relief filing a petition under Section 144 or 151, C.P.C. and that he will not be thrown to separate litigation. 

7. Mr. M.A. Rahim, the learned Counsel for the opposite party submits that the learned Subordinate Judge though did not assign any reason in staying the execution proceeding in fact applied his mind to the materials of the case and exercised his discretion under section 151, C.P.C. on sound judicial principle and as such his order does not deserve to be disturbed inasmuch as it aims at preventing both par- ties from being involved in further litigation. 

8. Heard the learned Counsel of both sides at length and also perused the impugned order dated 20.7.85. The impugned order is slip-shod, cryptic and non-speaking. Further proceeding of Title Execution case No. 16/77 was sought to be stayed by opposite party invoking aid of section 151, C.P.C. and the learned Subordinate Judge exercising his inherent power u/s 151 passed the impugned order of stay. No doubt court is competent to pass order staying further proceeding of Ex. case u/s 151, C.P.C. but before passing such order court has to be satisfied if it aims at securing ends of justice and prevent abuse of the process of court and this satisfaction must be based on some materials. If the court on application of judicial mind to materials placed before it, is of opinion that stay of proceeding in a case is required to prevent abuses of process of court and to secure ends of justice then only exercise of inherent power u/s 151, C.P.C. will be permissible. In other words it has to be exercised on sound judicial principle and not arbitrarily and whimsically. But unfortunately the impugned order of stay being non- speaking it is impossible to gather if Subordinate Judge applied judicial mind to material placed before him and was satisfied that in the circumstances of the case stay order needs to be passed to secure ends of justice and to prevent abuse of process of court. So, there is no escape from the finding that inherent power u/s 151, C.P.C. was exercised by the Sub- ordinate Judge, not on sound judicial principle rather it was exercised arbitrarily. 

9. Facts and circumstances of the case show that defendant Nos. 2 and 4 who are brothers, filed first re-hearing case (Misc. Case No. 100/74) and it was dismissed on contest on 29.3.75 and an appeal being Misc. Appeal No. 186 of 1975 was preferred but it was diminished on contest on 3.9.76 (Vide Annexure-D' & 'E'). Then another brother that is opposite party No.1 filed another re-hearing case under Order 9 Rule 13, but he allowed it to be dismissed for default vide Annexure-F. This act of filing rehearing cases by the opposite party reveals their nefarious design to deny the plaintiff-petitioner to enjoy the fruit of decree. Defendants opposite party having failed in their attempt to have the ex-parte decree passed in T.S. No. 336/70 set aside, another brother through whom the present Title Suit No. 239 of 1985 has been filed on 20-7-85 and stay order was obtained. The object for filing of T.S. No. 239/85 is nothing but to keep the Execution Proceeding stayed as long as they can, being guided by an evil motive to deny the plaintiff petitioner to enjoy the fruit of hard earned decree. This is one aspect of the matter. This fact seems to have been over looked by the Subordinate Judge who passed the impugned stay order. The facts involved in this case, do not warrant a conclusion that ends of justice will be secured if the Execution case is stayed till the disposal of T.S. No. 239/85. Rather it shows that impugned stay order aim at protecting the proceeding and thereby to cause harassment to petitioners. So having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case it cannot be said that the stay order was passed by the Subordinate Judge to secure the ends of justice or to prevent abuses of process of court. Rather impugned order aims at denying justice to petitioners. 

10. Now it is to be seen, if parties will be thrown to series of litigation if the stay order is vacated. In this connection Mr. Shaikh Razzaque Ali, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the question of parties being involved in series of litigation in the event of vacation of the stay order does not arise inasmuch as if opposite party succeeds in T.S.No. 239/85, they will be restored to former possession in respect of suit property by filing an application either under Section 144 or section 151; C.P.C. This contention appears to be well founded. In the event opposite parties succeeds in T.S. No. 239/85, they will not be thrown to another litigation as because they can obtain relief by filing a petition under section 144 C.P.C. In this connection Mr. Ra- him, learned Advocate for the opposite party, has submitted that remedy provided under Section 144 is not available if the decree is varied or set aside by separate suit. This contention does not appear to be based on sound proposition of law. 

11. The phrase "varied or reversed" in Section 144 C.P.C. is unqualified and ought to receive its full force and effect. There is no warrant for construing the section in a limited sense as meaning that the decree should be reversed or varied only by a superior Court in the same proceedings. The decree may be varied or reversed not only by an appeal but by revision to a superior Court. Similarly, a Court may review its own decree and set it aside. If a decree is obtained by fraud or granted by a Court that has no jurisdiction, such a decree may doubtless be varied or reversed by a suit brought in different Court. Court has jurisdiction to order restitution under section 144, even if the decree is modified or reversed by a Court of co-ordinate jurisdiction in a separate suit. The section does not provide for an order of restitution to be made in any particular form or proceeding or by any particular Court. 

Words of Limitation are not to be read into statute if it can be avoided. 

12. The remedy to the aggrieved party is under section 144, C.P.C. only. He can also seek remedy invoking aid of section 151, C.P.C. The principle enunciated by their Lordships of the Appellate Division in the case of Abdul Hamid Vs. Abdul Jabbar reported in 34 DLR (AD) 1982 at page 208, may be referred to. Their Lordships in enunciating the principle has observed as follows: 

"Following this decision of the Privy Council, different High Courts of the Sub-continent allowed restitution in the case of reversal of orders in exercise of their discretion under section 151 of the Code". Although facts involved in cited case is distinguishable from the facts of instant case, the principle enunciated by their Lordships will have full application in this case. Therefore, there is no manner of doubt that the parties will not be involved in a fresh litigation in the event of success of opposite party in Title Suit No. 239 of 1985 and the question of par- ties being involved in separate litigation in the event of success in Title suit No. 239 of 1985 does not arise. 

13. Thus having considered the facts and circumstances of the case, I have no hesitation to hold that the learned Subordinate Judge by passing the impugned order did not apply his judicial mind. Obviously the impugned order of stay has not been passed in the interest of justice rather it aims denying justice to petitioners by depriving them in enjoying the fruit of decree in T.S. No. 336 of 1978. In view of this matter, the stay order cannot be sustained in law and it is accordingly, vacated. 

In the result, the Rule is made absolute with cost. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J: -This First Appeal and the Civil Revision have been heard consecutively and will be disposed of by the same judgment as they arise out of the same suit.

2. The First Appeal preferred by the defendant No. 1 appellant is directed against the judgment anddecree dated 2.1.86 passed ex-parte by Mr. A.K.M. Fazlul Karim, Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 732 of 1985, decreeing the suit. 

3. The plaintiff No. 1- respondent M.H. Arif filed the suit for declarations that the said plaintiff is the legally appointed permanent Managing Director and Chairman of the plaintiff No. 2-company i.e. Bangladesh Light Costing CO. Ltd. that he cannot be removed from the saw posts unless he voluntarily resigns and that the resolutions dated 19.4.85 alleged to have been passed by the defendants removing the said plaintiff as the Managing Director and Chairman of the plaintiff-company and appointing the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 respectively in the said posts are illegal, malafide, void and of no legal effect. 

4. The averments in the plaint shortly were that the plaintiff No. 2 Bangladesh Light Casting Co. Ltd. is a private Limited company which was a purely family concern of Mr. M.A. Hassan, father of the plaintiff. It is the success or of a partnership firm. On 27.1.66 the brother of the plaintiff No.1 Mr. Hassan Dawood resigned as the Managing Director of the company. The Board of Directors in a meeting held on 27.1.66 unanimously made the plaintiff No. 1 the Managing Director in place of Mr. Hassan Dawood. In all extra-ordinary general meeting of the company held on l.11.67 the shareholders of the company unanimously passed a resolution that one male member of Mr. M.A. Hassan's family shall always be the Managing Director of the company. Accordingly on 1.11.67 all the shareholders unanimously made the plaintiff No. 1 the permanent Managing Director of the company unless he voluntarily resigns from the post in writing. 

5. On 20.3.75 the plaintiff No. 1 transferred some of his shares in the company to the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and their nominees, as the said defendants were good friends of the said plaintiff. But the transferee shareholders did not pay any money for their shares. These transfers were made in good faith for future consideration. 

6. On 24.3.79 Mr. M.A. Hassan the father of the plaintiff No. 1 resigned from the Chairmanship of the company and transferred his entire share to the plaintiff No. 1. The company took a resolution on 2. The First Appeal preferred by the defendant No. 1 appellant is directed against the judgment and arise out of the same suit. 24.3.79 that the plaintiff No. 1 shall be the Chairman of the company until he resigns voluntarily in writing. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 were parties to that resolution. 

7. Subsequently the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 did not honour their promise of giving shares to the plaintiff No. 1 in the company of defendant Nos. 1 and 2. Differences cropped up between them. After giving a long history of differences between the plaintiff No. 1 and the defendants the plaintiff states that the defendants passed a resolution on 19.4.85 removing the plaintiff No. 1 as the Managing Director and Chairman of the plaintiff-company and appointing the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 respectively in the said posts. He submits that the aforesaid meeting dated 19.4.85 was held in violation of an order of injunction from the Court. He also submits that he cannot be removed from those posts unless he voluntarily resigns. 

8. The suit was filed on 17.8.85. The defendant No.1 appeared on 18.9.85 and prayed for time to file a written statement. Time was allowed up to 21.11.85 to file a written statement. On 21.11.85 the defendant No. 1 did not file any written statement, nor took any steps. Hence the learned Subordinate Judge fixed the suit for ex-parte hearing on 22.12.85. 

9. On 22.12.85 the plaintiff filed hajira and the case was taken up for ex-parte hearing. P.W. 1 A.B. Siddique describing himself as General Manager of the plaintiff-company deposed as P.W. 1. Documents were marked as Exts. 1-3, 4-4(a). 5 and 6. P.W. 1 was directed to file his authority to depose in favour of the plaintiffs by 2.1.86. On 2.1.86 the learned Subordinate Judge saw the power of Attorney and the letter filed by the plaintiff. On perusal of the record documents and deposition of P.W. 1 he found the case to be proved and decreed the suit ex-parte against the defendants without costs. 

10. Thereafter the defendant No. 1 alone has filed this appeal. 

11. It has been urged by Mr. Asrarul Hossain, learned Advocate for the defendant No. 1-appellant that the learned Subordinate Judge posted the suit for ex-parte hearing without satisfying himself that summons were served on all the other defendants. 

12. When the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filed two miscellaneous cases under Order 9. Rule 13 C.P.C. setting aside the ex-parte decree, an enquiry was conducted by the learned Subordinate Judge in pursuance of an application from the plaintiff No. 1-respondent as to whether summons was served or not. The Nayeb-Nazir reported on 16.4.86 (at page 61 of the lower Court's records) that summons were served and returned to the sherista of the Court of the learned Subordinate Judge on 18.9.85 on due receipts. These returns are not in the record. It was also the Court's order dated 17.8.85 that the defendants were to be served additionally by registered post with acknowledgement due. The postal acknowledgement receipts are also not in the lower Court's records. From the order sheet we do not find any attempt on the part of the learned Subordinate Judge to satisfy himself before fixing the suit for ex parte hearing, that the other defendants were served with the summons of the suit. 

13. Mr. Rafique-ul-Hoque, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondents also concedes that there is nothing on record to show that the learned Subordinate Judge himself was satisfied about the service of summons upon the other defendants. 

14. Therefore upon the submissions of both sides it is a fit and proper case that the ex-parte decree should be set aside and the suit be sent back to the trial court for retrial in accordance with law. 

15. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, learned Advocate for the defendant No. 1 appellant and Mr. Moinul Huq, learned Advocate for the defendant No. 3 respondent have, however, argued that the suit should be dismissed by this appellate Court on various grounds. 

16. The ground common to the said two learned Advocates is that the suit is not maintainable. Their common contention is that the office of Managing Director is not a statutory office. It has got no legal character of status. It is purely a creature of contract. No declaratory suit is maintainable in defence of such an office. They have cited some decisions in support of the their arguments. 

17. Mr. Rafique-ul- Huq on the other hand submits that the office of Managing Director is very much a creature of the Companies Act and it is not based on contract. Managing Director is not a servant but an agent of the company. A suit is perfectly maintainable for a declaration in support of the office. 

18. Since these are contentious issues and ought properly to be disposed of after framing of issues and after consideration of the law and facts involved in the suit itself, we are not is a position to dismiss the suit straightaway on the ground of maintainability, nor are we in a position to hold that the tiffs suit is maintainable. The parties are free to raise No this issue at the trial court and we express no opinion whatsoever. 

19. It is next contended by both Mr. Asrarul Hossain and Mr. Moinul Huq that from the evidence of P.W. 1 and the exhibits filed in the case the plaintiff No. 1 has not at all proved that he was the permanent Managing Director and permanent Chairman of the plaintiff-company and that he would cease hold those offices only if he voluntarily resigns Both the learned Advocates have taken us through the evidence on record and have sought to argue that the evidence as it stands is just not enough to prove the plaintiffs case. 

20. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq, learned Advocate has submitted on the other hand that although in an ex-parte proceeding the plaintiff is obliged to prove his own case but still the burden of proof is not as heavy as in a contested case. He has cited some decisions in support of his submission. He has also taken us through the plaint and the evidence owner record and has argued that the plaintiff has proved his case as his assertions both in the plaint and in the evidence of P.W. 1 have gone unrebutted and unchallenged. As a measure of caution he has filed an application for adducing additional evidence of two resolutions which have been quoted in full in the plaint itself. Mr. Moinul Huq has objected to the reception of additional evidence on various grounds. 

21. As the case was one of no contest, and the plaintiff had a walkover at the trial Court he submitted his case as far as he thought necessary. The two resolutions were quoted in full on the body of the plaint and these were not refuted by the defendants by filing any written statement. He did not adduce any formal proof these two resolutions because none short controverted him. We do not think that we should dismiss his suit altogether because he did not prove and law those two resolutions at the ex-parte hearing had transpired during the course of hearing of the appeal that there were no averments with regard to these two resolutions and the plaintiff-respondent had no evidence at all to offer in respect of these two resolutions then of course we would have considered whether it was at all worth the while to send the case back for retrial. But the plain fact is that the plain have quoted the resolution in fully in the plaint. one controverted them and the suit cannot be dis- missed simply because they did not formally prove the resolutions. 

	22. Mr. Moinul Huq has further assailed the two resolutions on various grounds. He has also filed an application for taking judicial notice of the High Court Division's order in company Matter No. 29 of 1985 and the plaintiff-respondent's Special to Leave petition before the Appellate Division. He .argued that on the plaintiff-respondent's own showing, he has appointed a permanent-Managing Director by the shareholders in an extra-ordinary general meeting. By the same token he can also be removed by the shareholders in a general meeting of the company which the shareholders have done subsequently after the High Court Division directed the holding of the Annual General Meeting of the company. He submits that this Court should take notice of subsequent developments after the suit was filed and should hold that the plaintiff-respondent has no long any cause of action and that he has ceased to be fully the Managing Director and Chairman. 

23. We are in fact being called upon to trans- form ourselves into a primary Court of fact and law. We arc called upon to take judicial notice of certain judgments and petitions. The plaintiff-respondent on the other hand prays for adducing additional evidence. The justification for this exercise is that in any event complex issues of maintainability of the suit, the true meaning and import of the proceedings under section 76 of the Companies Act and the interpretation of the Articles of Association of the company will come up for resolution by the High Court Division itself whatever be the result of the suit in the trial Court. Why not do it now? 

24. In other words we are called upon to make a -circuit of the procedure provided in the Code and transform ourselves into a primary Court of fact when admittedly the parties have not adduced. If it full evidence in the case nor have the defendants filed any written statement. 

25. Needles to say that we are not prepared to assume such a role in the facts and circumstances of the present case. We set aside the decree and send the suit back to the trial Court for retrial and there it should rest for the present. 

26. As such the appeal is allowed. The judgment and decree dated 2.1.86 passed ex-parte by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 732 of 1985 are set aside and the said suit is sent back to the trial Court for fresh trial in accordance with law. 

27. There will be no order as to costs. 

28. In the connected Civil Revision No. 197 of 1986 the facts are that the defendant No. 1 of the above suit, who is the appellant in F. A. No. 28 of 1986, instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 238 of 1986 under Order 9 Rule 13 C.P.C. for setting aside the ex-parte decree dated 2.1.86 passed in Title Suit No. 732 of 1985. On 12.3.86, upon the prayer of the defendant No.1 the learned Subordinate Judge stayed the operation of the judgment and decree till the disposal of the miscellaneous case. Against the said order the plaintiff-respondents as petitioners have obtained the present Rule. 

29. As we have already allowed the appeal in F.A. No. 28 of 1986 and set aside the ex-parte decree passed on 2.1.86 the Rule has become infructuous. 30. As such the rule is discharged without any order as to costs. 

Md. Mozammel Hoque, J: I agree. 

End.

In this Rule I am invited to consider the propriety of the order dated 9.5.87 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 307 of 1988 pending before him. In order to make the question clear it is necessary to make a brief statement of facts.

2. The petitioner being plaintiff instituted, in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka a suit being Title Suit No. 6 of 1983 against the opposite party and several others for declaration of his title and recovery of khas possession in certain land. The suit was decreed ex parte on 18.8.84. On behalf of the opposite party an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, hereinafter referred to as the Code, was thereupon filed to have the decree set aside. It was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 307 of 1986. There being a failure on the part of the opposite party to make his co-defendants parties the petitioner took an objection that it was not maintainable for non-joinder of necessary parties and prayed for rejection of the application. By the impunged order dated 9.5.87 the learned Subordinate Judge refused the prayer. The petitioner now contends that the decision is wrong.

3. The question that emerges, therefore, is whether one of the defendants can maintain an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code without impleading his co-defendants.

Order 9 rule 13 of the Code reads thus:

"In any case in which a decree is passed ex parte against a defendant, he may apply to the court by which the decree was passed for an order to set aside; and if he satisfies the Court that the summons was not duly served, or that he was prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing, the Court shall make an order setting aside the decree as against him upon such terms as to costs, payment into Court or otherwise as it thinks fit, and shall appoint a day for proceedings with the suit.;

Provided that where the decree is such a nature that it cannot be set aside as against such defendant only it may be set aside against all or any of the other defendants also."

<u>4. There is nothing in the language of this provision which makes it obligatory on the part of an applicant under the Rule to make all other defendants parties to the proceeding. But rule 14 of the Order lays down that the decree shall not be set aside unless notice of the application to set it aside has been served on the opposite party. In Apil Bibi Vs. Ayatullah, 6 DLR 461, Dulal Chandra Chowdhury Vs. Atul Krishna Roy, 39 CWN 863 and Sultan Hossain Khan Vs. Satnarain Lal AIR 1953 Hyd. 191 it has been held that the expression 'opposite party', means the person in whose favour the ex parte decree was passed. Therefore, all that is required in an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code is to implead the person or persons in whose favour the decree is passed and not others. Since the petitioner who is the decree holder has been impleaded in this case, it cannot be said that the Miscellaneous case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code suffers from any defect of party.</u>

In that view of the matter the Rule is discharged with costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Ranadhir Sen, J.-This appeal at the instance of the decree holder is directed against the judgment and order dated 30-1-80 of the learned Subordinate Judge allowing an application under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The judgment-debtor alleged that the Suit decree holder obtained a decree in Money Suit No. 8 of 1977 for realization of the rental compensation from the judgment-debtor for a house under the control and management of the judgment debtor as abandoned property within the meaning of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. The decree-holder obtained an expert decree and filed money Execution Case No. 5 of 1979 for recovery of the decretal amount.

3. The decree holder filed a written objection against the petition of the judgment-debtor contending, inter alia, that the house in question was released by the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in terms of the judgment and order in Writ Petition No. 287 of 1975 holding that the house was not an abandoned property and the management of the judgment-debtor was without lawful authority. For the illegal management and control of the house the decree holder obtained a valid decree for realization of the rents of the house which was received by the judgment-debtor in course of its possession during the years in question. It was contended by the decree-holder that the decree in question was passed by a competent Court with jurisdiction to pass the decree. The executing Court was not authorized in law to go behind the decree.

The learned Subordinate Judge raised point for determination "as to whether the executing Court can go behind the decree."

Considering the relevant facts and law the learned Subordinate Judge was of the opinion that the decree has been passed by a Court without jurisdiction and the decree stood abated and as such the decree was not executable. The learned Subordinate Judge held that the decree passed in Money Suit No. 8 of 1977 dated 7.3.78 is without jurisdiction."

Accordingly he allowed the petition under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Subordinate Judge appears to have considered the Provision of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and M.L.R. 7 of 1977 while reaching the conclusion referred to above.

4. Mr. MJ. Farooqui, the learned Advocate appearing for the appeal contends that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in going behind that decree while holding that the decree in Money Suit No. 8 of 1977 dated 7.3.78 was without jurisdiction. According to Mr. Farooqui, the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in construing provisions of Article 23 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 read with Article 5 of M.L.R. No.7 of 1971. Article 23 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 runs as follows:

"No suit, prosecution of other legal proceeding shall lie against the Government or any person for anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done under this Order or the Rule made thereunder."

5. According to Mr. Farooqui, this barring provision has no application in the fact of the instant case. Since the decision in Writ Petition No. 287 of 1975 clearly concluded the question whether the action of the Government was protected within the meaning and scope of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. In the said Writ Petition an objection was raised in justification of the action taken by the Government while treating the disputed property as an abandoned property. The High Court "Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh held "that action of the Government treating the Petitioner's house as all abandoned property is without any lawful authority and of no legal effect. The respondents are directed to make over possession of the house to the petitioner at once."

6. It is admitted that in terms of the aforesaid decision in Writ Petition, the Government made over possession of the disputed property to the petitioner. Money Suit No. 8 of 1977 was filed for recovery of the amount of rent received by the Government during the period of its control and management. The suit was decreed ex-parte on 7.3.78. Thereafter, Money Execution Case No. 5 of 1979 was started for recovery of the decretal dues. The objection under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure aimed at a question to oust the jurisdiction of the Court so far as the money suit was concerned. According to the Government, the learned Subordinate Judge had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit and to pass the decree in view of the bar of Article 23 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. Mr. Farooqui has drawn our attention to the case of Bangladeshi Steel Mills Vs. Masud Reza 30 D.L.R. (SC) 169 for the proposition that if the property does not answer the description of abandoned property, no occasion arises for application of the abandoned property order. We have already referred to the judgment of this Court in Writ Petition No. 287 of 1975, where it was held that "the action of the Government treating the petitioner s house as abandoned property is without lawful authority and of no legal effect."

7. In the case of Abdur Rauf and others Vs. Abdul Hamid Khan and others reported in 17 D.L.R 515 it has been held that the Civil Court's jurisdiction is not barred and the distinction between an Order passed under the Act or under the chapter was considered. Their Lordships noticed that civil Courts have jurisdiction as under section 9, Civil Procedure Code, to try all suits of a civil nature excepting those the trial of which is expressly or impliedly barred. The alleged action in the instant case claimed to be protected under the Act, namely under the President's Order No. 16 of 1972. The learned Judges of the Pakistan Supreme Court in the aforesaid case expressed this in the following words:-

"We are quite familiar with the words "under the Act" or 'under Chapter……………..", No order is an order passed "under the Act" if it was not passed in exercise of powers granted by the Act and was therefore without jurisdiction In 11 particular Act the words "under the Act" or "under Chapter…………….." may not appear and words of similar import may be used. But whatever the phraseology employed any provision in an enactment saying that orders passed under the enactment or by virtue of the powers conferred by the enactment would not be liable to challenge in a Court of law has reference only to orders passed with jurisdiction."

In view of the decision-in writ petition No. 287 of 1975, it cannot be said that the order passed and action taken were under President's Order No. 16 of 1972. Thus the protection of Article 23 of P.O. 16 of 1972 does not appear to be applicable in the facts of the instant case.

Similar view was expressed in the case of Nasiruddin Vs. Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh reported in D.L.R. 32, 31 (AD) 216. In that case protection under M. L.R. No. 7 failed to attract the action taken in the said case.

8. Mr. Ismailuddin Sarker, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing in support of the Government has strenuously contended that the actions taken are protected under Article .23 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and Article 5 of M.L.R. No.7 of 1977. We may quote here the Provisions of Article 5 of M.L.R No. 7 of 1977 which runs as follows:

"(1). Save as provided in the President' Order, no such taking over or vesting of property as is referred to in paragraph 4 shall be called in question on any ground whatsoever before any authority or in any Court; nor shall any such taking over or vesting of property give rise to any claim to compensation.

(2) All suits, appeals, petitions, applications, and other legal proceedings immediately before the commencement of this Regulation in any Court in which any such taking over or vesting of property as is referred to in paragraph 4 has been called in question in any manner whatsoever shall abate forthwith and shall not be further proceeded with."

9. Referring to the expression "nor shall any such taking over of vesting of property give rise to any claim to compensation", the learned Assistant Attorney General contends that the decree was without jurisdiction since the bar by Article 5 of M. L.R. No. 7 of 1977 applied to the instant case. It was not a suit for any claim of compensation but it was suit for recovery of the money received by the Government by way of rent for the relevant period. It was not receiveable by the Government on the strength of its action under President's Order No. 16 of 1972. The contention of the learned Assistant Attorney General does not hold well in view of the facts of the instant case and the nature of suit. The suit was decreed ex-parte. It was not a suit for recovery of any compensation for the wrongful act nor it was the suit for mesne profits. It is evident from the materials one record that the suit was one for recovery of the amount received by the judgment debtor without any lawful authority. Such a suit does not appear to be protected under the mischief of Article 5 of M.L.R. No. 7 of 1977.

10. Having considered the aforesaid decision we are of the opinion that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in going beyond the decree while holding that the decree was without jurisdiction. The cases referred to above may be considered in the light of the case of the Secretary of State Vs. Mask and Co. 44 C. W.N. page 709. This decision clearly applies in the facts and circumstance of the instant case. The learned Subordinate Judge did not take into consideration the principles laid down in the cases referred to above while striking down the execution case.

11. It has been contended by Mr. Faruqui that the scope of section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure is limited to the extent of investigation as to whether the court which passed the decree did so without jurisdiction. The illegal exercise of jurisdiction or illegality in the decision is not within the scope of section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Faruqui has referred to the case of Gora Chand Halder Vs. Prafulla Kumar Roy and others reported in 29 C.WN. page 948. In this Full Bench case it was held that "where the decree presented for execution was made by Court which apparently had no jurisdiction, whether pecuniary or territorial or in respect of judgment debtor's person to make the decree the executing Court is entitled to refuse to execute it on the ground that it was made without jurisdiction. Within these narrow limits the executing Court is authorized to question the validity of the decree." This decision of the Full Bench appears to have been uniformly followed. Mr. Sarkar has also referred to the case of Lunatic Kumar Chanchal Kumar Ray Vs. Kumar Jagadish Ch. Singha represented by the Manager, Paik Para Raj Wards Estate reported in 6 D.L.R. Page 561. A Division Bench of the Dacca High Court considered the scope of section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure and explained the aforesaid Full Bench decision in the following terms :-

"It is only in very exceptional cases, where on the face of the decree it is clear that the Court which passed the decree had no inherent jurisdiction to do so, that the executing Court can refuse to execute the decree, but otherwise, it is not open to the executing Court to go behind the decree and determine for itself whether the decree passed by the Court having jurisdiction is valid or not."

12. In the aforesaid case their Lordships of the Dacca High Court discussed a large number of decisions resting on the question.

13. A similar view was also taken in the case of Islamic Republic of Pakistan Vs. Mohammad Saeed reported in 13 D.L R. (S.C) page 84. Hamoodur Rahman. J, as his Lordship was then, expressed his views in the following terms:-

"It is next urged that since no appeal has been preferred against the original order in the Writ petition itself the appellant should not be allowed to challenge or go behind that order in this appeal. We see no substance in this contention, for even in execution proceedings questions relating to the excitability of an order, of decree can be raised and it is open to the party against whom it is sought to be executed to show that it is null and void or had been made without jurisdiction or that it is incapable of execution."

14. In the instant case, the Government judgment-debtor produced no materials before the executing Court to hold that the decree in question was passed by a Court without jurisdiction or that the decree itself was null and void or that it was incapable of execution. The illegal or improper exercise of jurisdiction or illegality of the decision are no grounds for challenging the decree under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure. A similar view has also been taken in a recent decision in the case of Hajee Md. Ahsanullah Vs. Arafatunnessa Bibi being dead her heirs Ali Ahmad and others in 33 D.L.R. (A.D) 17. In the case it has been held that "where the decree presented for execution was made by a Court which apparently had no jurisdiction whether pecuniary or territorial or in respect of the judgment debtor's person to make the decree, the executing Court is entitled to refuse to execute it on the ground that it was made without jurisdiction. Within these narrow limits the executing Court is empowered to question validity of the decree."

<u>15. It may be said that a decree to be without jurisdiction must be of such a nature as to make it a void decree or a nullity, In the facts and circumstances of the instant case, we have not been presented with any material to hold that the decree was void or that it was a nullity. The total absence of jurisdiction of the Court which passed the decree has not been proved in the facts and circumstances of the case. Accordingly we hold that the decree was not without jurisdiction. The learned Subordinate Judge, as an executing Court, erred in law in going behind the decree. On a consideration of the aforesaid decisions we hold that the executing Court went wrong in not taking into consideration the proper scope of section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure as authorized in law and supported by a long chain of decisions. Therefore, the judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge are liable to be set aside.</u>

16. We have been taken through the objection petition filed by the Government under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In paragraph 4 of the objection petition it has been stated that Tk. 1,74,896/- have been paid for renovation and repair or the house in question. So the execution case cannot proceed for the entire decretal amount. The learned Subordinate Judge does not appear to have directed his consideration towards the aforesaid objection. We need not say anything as to the merits or otherwise of the said objection.

17. For the aforesaid reasons the judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge are set aside and Money Execution case No. 5 of 1979 is restored to file, Miscellaneous Case No. 121 of 1979 is remitted to the Executing Court for disposal according to law and on evidence as may be adduced by the parties.

18. In the result the appeal succeeds and is allowed without any order as to costs. Money Execution Case No. 5 of 1979 is restored to file and Miscellaneous Case No. 121 of 1979 arising out of the said Money Execution Case under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure do proceed according to law and in the light of the observations made above.

Send down the records expeditiously.

Abdul Matin Khan Chowdhury J.-I agree.

End.

full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal J: This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 13.2.85 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division, Dhaka in Civil Order No. 98 of 1985 summarily rejecting the appellant's application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and affirming the concurrent judgments and orders of the Courts below dismissing the appellants Miscellaneous Case No. 151 of 1981 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. Plaintiff-respondent Nos. 1-4 instituted Title Suit No. 589 of 1980 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for declaration of title to the suit land. The suit was decreed ex parte on 1.12.80 The defendant-appellants filed Miscellaneous Case No. 151 of 1981 on 5.8.81 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree on the averments, inter alia, that the decree was obtained behind the back of the appellants without service of any summons upon them. The appellants and the respondents were parties in another suit, namely, Title Suit No. 637 of 1976 of the 1st Court of Munsif, Dhaka. On 20.7.81 when the appellants had been in the said Court in connection with the hearing of the said suit, they came to learn about the ex parte disposal of Title Suit No. 589 of 1980. On search the appellants came to know definitely on 28.7.81 about the impugned decree.

3. The respondents contested the case by filing a written objection contending inter alia that the summons and notices of the suit were duly served upon the appellants. They were aware of the filing of the suit but they did not appear to contest the suit intentionally.

4. In support of their respective cases the appellants examined only one witness, appellant no. 3 Mohammad Hossain as PW 1. The respondents examined OPW No. 1, Nurul Islam, husband of respondent no 1 and OPW no. 2 Motalib Bhuiyan, the process-server who served the summons in the suit.

5. The learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka by his judgment and order dated 27.7.83 dismissed the miscellaneous case on the finding that the appellants having failed to prove sufficiently their date of knowledge on 20.7.81 the miscellaneous case was barred by limitation. Further, the process server OPW No. 2 has proved the service returns Exts. A and A1 showing service of summons upon the appellants on 2.7.80. He has also proved Exts. A to A5 showing service of show cause and notices of ad interim injunction.

6. The miscellaneous case was thus dismissed.

7. On appeal the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka by his judgment and order dated 31.12.84 and on revision a Division Bench of the High Court Division, Dhaka by judgment and order dated 13.2.85 affirmed the findings and decision of the learned Subordinate Judge.

8. Before filing the present Title Suit No. 589 of 1980 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka the respondents instituted Title Suit No. 637 of 1976 in the First Court of Munsif, Dhaka for permanent injunction against the appellants in respect of the self-same suit land. The earlier suit was pending between the parties when the ex parte decree was passed in the later suit. In Title Suit No. 637 of 1976 the respondents prayer for temporary injunction was refused on contest up to the High Court Division. Leave was granted in this appeal to consider as to whether the subsequent suit was surreptitiously filed by the same plaintiff-respondents against the same defendant-appellants seeking declaration of title in the same suit land and whether in view of the pendency of the earlier suit between the parties the allegation of fraudulent suppression of summons adds a new dimension to the case. Leave was also granted to consider whether the Courts below and the High Court Division applied their judicial mind particularly in respect of the fact that the process-server OPW No. 2 did not give the address of the mokabila witnesses in the service return and whether the Court below ought to have relied upon the evidence of the process-server without examining the mokabila witnesses.

9. Mr. Rafique-ul Huq, learned Counsel for the defendant-appellants, has taken us through the plaints of the earlier suit, namely, Title Suit No. 637 of 1976 and the present Title Suit No. 589 of 1980. It is clear that the earlier suit was for a decree of permanent injunction and the present suit is for declaration of title in respect of the same land. The averments in the two plaints are almost interchangeable. It is also clear that in the present suit there is a complete suppression of the fact that the respondents filed an earlier suit in respect of the same suit land against the same defendants. Mr. Rafique-ul Huq has further shown that in the earlier suit the temporary injunction matter was contested upto the High Court Division and the parties were directed to maintain status quo. Mr. Rafique-ul Huq submits that there was no earthly reason for the appellants not to contest Title Suit No. 589 of 1980 if they had received the summons of the suit, particularly in view of the fact that they had been contesting diligently the temporary injunction matter arising out of the suit for permanent injunction in respect of the same suit land. He submits that it is against human nature to stand by when an adversary was aiming at inflicting a bigger harm when the attempted smaller harm was diligently faced and contested. Mr. Rafique-ul Huq submits that suppression of the fact that a suit was pending between the parties over the self-same suit land is indicative of fraud on the part of the respondents and both the Courts below and the High Court Division failed to consider that the miscellaneous case was liable to be allowed on the ground of fraud alone.

10. Mr. M Nurullah, learned Counsel for the plaintiff-respondents, submits, on the other hand, that the cause of action and the reliefs prayed for in the two suits are vastly dissimilar, suit land being the same. The respondents every right under the law to file any number of suits over the same cause of action. The only limitation is that the last suit will be stayed under section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The respondents did not think it necessary to state that an earlier suit was pending between the parties, as the present suit sought a different relief and arose out of a separate cause of action. No fraud can be deduced therefrom, he submits.

11. The appellants clearly stated in their application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure about the pendency of the earlier suit between the parties. The fact that they were diligently pursuing the temporary injunction matter arising out of the earlier suit for permanent injunction is also a matter of record. It should have struck the Courts below that litigants who were contesting without laches a suit for permanent injunction in respect of the suit land would not ordinarily become disinterested to contest a subsequent suit for declaration of title in respect of the same suit land, if they have received the summons of the suit. In the temporary injunction matter arising out of the title suit for permanent injunction a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division passed the last order on 24.1.79 in Civil Revision No. 47 with Civil Revision No. 890(R) of 1978, directing the parties to maintain status quo till the disposal of the earlier suit and directing the learned Munsif to dispose of the suit within 30th June, 1980 positively.

12. The respondents filed Title Suit No. 589 of 1980 on the 13th June, 1980. We are informed that the earlier suit namely, Title Suit No. 637 of 1976 is still pending. The filing of the second suit 2-1/2 weeks before the expiry of the deadline set by the High Court Division tantamounts to opening of a second front from behind while the first front was still active. The respondents did not at all disclose in the plaint of the last suit as to the existence of a suit between the parties over the same suit land. The reliefs prayed for in the two suits may be different but the suppression of this information cannot but throw a cloud over the intention of the respondents.

13. This background has to be kept in mind while considering the question of service of summons in the second suit. The two Courts below and the High Court Division were oblivious of it.

14. Mr. Rafique-ul Huq has drawn our attention to the order sheet of the learned Subordinate Judge after registering Title Suit No. 589 of 1980.

Order nos. 4-7 read as follows:

"4. 12.7.80. Summons served. Plaintiff files hazira. Service report appears to be not satisfactory. Issue summons upon the defendants through regd post. To 24.7.80 for requisites.

Sd /- ZH Md Daud

5. 14.7.80 Plaintiff files a petition praying for making the order of ad-interim injunction absolute and grant temporary injunction on the ground stated therein. Service of notice appears to be not satisfactory. Plaintiff to take step for the same by regd. post by the date fixed.

Sd/-ZH Md. Daud.

6. 24.7.80. Requisites put in. Issue the same fixing 10.9.80 for A/D. Plaintiff to put in receipt by the date fixed.

Sd/-ZH Md. Daud. 7. 10.9.80. Plaintiff files hazira. Registered summons served. None appeared on behalf of the defdts. To 29.9.80 for ex parte hearing.

Sd/-ZH Md. Daud.

15. It is very clear that on 12.7.80 the learned Subordinate Judge found that the report of service of summons of the suit was not satisfactory. On 14.7.80 the learned Subordinate Judge found service of notice of ad-interim injunction to be not satisfactory. He passed orders for issuance of summons upon the appellants through registered post. It is not clear why the learned Subordinate Judge did not pass orders for fresh service of summons through Court.

<u>16. At the hearing of the miscellaneous case OPW 2, the process-server deposed and proved Ext. A series. It was a case of service by hanging as the appellants allegedly refused to receive the notices. These Ext. A series were found to be not satisfactory on a bare perusal by the learned Subordinate Judge himself. Rule 69 of the Civil Rules and Orders provides that "service should always be personal wherever practicable (Ord. V r. 12) and the Courts ought not in ex parte cases to act upon anything short of personal service until they are satisfied that personal service could not reasonably be effected". It is not understood how on appearance of the process server as a witness the same reports, Ext. A series, gained acceptance by the same Court OPW 2 did not improve upon his earlier reports by personal appearance in the Court. He did not throw any further light upon Ext. A series. The reports remained as they were. In particular, the names and addresses of mokabila witnesses were not noted in the service reports. The reports were found to be unsatisfactory by the learned Subordinate Judge earlier clearly because these were one-man show by the process-server himself, unsupported and uncorroborated by any mokabila witness. The same malady persisted. when the process-server was examined in Court. Surely the same unacceptable reports could not gain acceptance by mere personal appearance of the process-server.</u>

17. Since this is allegedly a case of refusal to accept service, the following provisions of Order 5 rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure arc to be kept in view:

"17. Where the defendant or his agent or such other person as aforesaid refuses to sign the acknowledgement, or where the serving officer, after using all due and reasonable diligence, cannot find the defendant, and there is no agent empowered to accept service of the summons on his behalf, nor any other person on whom service can be made, the serving officer shall affix a copy of the summons on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain, and shall then return the original to the Court from which it was issued, with a report endorsed thereon or annexed thereto stating that he has so affixed the copy, the circumstances under which he did so, and the name and address of the person (if any) by whom the house was identified and in whose presence the copy was affixed".

18. It is, therefore, obligatory upon the process-server to mention in his report the name and address of the person, if any, by whom the house was identified and in whose presence the copy was affixed.

19. Also relevant is rule 84 (e) of the Civil Rules and Orders which provides as follows:

"(e) Where a person refuses to accept the process the grounds thereof, if any, and the names of the persons witnessing the refusal should be given."

20. The service reports, Ext. A series, are devoid of these essential information. The Courts below and the High Court Division have failed to consider the Order Sheet and the relevant provisions of law.

<u>21. Although the service of summons of the suit was sought to be effected by registered post with acknowledgement due and although by Order No. 7 dated 10.9.80 the learned Subordinate Judge noted that registered summons were served, it is clear from the cross examination of OPW 1 Nurul Islam that the postal notices and acknowledgement dues were not in the records. In any case it is not the finding of the Courts below that the summons of the suit was served by registered notices. The two Courts below have found the summons to be served by the process-server. In the face of the contrary postures of the trial Court lingering doubts remain as to whether the process-server had at all effected any service when his uncorroborated reports were not relied upon earlier by the trial Court itself and when in the Court he presented himself alone without corroboration.</u>

22. The trial Court has held that the appellants could not prove satisfactorily that they came to know of the impugned decree for the first time on 20.7.81 during the hearing of the earlier suit in the 1st Court of Munsif, Dhaka, because they did not examine any other witness to corroborate the said story.

23. The Courts below have simply overlooked that the appellants and the respondents were contesting two suits at the same time over the same suit land. There has been a total non-application of mind insofar as this aspect of the appellants case is concerned. The appellants are on record to have prosecuted the earlier suit diligently and there can be no earthly reason for them not to be present in Court on 20.7.81 for hearing of the earlier suit. It is also natural for the respondents to express themselves joyously over the fate of the subsequent suit, implying that they had no stake in the earlier suit any more. OPW 1 Nurul Islam admitted that he was present in the 1st Court of Munsif on 20.7.81, which shows that the appellants statement regarding the date of hearing of the earlier suit was correct. OPW 1 of course stated that on that date appellant no. 2 Priya Dasi was present, but appellant no. 3 Md. Hossain was not present. Appellant no. 2 in both the earlier suit and the present suit is Priya Dasi, wife of appellant no. 1 Upendra Chandra Rishi. She is the only lady in both the suits. All other defendants in the two suits are men. Appellant no. 3 was added as a party to the earlier suit on an application under Order 1 rule 10 CPC. It is inconceivable that only a lady was present on 20. 7.81 during the hearing of the earlier suit, but the appellant no. 3, a person who on his own added himself as a party defendant in the earlier suit, was not present. These aspects were totally left out of consideration by the trial Court and the Court of appeal below. The appellants have convincingly proved that they came to know of the ex parte decree for the first time on 20.7.81. The miscellaneous case having been filed on 5.8.81, the same was not barred by limitation.

Hence the appeal is allowed with costs. The ex parte decree dated 1.12.80 passed in Title Suit No. 789 of 1980 is set aside and the said suit is restored to its file and number.

End.

full_judgment:
Facts leading to the Rule are the following:

Plaintiff petitioner filed Title suit No. 204 of 1970 for declaration of title in the suit land against opposite party principal-defendants Nos. 1-9. In the suit, opposite party Nos. 10-17 were made proforma defendants. Defendants Nos. 1-9 entered appearance but later on compromised the suit with the plaintiff. The suit was decreed on compromise against the defendants 1-9 and ex-parte against defendants 10-17 by order dated 5.7.71. Thereafter, defendants Nos. 1 to 3 filed an application before the learned Munsif on 3.10.72 for setting aside the decree and for restoration of the suit under P.O. 12 of 1972.

2. The learned Munsif by order No. 18 dated 17.3.73 set aside the ex-parte order dated 5.7.71 and restored the original suit. An application filed by the plaintiff under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 18.6.73 was also rejected on 20.7 73 by order No. 24 dated 20.7.73.

Being aggrieved the plaintiff moved this court in its revisional jurisdiction and obtained this Rule.

Mr. Md. Ayub, learned Advocate, has appeared for the petitioners who are the heirs of the original petitioner who died during the pendency of this Rule and was substituted by his heirs. None has appeared for the opposite party defendants.

3. The learned Advocate for the petitioners contends that under P.O. 12/72 relied upon by the learned Munsif all judgments, decrees and orders passed ex-parte by any court after 1st day of March, 1971 and before the commencement of the order which is 7.2.72 were declared null and void. But in this case the decree passed against defendants 1-9 was decreed on compromise. No doubt the decree is so far as it related to defendants 10-17 was exparte but defendants 10-17 was merely proforma defendants and against them no relief was claimed. In the circumstances of the case the decree is so far as it related to defendant 1-9 did not come within the mischief of P.0 12 of 1972.

I see substance in the contention of the learned Advocate. Article 3, which is relevant, of P0 12/72 is quoted below:-

"3. Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, all judgments, decrees of order passed ex-parte by any court or tribunal or orders disposing of matter due to default in compliance with any direction of any court or tribunal in any legal proceedings at any time after the 1st day of March, 1971, and before the commencement of this Order are hereby declared null and void and the proceedings shall, on the commencement of this Order, continue in accordance with the law.

<u>4. It is patent that only ex-parte judgments, decrees or orders passed during the period mentioned in article 3, of P.O. 12 of 1972 came under the mischief of the section. Compromise decrees did not come within the mischief of the section. There is no doubt that the decrees against defendants 10- 17 came under the mischief of section 3 of P.O No.121 72 but this by itself could not justify the setting aside of the decree as a whole and restoration of the suit without a finding that if ex-parte decree against defendants 10-17 was null and void, the compromise decree against defendants 1-9 could not be maintained. The learned Munsif in his order dated 17.3.73 has not made any such finding. Defendants 10-17 were made merely proforma-defendants and no relief was claimed against them. The learned Munsif ought to have maintained the compromise decree passed against defendants 1-9 and set aside the ex-parte decree passed against defendants 10-7 There was no reason for him to restore the suit which in effect has resulted in a setting aside of the decree in its entirety. I am of the opinion that the learned Munsif has acted illegally and with material irregularity in the exercise of his jurisdiction in setting aside the decree in effect in the entirety applying the provision of P.O. 12/72 and restoring the suit. The order dated 17.3.73 made by the learned Munsif cannot therefore be sustained. The compromise decree passed against defendants 1-9 did not come within the mischief of P.O.12/72 and could not be disturbed.</u>

5. The Rule is therefore made absolute. The compromise decree passed against defendants 1-9 on 5.7.71 is maintained. The ex-parte decree passed against defendants 10-17 by the same order will however, stand set aside being null and void and the name of the defendants10-17 will be struck of the decree

The order of the learned Munsif for restoration of the said order is set aside.

End.

full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J.: This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1067 of 1981.

<u>2. Leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division was correct in taking the view that the suit filed by the plaintiff was hit by res judicata.</u>

3. Plaintiffs are the appellants. They filed the suit being O.C. Suit No. 136/1965/13/1966 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Mymensingh for declaration of title to the suit land. Their case in short was that they took lease of the suit land from the Jamindar and relied on pattannama exhibit 1, Amin's report exhibit 2, Dakhila Exhibit 3 series, Kabuliyats Ext. 4 and 5 in support of their case. Government contested the suit and filed written statement stating that the suit land is 'beel' which is not retainable under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the rent receiving interest of this landlord namely, Bhabanipur Estate was acquired. Respondent Nos. 2-12 contested the suit by filing written statement. Their case was that they took lease from the Government and the Government collected the price of borga crops of the suit land ever since they were inducted into possession of the suit land. The trial Court considered the evidence and noted the admission of the plaintiffs that the defendants were in possession of the suit land before filing of the suit. The trial Court disbelieved the evidence produced by the plaintiffs and no reliance was placed on the kabuliyat and the pattannama. Dakhilas were is believed so also the Amin's report exhibit 2. In this view of the matter the suit was dismissed.

4. The plaintiffs then filed appeal being O.C. Appeal No. 28 of 1969. The learned Additional District Judge, Mymensingh concurred the decision of the trial court and accordingly dismissed the appeal.

5. Now the second round. The plaintiffs filed present suit being Title Suit No. 30 of 1972 which was re-numbered as 31 of 1977 in the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Additional Court, Mymensingh against the same set of defendants for declaration of title in respect of the self-same suit land. The trial Court decreed the suit and noticed that since the earlier suit was dismissed on the ground that the plaintiff was out of possession and a suit for declaration simpliciter is not maintainable, the findings of the said suit are not res judicata in the present suit. Reliance was placed on the case of K.B. Kishore Acharayya Chowdhury and others Vs. Province of East Bengal, 6 DLR page 1. The Appellate Court affirmed this view and decreed the suit. It was in the High Court Division that the question of res judicata was considered fully and the learned Single Judge (Mustafa Kamal, J:) exhaustively considered the pleadings of both the suits and perused the previous judgment and observed-

"In the present case the earlier suit filed by the plaintiff was apparently not dismissed on a preliminary point. Both the trial Court and the appellate Court had gone into details with regard to the title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. After exhaustively discussing the same the courts below found that the plaintiff himself admitted in his evidence that the defendants 2-12 were in possession of the suit land."

<u>6. The learned Judge concluded that the plaintiffs' earlier suit failed not primarily because it was not by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act but because he failed to prove the totality of his case, including his title. In this view of the matter, the High Court Division took the view that the suit is barred by principles of res judicata.</u>

<u>7. Mr. M.H. Khandker, the learned counsel appearing for the plaintiffs-appellants, canvassed that the earlier suit was for mere declaration of title whereas the instant suit is for declaration of title and recovery of possession and further the earlier suit was dismissed in the absence of any prayer for recovery of possession and as such the decree in that suit does not operate as res judicata in the present suit. This point has no substance. Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure clearly comes into play and Explanation IV is to the following terms:-</u>

<u>"Any matter which might and ought to have been made ground of defence or attack in such former suit shall be deemed to have been a matter directly and substantially in issue in such suit."</u>

<u>8. In view of section 11 C.P.C. there is no hesitation in saying that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division was correct in taking the view.</u>

This appeal is, therefore, dismissed without any order as to cost.

End.
